I

RUSSELL E. CHARVONIA
Grand Master – 2014-2015

Russ Charvonia was raised in Phoenix Arizona, and moved to California
in 1987. He was raised a Master Mason in 1992 in San Buenaventura Lodge
No. 214 (now Channel Islands Lodge No. 214) in Ventura and served as Master
in 1996. He served his lodge as Treasurer for eight years and in 2002 he was
presented with the Hiram Award.
His service to California Freemasonry began in 1995 with his
appointment to the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance, during which he served
seven terms, including two as chairman. He served 13 terms on the Committee on
Investments, including seven as chairman. He also served on the Audit Committee
and the special Committee of Twenty. In 2006 he was appointed director of the
Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and served as president of that board. He was also
a member of the boards of the California Masonic Foundation, Masonic Homes
of California and Acacia Creek.
Russ served as Grand Orator in 2009 under Most Worshipful Larry
Adamson and served two terms as Inspector-at-Large for Division V.
He is a 33° Inspector General Honorary of the Valley of Ventura Scottish
Rite Bodies. He is a member of the Ventura Chapter No. 50 Royal Arch Masons
and Ventura Council No. 15 Cryptic Masons and the Al Malaikah Shriners in Los
Angeles. He is also a member of the Lodge of the Holy Land, No. 50 in Israel,
Kona Lodge in Hawaii, Tanana Lodge No. 3 in Fairbanks, Alaska and Internet
Lodge No. 9659. He received the DeMolay Honorary Legion of Honor in August
2012 and is a Certified Adult Volunteer for all three Masonic Youth Orders,
DeMolay, Job’s Daughters and Rainbow for Girls.

RUSSELL E. CHARVONIA

Grand Master
October 12, 2014 – October 10, 2015

II

Russ has been in the financial services industry since 1980. He is
a founding partner and owner of Channel Islands Financial Group in Ventura,
providing financial planning and investment services. He earned his Juris Doctor
degree from Ventura College of Law in 2003 and was admitted to the California
Bar in 2004. He is a founding partner of Channel Islands Law Group, specializing
in estate planning, including the drafting of wills and trusts along with charitable
and wealth planning.
Russ is active in his community, and has spent many years volunteering
his professional services with non-profit organizations, particularly those focused
on protecting senior citizens from financial abuse. Russ is a member of Temple
Beth Torah in Ventura where he served a two-year term as president of the Board
of Directors. He serves as advisory board member for the Rubicon Theatre and
III

2014-2015 Grand Lodge Officers

Russ lives in Ventura with his wife of 22 years, Linda, who is a Past
Honored Queen and recipient of the Degree of Royal Purple in Bethel 89,
Ventura. He has a daughter, Alissa; son and daughter-in-law, Keith and Kendall;
and grandsons, Tanner and Hudson. His father-in-law, Most Worshipful Harry L.
Maynard, served as the 117th Grand Master of Masons of California and Hawaii
in 1982-83.

3

One Hundred Sixty-Sixth
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 9, 2015
The 166th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
Russell E. Charvonia on Friday, October 9, 2015 at 1:00 p.m.
Worshipful Brother Emanuel A. Rose, Master of Humboldt Lodge
No. 79, raised the opening session of Grand Lodge. The gavel used to raise Grand
Lodge was presented to the Grand Master when he was installed as Grand Master
on October 12, 2014 by Worshipful Brother Larry Cook, Past Master of Santa
Barbara Lodge No. 192.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at
the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following
which the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our
Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters
were then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master
then directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the
usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Saturday Morning, October 10, 2015

After delivering the Decision and Recommendations, the Grand
Master resumed his station and directed attention to the screen for a
video presentation.
Video Presentation
The Grand Lodge of California premiered a new video entitled “Diverse,
Yet United: California’s Masonic Mosaic.” This video explores the many aspects
of California Masonry’s rich cultural influences – from those of the state’s original
settlers to new immigrants who have made California their home today. It shares
how our fraternity has been shaped by members’ diverse heritages, and how these
varied global influences continue to inspire California Masonry today.
At 5:17 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 10.

11

The Grand Lodge convened at 8:32 a.m., and after prayer by the Grand
Chaplain, the Grand Master noted that Grand Lodge was raised by Worshipful
Brother John L. McGoldrick, Past Master of Fallbrook No. 317.
Brother John L. McGoldrick raised Grand Lodge using a gavel that was presented
to the Grand Master by Brother Robert N. Jordan of Fallbrook No. 317 on the
occasion of our dedicating a flagpole at the Fallbrook Masonic Cemetery last
month.

15

The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Gary C. Silverman,
Grand Chaplain, to present the following service of remembrance for our departed
brethren. The Grand Chaplain gave the following remarks.
To take pause for the purpose of remembering brothers, who, have been
called from labor to reside in the Celestial Lodge above since our last gathering
is a solemnity of respect delayed too long. For these two Grand Lodge brothers
have entered that house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, and now use
their trowels to inspire and influence our unfinished work in the quarries of life.
For many of us, their memories and deeds are shining examples of our
gentle Craft’s impact, and their influences are reflected in our hearts and minds as
we go about our daily lives. For nobody gets through life without losing someone
they love, someone they need, or something that they thought was meant to
be. But it is these losses that make us stronger and eventually move us toward
future opportunities.
As a poignant a reminder of those who have gone on ahead, let us, in
honor of their memory, vow right today to turn to our friends, family, and brethren
whom we respect, cherish, and love, before they are taken from our midst, and
express our appreciation for having them in our lives. Since the grains of sand in
each of our hourglasses is unknown, the opportunity to appreciate and honor them
now is a blessing not to be squandered.
Creator of light and life, guardian of the Eternal Flame, in your loving
care are our brothers and loved ones for whom you have opened your heart.
Reward them with eternal glory, happiness, and peace. In the ancient words of
the sages Zichrona Livracha, ‘May their memory be for a blessing...’ AMEN “So
Mote it be.”
Very Worshipful Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer, delivered a eulogy for
the late Past Grand Lecturer Joseph Hammond.

Eulogy
Joseph Hammond

422nd Masonic District Officers Association, Past President of the 427th Masonic
District Officers Association, and Associate Bethel Guardian for Bethel No. 134
in Corcoran.

Very Worshipful Joe Hammond Jr, the 37th custodian of our ritual and
the 13th elected Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of California, son of Joseph
and Grace Hammond, was born on November 13, 1929, in Corcoran California,
and called from labor to refreshment in that Celestial Lodge above on February
17, 2015, at the age of 85 years, 3 months, and 2 days.
“Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy resting place! Bright and
glorious be thy rising from it!
It is only fitting that Very Worshipful Joe’s eulogy begin with this phrase
from our funeral ritual. You see, among Joe’s many accomplishments as Grand
Lecturer was the requirement that all Funeral Masters be certified to ensure the
last tribute of affection to our departed Brethren was delivered appropriately
before the public.
Joe graduated from Corcoran High School in 1947, married the love
of his life, Ida Lee Johnson, in 1949 and together raised their sons Scott and
Steve (both Senior DeMolays) and daughter Debra (a Past Honored Queen of
the International Order of Job’s Daughters) in Corcoran. Joe graduated from the
College of the Sequoias and in 1953 followed in his father’s footsteps when he
became the owner and President of Hammond’s Home Furnishings, Inc. until his
retirement in 1997.
Public service was a huge part of Joe’s life and he was an active member
of the First United Methodist Church in Corcoran. The boards that Joe served on
and chaired over his lifetime are really too numerous to read here today, but to
name a few, he was a Past President of the County Appliance Dealers Association;
Director of the Corcoran Chamber of Commerce; Commissioner (and 2 years as
Vice President) of the Corcoran City Planning Commission; Member of the Crown
Development Corporation; Member of the Kings County Economic Development
Commission; Member of the Executive Committee for the Kaweah and Tule Dam
Expansion projects; Member of the Kings County Board of Equalization; Member
of the High Speed Rail Corridor Study Group; and Director of the San Joaquin
Valley United Air Pollution District.
Joe was elected and served as Kings County District 2 Supervisor for 16
years and served since 2001 as a trustee of the Kings County Board of Education.
In 2013 and 2014, Joe served as president of the Board of Education. Joe was a
tireless worker who was very generous with his time.
Joe was a member of the Tulare Chapter Order of DeMolay. He petitioned
for the degrees of Masonry on April 4, 1961 and raised to the Sublime Degree of
Master Mason in Corcoran Lodge No. 490 (now Olive Branch No. 269) on June 1,
1961, where he served as Master in 1967. He served as Past Vice President of the

Between 1967 and 1969, Joe was a speaker for the Grand Lodge Public
Schools Committee.
Joe was a firm believer in and supporter of our Masonic youth orders,
and in 1968 was appointed to the Grand Lodge Youth Orders Committee where
he served for six years. In 1969, he was appointed Inspector where he served for
eight years before being promoted to Assistant Grand Lecturer in 1976. He served
for five years before being elected Grand Lecturer in 1981.
In 1971 Joe joined the Fresno Valley Scottish Rite and in 1979 he was
decorated with the rank of 32º Knight Commander of the Court of Honor. In 1984
he received the DeMolay Legion of Honor. He was a Noble in the Tehran Shrine
in Fresno and a member of the Royal Order of Scotland.
In Joe’s reports to the Grand Lodge, he noted that when he was appointed
Grand Lecturer there were 188,535 Masons; today are only 54,541 Masons, a
drop of some 134,000 Masons. During Joe’s tenure as Grand Lecturer he provided
both ritual and administrative guidance to the members of the Ritual Committee.
Joe was a great ritualist who taught our ritual with a soft but determined voice.
He never failed to acknowledge the successful work of others while providing
welcomed encouragement to those who needed to improve. In 1985, Joe retired
as Grand Lecturer.
Near the end of Joe’s tenure as Grand Lecturer, he had heart surgery after
which he began a stringent exercise regimen where for over 28 years, without
fail, he walked along Whitley Avenue near his home. Those who live in Corcoran
remember seeing Joe every morning wearing his 1974 Corcoran Boosters
windbreaker with pride.
Each day his walks took him by the Kings County Fire Department in
Corcoran where he always stopped by to pay his respects to the firefighters and
join them in morning coffee and discussions about community improvement.
The Fire Department became Joe’s personal coffee shop. Joe was so
welcomed at the Fire Department that the Fire Chief provided him with the
station’s access code so, if they were not present, he could enter, prepare the coffee
and await their later arrival. Every member of the Fire Department treasured their
daily visits with our Brother Joe.
Joe was an inspiration to all who knew him, both in his public and
Masonic lives. He led others with a gentle hand, taught others by setting the
example, and was truthful to all. We will forever remember Joe for his energetic
and heartfelt pursuit of programs to educate and inform Masons about our ritual
and its rich history.

18

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

His legacy will live on in the lives of his brethren, family, and community
who were cheered and inspired by his dedication, wisdom, and company.
In closing I think it is only fitting that, just as we began this eulogy with a
reference to the ritual, so we should also conclude it with another reference to our
ritual when I say, “how important it is that we should endeavor to imitate” Very
Worshipful Joe, “in his truly exalted and exemplary character, in his unfeigned
piety to God, and in his inflexible fidelity to his trust;” thus proving that he is, after
all, “an example, my Brethren, worthy of all imitation.’
Very Worshipful Joe, today we surround your memory with the ritual
you so lovingly adored and protected. Just as you always remembered to say
“Thank you” to others for their service we now say, “Thank you,” to you for your
service to our Craft until such time as we meet again “in realms beyond the skies.
Until then, dear brother, until then, farewell.”

JOSEPH HAMMOND
Past Grand Lecturer
November 13, 1929 - February 17, 2015

Most Worshipful Frank Loui, Past Grand Master, delivered a eulogy for
the late Past Grand Lecturer Ulysses G. Patropulos.

Eulogy
ULYSSES G. PATROPULOS
Ulysses George Patropulos was born on May 1, 1917 in San
Francisco, California.
Ulysses was known as a fighter. He showed bravery at a very young age.
When he was 13 years old, a robber desperate for money entered his family’s
residence and attacked his mother with a knife. Little Ulysses heard the noise,
rushed into the room, seized a bottle and flung it into the face of the holdup man,
knocking him to the floor and detained him by sitting on him until the police
arrived. He helped his father in the grocery store as a young boy and eventually
took over the business until his retirement in 1969.
Ulysses was raised a Master Mason in King Solomon Lodge No. 260 on
May 20, 1940, which later became Pacific-Starr King Lodge No. 136. He served
as Master in 1946 and began his career as a ritualist and teacher. He was the
Officers’ coach for ten years after his term as Master. Ulysses became District
Inspector in 1957. In 1966, he was appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer and served
for 20 years. He was elected Grand Lecturer in 1986 and served until 2001.

ULYSSES G. PATROPULOS
Past Grand Lecturer
May 1, 1917 - May 17, 2015

Very Worshipful Ulysses was a member of the York Rite, Shrine and
Scottish Rite. In Scottish Rite, he received his 32º on December 12, 1947 and
was coroneted a 33º Inspectors General Honorary on November 25, 1989. Most
recently he served as the Assistant to the Personal Representative and Almoner
of the San Francisco Valley Scottish Rite. When I came to the Scottish Rite as
General Secretary in 2007, I asked Very Worshipful Ulysses to come to the office
on a regular basis and be an ambassador for the Valley. He did that for 7 years with
distinction. He became my “Girl Friday” and never let the phone ring more than
once before answering.
Very Worshipful laid down his working tools on May 17, 2015, just three
days short of his actual 75th Masonic Anniversary. It was my pleasure, privilege
and honor to present his Diamond Anniversary pin and certificate. They were
presented on his 98th birthday. His certificate still hangs on our office wall at the
San Francisco Scottish Rite office.
To those of us who came up the line during his time as Assistant Grand
Lecturer and Grand Lecturer, we know of his dedication to the Craft and his
willingness to reach out and give friendly advice. He had many stories to share

22

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

and his memory was sharp as ever. He had a great sense of humor. We will always
remember his schools of instruction in the second section of the third degree
wearing his white socks and different color baseball caps.

Saturday Afternoon, October 11, 2014

Ulysses was predeceased by wife Belle and son Chris who was also a
Master Mason. He is survived by daughter Georgette Kritikopoulos, son-in-law,
George, and daughter-in-law, Mavra.
He will be sadly missed by all. Until we meet again – farewell,
my brother.

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award

Presentation of the Civility Medals

The Grand Master was pleased to present an award in memory of our late
Brother Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576 for 17
yeas as secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer, and chaplain. He exemplified
Masonic relief and brotherly love. He reached out to members and widows on
a weekly basis, assisted with numerous applications to MOS and the Masonic
Homes, frequently called Masonic Assistance to check the status of his member’s
applications, and helped expedite the paperwork process.
The Grand Master went on to explain that the Joe Jackson Lodge
Outreach Award is given to a lodge that has demonstrated excellence in outreach
to their members and widows. The Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award was
presented to Reading Lodge No. 254 in Redding for their extraordinary outreach
efforts this year.
Grand Master Charvonia spoke about the outreach program and all of the
programs of the Masonic Homes.
Those present enjoyed a presentation by Mr. Laffit Pincay, III, a talented
horseracing analyst.

JACOB F. GALBA-BRIGHT

Africa. Brother Jacob Galba-Bright has been an active Mason for 49 years. He is

Lodge No. 804 in Moreno Valley, where he serves as youth order ambassador.
Brother Galba-Bright has long served Masonry and our youth orders,

advisory council chairman, and membership director for the chapter and league.
In recognition of his outstanding leadership and support, Brother Galba-Bright
was honored as the 2011 Southern California Jurisdiction advisor of the year, and

Today, in addition to his role as assistant executive officer of Southern

Brother Galba-Bright makes an effort to help DeMolay members in
every chapter that he visits, and has shown true dedication by attending almost
all activities throughout Southern California and beyond. Brother Galba-Bright is
positively a perfect role model of what all advisors strive to achieve – dedication
and putting our youth first.

Brother Killmer has devoted his career to service as well. He is a

community, giving back through service and volunteering. He engenders a positive
impression of DeMolay and Masonry as value-centered, vibrant organizations.
Brother Killmer is a perfect of example of what a Master Mason
should be, and he is very worthy of emulation by our youth. His devotion to
service and Masonic values will continue to inspire the next generation of our
fraternal leaders.

Grand Master’s Message
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State
of California:
Past Grand Masters, Past Grand Officers, Grand Officers, Worshipful
Masters, my brethren all.
Welcome to the 166th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
California, here in the City and County of San Francisco.
Among the duties of the Grand Master under §404.130 of our Masonic
Code is that he present, at each Annual Communication, a written message
setting forth:
All of his official acts during the year;
The general condition of Masonry within this Jurisdiction; and
 ecommending such legislation as he deems necessary or expedient for
R
the welfare of the Craft.
It is now my pleasant duty to comply with this requirement.
While I will cover some of the official acts of the past year in this address,
the detail of all of such acts will be presented in the written proceedings of this
Annual Communication. My single Decision and several Recommendations will
be presented separately when we consider the legislation later in this session.
As far as the state of our Craft, I am able to stand before you this
afternoon, my brethren, and proclaim that Masonry in general is more relevant to
society today than it has been in recent memory; and perhaps ever.
And I am also pleased to inform you that California Masonry today is a
strong and vital influence on individuals and society. Young men are knocking at
our doors, seeking the light from our gentle Craft that they are not finding elsewhere
in their lives. Our brethren, their families and our Masonic youth are looking ways
to grow and better themselves, as well as to improve their communities.
I don’t believe the interest in our Masonic ideals is by happenstance,
or simply a result of the regular ebb and flow of the tide. The world about us
is growing increasingly treacherous and uncivil. Whether it is our presidential
candidates slinging personal barbs at one another, ISIS brutally slaughtering

44

45

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

innocent people and destroying sacred antiquities, or high school football players
intentionally plowing into an official during play at the direction of their coach,
we witness revolting acts of incivility on a daily basis.

The second objective we have asked the leaders of our lodges to address
is to see that every brother feels rewarded for being a part of our cherished Craft.
When we can contribute to the greater good, we experience personal growth
and reward.

Yet Freemasonry continues to endure and to provide a needed refuge
from such profanity. Why? In short, the practice of the art of Freemasonry allows
us to build a temple of humanity within ourselves. As we work to improve
ourselves, we are able to go about repairing the world about us.
We are wrapping up our current five-year strategic plan, and are
developing our next 2020 Vision Plan. I am proud to report that we have been
very successful in implementing the strategies identified in our current plan.
As part of the development of our new plan, we have received input
from thousands of you. When we do such strategic planning, it is important that
we attempt to anticipate the needs of the next generation of Masons, while we
simultaneously focus on intermediate term implementation.
This year, we have asked our lodges to focus on three objectives; for by
doing so, I believe that many of the challenges our Fraternity faces today will be
resolved in due time as our lodges address and master these goals.
The first objective is to continue to elevate our ritual, to the point that
every degree we confer makes a deep and lasting impression upon our new
brother’s mind. Can you just imagine how dedicated to our lodges and the purposes
of Masonry our new brethren will be if each is deeply moved and transformed by
the experience?
Very Worshipful Jack Rose, as chair of our Ritual Committee, and our
ten Assistant Grand Lecturers have done a great job of helping to bring this closer
to reality, and they are always looking for creative ways to enhance the candidate
experience. I have also witnessed a renewed focus in our lodges on conferring
quality, meaningful degrees.
It is important that we honor and elevate the esteem of our candidates’
and officers’ coaches; for these men are the direct linkages to bringing our ritual
to life. We have implemented several ideas to achieve this.
We will soon consider legislation aimed at enhancing our ritual
experience for the candidate, officer and the sideliner.
One thing that each Lodge can immediately implement is to offer
the online Candidate Learning Center to its candidates. The feedback we are
receiving from candidates, their coaches and lodge masters is that this tool is a
tremendous asset in helping to solidify the Masonic teachings in the minds of our
newly obligated brethren.

Among the ways we have helped to provide a rewarding membership
experience is by enhancing our community outreach opportunities. Many of our
lodges are distributing the In Case of Emergency “ICE” Packs when they are at
community events, served others at Make a Difference Days, and found numerous
other ways to improve the lives of others.
Throughout this year, your Grand Lodge officers and families have
worked closely with the local lodge brethren, youth orders and their families
to repair the world by performing various types of community service projects.
We packed books for underprivileged kids, served food in VA hospitals, provide
face lifts to lodges and schools, cleaned up cemeteries and tended to gardens.
In addition to feeling we have done a small part to improve our communities,
I believe our activities have inspired many lodges, Job’s Daughters bethels,
Rainbow assemblies and DeMolay chapters to regularly schedule service projects,
creating an additional bond among the brethren and their local community.
I have also seen our lodges increasingly reaching out to the brethren and
widows whom they don’t see very often, to simply offer a helping hand and look
for ways to re-engage with them.
The final objective we have asked our lodge leadership to address is to do
all we can to ensure that our lodges and hall associations are operating in a smooth
and sound manner. My brothers, poor operational management is the primary
cause of a lodge’s failure. All too often, well-intended members who lack the
knowledge, experience or ability to properly manage the business operations of
their lodges and hall associations are operating multi-million dollar assets whose
actions impact hundreds of people, and when the lodge breaks down functionally,
it causes disharmony and dissention among the brethren.
We have done much over the years to address this particular objective,
including streamlining lodge business systems, such as the implementation of
i-Member, the Member Center and Intacct. We strive to balance providing services
and guidance to our lodges, and training their leaders in order that they can focus
more of their time and attention on the practice of Freemasonry, while always
honoring the autonomy of our lodges.
Our Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Ray Schmalz, as well as our
Finance, Investment, Insurance, Membership Development, Masonic Properties,
and certainly not least, our Lodge Support Committees are among the resources

46

47

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

that we have made available to our lodges to address these challenges. In addition,
our incredible Grand Lodge staff members have gone above and beyond to support
the brethren. To all of these people, I am incredibly grateful.

We have worked hard this year to not only bridge our differences, but to
learn to appreciate and celebrate these distinctions. When we recognize each other
as an individual tile, which, when united, forms a unique and beautiful mosaic,
then we can accomplish great things.

We have many lodges that are successful at all three of these objectives;
others that are doing fairly well; and others that, unfortunately, are severely
missing the mark.
This year, I continued the suspension of the charters for Foothill
Lodge No. 305, Three Great Lights Lodge No. 651 and North Hollywood
Lodge No. 542.
Major efforts and resources have been poured into each of these lodges
over the years, with varying degrees of success. The brethren of Foothill Lodge,
along with three others: Concord No. 117, Provident Three Pillars No. 609 and
Santa Clara Valley Daylight No. 844 have chosen to surrender their charters. In
each of these cases, the lodges were suffering from declining membership and
the inability to adequately field officers and confer degrees. We have worked
closely with the brethren of each of these lodges to let them know their options
and to wrap up operations. Plumas Lodge No. 60 voted to surrender their charter
in December in order to form a historic lodge.
I am pleased that I have not had to suspend any lodge charters this year,
although we do have several lodges that are struggling mightily. In each of these
cases, we have advised them of the resources available to them. However, our
various leaders and committees can’t want their success more than they do.
My greatest frustration is that so many of the problems within our
lodges are simply caused by certain groups of brothers who are, for whatever
reason, unable to get along with one another. If we, as Masons who share certain
obligations and ideals can’t navigate our way through difficult situations, how can
we possibly expect the rest of society to do so? We must, using all the tools at our
disposal, endeavor to keep peace in our own houses.
We never want to lose any lodge. However, a lodge has a right to die,
even if we don’t want them to disappear from our ranks.
We have encouraged brothers in many parts of the state to consider
establishing new lodges, including in the community of Benicia, where we lost
Sublime-Benicia Lodge No. 5 last year. It is my firm belief that where we have
the right men looking to form a new lodge, in the right area, at the right time,
and most importantly, for the right reasons, then we have a very good chance at
establishing a successful and vital lodge. I welcome Worshipful Jordan Yelinek to
our Grand Lodge staff to lead the effort of establishing new lodges.

There was no greater illustration of this than an event that occurred during
my Grand Master’s trip to Israel this past May. In the Quarries of Solomon’s
Temple, 150 brothers, from ten countries, representing 60 lodges, initiated an
Arab Christian man into our Craft. We learned about cultures and religions other
than our own. And we brought the message of civility and unity to a region in
desperate need of it.
We brought some of this fellowship home with us when we held four
Brotherhood Degree Exemplifications across the state. Brethren exemplified
significant portions of our degrees in their native languages. And of course we
enjoyed the food of these cultures. I am confident that everybody in attendance
gained a greater appreciation, not only of our differences, but also of the
universal meaning of our ritual. My thanks go out to all who participated in these
unique experiences.
I also feel California Masonry has turned a new chapter in our
relationship with our Prince Hall Brethren.
Masonry still has room to improve its diversification and acceptance of
other cultures; but we have made tremendous strides in showing the world what
can be accomplished when we work together. I am very grateful to Past Grand
Master Lovell Morgan and current Grand Master Dr. Donald Ware, not only for
the relationships we have forged, but also for all you have done for Freemasonry.
The names of both of our Grand Lodges are now indelibly inscribed on the
cornerstones of three important buildings across the state. We have also initiated
conversations about how we can work even more collaboratively and capitalize
on our collective strengths.
Most Worshipful Tomas Rentoy III, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines and I recently issued a joint statement regarding the proper practice
of our Craft in California as well as in the Philippines. I am extremely grateful to
you, Most Worshipful Rentoy for your willingness to address this difficult issue in
such a professional way, as well as for the friendship we have developed.
Among this year’s accomplishments of which I am most proud is
the progress made with the Civility Effort. We are now working with civility
ambassadors from Prince Hall, the Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile, Baja Mexico,
Canada, Israel and the Philippines, making this a truly worldwide effort. We have
released the civility toolkit and developed a definition of “civility” for Wikipedia.

48

49

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

And perhaps most exciting, we are close to releasing the Civility Scorecard that
will, in real time, provide voters with objective comparisons of the level of civility
of each of the presidential candidates’ speeches. It is our hope that mainstream
media will make frequent use of the Civility Score in their reporting and that as a
result, we can start to reward civil dialogue among the candidates and encourage
them to focus on discussing real issues and not sound bites.

We can all take pride in our award-winning Freemason magazine that
keeps us connected with the Masonic family across the globe. I am also proud of
how we are connecting with our members and the public via social media. Later,
we will hear Very Worshipful Allan Casalou introduce our new Lodge app that
will be an incredible tool to stay in touch with your lodge brethren.

I am also pleased to report tremendous progress with our Masonic Youth
Orders, and to admit that our involvement with our Masonic youth has been
among the highlights of this year. We dedicated DeMolay Drive at our Union City
Masonic Home, shared dunk tanks in Covina, hung out at baseball games and
initiated many new Job’s Daughters, Rainbow Girls and DeMolay.
Working with and beside these young men and women has been very
uplifting and inspiring. My special thanks to Very Worshipful Glenn Woody
who so ably chaired our Youth Orders Committee this year. Brother Glenn, you
definitely moved the needle. I also thank all the adult youth order leaders who
are helping to shape these boys and girls into strong citizens who will contribute
greatly to making our world a better place.

As impressive as these high tech communications resources are, it is
critical that while we go high tech, we never lose our high touch with our brethren
and families. Nothing should ever replace our personal connections. A sign of this
is our recent decision to reestablish our Widows Committee.
While every loss among our Masonic family is painful, there are certain
deaths that are more palpable than others. I am very grateful that none of our Past
Grand Masters were called to the Celestial Lodge Above this past year.
However, early this year, the sudden passing of Pam Whitmore, beloved
wife of our Assistant Grand Lecturer, George Whitmore, stunned us all. In the
relatively short time Pam was a part of our Grand Lodge family, she made deep
and lasting impressions on so many of us.

Your California Masonic Foundation has offered a new grant to our
California youth orders to help them achieve far more than they are able with their
current resources. I am impressed with some of the ideas being generated and am
very proud of our Foundation for finding productive ways to support our youth.

We also lost two dear and influential brothers who served our Craft as
Grand Lecturer: Very Worshipful Brothers Ulysses Patropulos and Joe Hammond.
There is no question that we are the beneficiaries of the legacy left by both of
these dear brothers and friends.

Among our focuses this year was enhancing all forms of our
communications, and I am pleased to report good progress on this front. Hopefully,
you have seen the On the Level recordings that I prepared every three weeks this
year. These were intended to connect with the brethren everywhere in California,
share our successes and impart important information.

Our hearts also ache at the loss of Greta Alexander, wife of our Past
Grand Master Charlie Alexander and Ginny Weiss, wife of our Past Grand Master
Al Weiss. Both of these ladies truly exemplified class as they represented the
Masonic family as first ladies.

We also established new Lodge Communications awards, and tomorrow
night we will recognize four lodges for outstanding internal, public and social
media communications. In establishing these awards, we have discovered some
great techniques, which we will be sharing.
Our lodges are doing a better job in using the local press to share
newsworthy items with their community. Our outstanding Communications
Department is able to help with this and has produced media kits and press
release templates.

Worshipful Don Taylor, a 50-year Mason who ably served our Grand
Lodge for a decade as Grand Tiler, was laid to rest just two weeks ago. Worshipful
Don was a tireless worker in the quarries of Freemasonry, and California Masonry
is better today because of our dear friend and brother.
May the Great Architect of the Universal bless and watch over each of
these gentle souls and provide those nearest to them solace in their time of grief.
I also ask for your prayers for members of our Masonic family
who were victims of the recent fires in the north part of our state. The actions
taken by the lodge brethren in support of these families have been swift and
incredibly compassionate.

My brothers, California Masonry is honored, respected and revered by
many across the globe. This is due in no small part to our incredibly dedicated
staff. This level of competence and commitment can be attributed almost entirely
to the leadership of Very Worshipful Allan Casalou. Allan, your vision and
perspective have been an invaluable aid to me this year. I will forever treasure
our friendship and am indebted for all you and your team have done for our
Fraternity and me.

To paraphrase Past Grand Bethel Honored Queen, Dailey Roche, Grand
Master was not my title this year, but rather it was my role. It has indeed been a
great privilege to serve you, my brethren.

Nobody is born a Mason. Yet, Masonry is within every good man,
waiting to be discovered.
This brings me to the conclusion of my message as Grand Master, and
in closing I wish to share my gratitude to those who have helped make this year a
successful one for California Masonry.
I continue to be amazed and impressed by the dedication of the brethren
who serve on our various boards, committees and task forces. To each of you,
thank you from the bottom of my heart for all you do for our beloved Craft.
To my Grand Lodge officers—you have demonstrated how a group of
rather ordinary people can achieve extraordinary successes. Thank you for being
a part of an incredible family. Linda and I will forever cherish the relationships
we have built.
A special thanks to Very Worshipful Brother Ray Schmalz, who has been
a steady hand to me during his three years as Grand Treasurer. I thank you for your
service to our Craft, my brother.
Right Worshipful Dave, I am excited for what you and your team have
in store for us. I am always willing to hold the nail for you as you show us how to
Rise and Build. My only advice to you is that you exchange your 24-inch gauge
for a 36-inch one, as you will need it!
And although my wife Linda is not with us this afternoon, I will make
sure she knows how critical it was having her presence by my side throughout this
remarkable journey. She has truly been my oak tree, my ballast, not only an extra
passenger for the HOV lane, but also by keeping me level and on solid footing
at all times.
This year has at times been grueling, yet always rewarding beyond
my comprehension. There is no question that I have received far more from the
experience than I have invested. A great return on my investment.

Before long, however, I will return the emblems of authority that you
have so graciously granted me, and I will humbly replace this apron with a white
lambskin, and return to my lodge which spake me into my Masonic existence. I
can think of no greater reward at the end of a most remarkable journey.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Russell E. Charvonia, Grand Master

Appendix B

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

71

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2014/2015 Grand Lodge Budget
M. David Perry, Deputy Grand Master

Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
At the last Annual Communication, the Masters and Wardens of our
Constituent Lodges along with the other members of Grand Lodge approved the
per capita proposal I made as Senior Grand Warden. I am grateful for the support
and I’m pleased to present this budget for your consideration at the upcoming
Annual Communication.
The budget is very close to the budget I presented last year. We have
made refinements to the projections based on the actual membership numbers
that we have now finalized and a more clear idea of the actual expenses of some
of the time sensitive expenses like lodge insurance and health care. In the spring,
I presented this budget to the Masters and Wardens who attended the leadership
retreats. A number of them have been in communication with me and I appreciate
their interest and input. Now that we have the benefit of the latest information,
the expenses in the final budget are actually less than in the budget I presented
at the retreats. In addition to the support from our Masters and Wardens, I have
received great assistance in preparing this budget from the Grand Lodge Finance
and Insurance Committees, the Executive Committee, the Grand Treasurer, the
Grand Secretary, our Chief Financial Officer and the entire finance team. I really
appreciate the collaboration and teamwork on this effort. I am confident we have
given the budget thorough consideration.
The total membership ended up lower than we anticipated last year. The
assumption we used when I requested a Per Capita rate of $39.50 was 50,752
billable members. The actual number came in at 49,536. As it turns out, the number
of members of the Grand Master’s Lodge rose this year and the dividend from the
Nob Hill Masonic Center came is slightly higher than expected. Because of these
increases, the total decrease in revenue was only $14,000 less than originally
planned. The final expenses ended up $16,000 less than originally planned so I
am able to present a balanced budget.
Total Income for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,964,681.
Expenses exclusive of depreciation for the next fiscal year are estimated to be
$2,946,241. In many areas, we have kept expenses at the same level as the current
year. The following represent the changes in expenses.
Our Grand Lodge will host the World Conference of Regular Masonic
Grand Lodges in November. We have budgeted $50,000 to help underwrite this
worldwide event.

72

Proceedings of the

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA

The projected net revenue after expenses is approximately $5,000.
As you can see, this is a thin margin. We will need to monitor our income and
expenses very carefully to make this budget work.
With the adoption of this budget, we will be able to maintain the
programs and services we now provide to our lodges and members and we will
make an important investment in the future by focusing on meaningful degrees,
a rewarding member experience, strong lodges and halls, and our impact on
society. We will continue to improve our leadership training, offer ongoing and
new business systems to lodges like the new app, and create new lodges where
there is the interest and need to do so.
I thank you, again, for your previous support and ask for your support
now as we consider this budget for our coming fiscal year.
Respectfully submitted by,
M. David Perry, Deputy Grand Master

Fiscal Year 2015/2016
M. David Perry, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

Fiscal Year 2015/2016
M. David Perry, Deputy Grand Master
Expense Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been
Per Capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates
income from the investment return. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a four and a
half-percent spending policy has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year average valuation to
protect the fund principle. The Grand Lodge may from time to time have other income, such as interest
from bank accounts and other financial instruments. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation
included in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now
provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication
adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for the degrees of Masonry
and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different service bureaus throughout the state
and receives reimbursement for expenses incurred with the performance of those services. The Grand
Lodge also manages the investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the
cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic
Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of this Corporation.

Freemasonry has always been about building. Masons are builders. In
ancient times, we were craftsmen that possessed a unique knowledge of geometry,
the use of stone material and the physics needed to build the greatest cathedrals
and temples known to man. Many still stand today. The craftsmen quarried
stone and applied the tools of their trade, making each stone fit for the builders
use. They mastered the square, plum, level, compass, trowel and gavel. The
apprentice prepared and shaped the stone. The fellow craft tested his work and
proofed it. Then, he passed the stone to the master who determined the plan and
purpose for it.
Masons today are builders still, yet we build with stones far more fragile,
precious and valuable. In fact, we are the stones used to form temples now. Masons
are builders of men as living stones. Every man that walks through our doors is a
stone to shape, mold, proof and find a purpose for.

For 300 years, amidst major and ongoing world change, the fraternity
has remained relevant and continues to attract and retain members. That is a
major accomplishment. I’m convinced Freemasonry has withstood the test of
time because we have remained builders of men. We’ve sought to bring out the
best in men. We’ve sought to build lifelong friendships. These are aims that do
not diminish with time.
Building is contagious. We just need a spark to light our fire so we can
build something great.
This year, we will be that spark and we will “Rise and Build” together.
We will share and support our youth. We will buildup brothers that need
encouragement. We will build new lodges and restore others that have lost their
way. We will connect with each other and form strong friendships.
Building is a way of life. A builder is always prepared with his working
tools and his plan. And, when things fail or don’t go as planned, then it’s time to
check the plan. The key is to have a plan. Our fraternity in California is completing
a five-year plan that was launched in 2010.

Together, we accomplished a lot. We improved the application and
investigation process. We’re more careful about who we bring into our lodges as
we put quality over quantity. We gave Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons
more opportunities to engage in the lodge. We improved our communications. We
introduced new resources like Intacct and the Vault. We expanded our Masonic

82

83

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

education programs. Today, more and more lodges are offering outstanding
education programs. We created a statewide program to support public education,
raising more than $1.2 million to give Raising A Reader to more than 50,000
California students. We expanded Masonic Homes outreach services to serve
more brothers and widows in their own homes than ever before.

The plan calls for ensuring long-term growth with a sustainable model
for developing new lodges. Interest in the fraternity remains high and there is
room for lodge growth in the state. Our most populated cities are significantly
underserved by Freemasonry. Half of the cities and towns in California do not
have a Masonic lodge. New lodges will open in the right location, with the right
people, for the right reason.

This year, we’ve had a substantial conversation about the next five years.
We engaged over 1,300 brothers in face-to-face conversations and another 4,800
in an online survey. Together more than 6,000 brothers help create what we launch
today – our Fraternity’s 2020 Plan.
The 2020 Plan has four main objectives: a rewarding member experience,
meaningful degrees, strong lodges and halls, and our impact on society. Let’s look
at these priorities and what we hope to achieve.
Rewarding Member Experience. We will engage members in a
fraternal experience that unites us and bridges our differences. The objective is to
create a deep sense of fraternity in the lodge that creates a rewarding experience.
Our brothers told us what makes it rewarding. Masons believe that their lodge
experience is rewarding when they can say three things. “I am making true
friends.” “I am learning and improving myself.” “I am having an impact.” This
will be our goal –that every Mason can speak these words when he is asked about
his lodge experience. And we are poised to achieve this. Is there a better place in
the community where a man can make true friendships, improve himself and have
an impact on society? Our lodges are the perfect place for this and it must be our
highest priority.
Meaningful Degrees. Almost all of our members, 81% of those that
took the survey, said that degree conferrals were the most meaningful and
interesting to them of all lodge activities. Our plan’s objective is to deepen our
understanding of the ritual and provide opportunities for further learning. Every
time a candidate enters our lodge room, we want him to be profoundly affected.
A deep understanding of the principles in these degrees leads us to apply them
outside the lodge.
Strong Lodge and Halls. This objective is to strengthen our existing
lodges and halls, and create new lodges to ensure our long-term growth. The plan
calls for cultivating a succession of skilled, effective lodge officers. The interest
is there. Over 1,400 brothers requested information about serving as an officer.
We will connect with these individuals and help lodges identify them and work
together to prepare them.
The plan calls for reducing the administrative burden associated with
managing lodges and halls. We will do this by simplifying, streamlining, and
automating as many tasks and processes as possible. And we will create more
powerful and useful tools and systems.

Our Impact on Society. We will realize our vision of making a positive
difference in the world. When asked, 97% of members say they make a impact on
society. They say they use lessons shared in lodge to improve their home life, their
work life and their interactions with the public.
You have either heard or spoken the words, “And the greatest of these
is charity.” Freemasonry is not a charity; it’s a fraternity. Charity is a core value
of the organization. Masons are charitable by nature. Masonic lodges provide
relief to members and families in need, and work to improve our communities.
We take care of our Masonic widows. We invest in our children and improve our
neighborhoods. In doing so we give of our time and talent, and make financial
contributions to Masonic and other public charities.
Our brethren have told us that a unified charitable focus for the fraternity
is needed. Therefore, I will not have a Grand Master’s project. However, my
hope is to lead our fraternity to some of our most charitable days. Your Grand
Lodge leadership will work to establish a campaign that will be consistent for
several years, which will benefit our Masonic charities - the Masonic Homes and
the California Masonic Foundation. We are so proud of the great work of these
charities and they will be the focus of our efforts.
As we implement the 2020 Plan, I hope each lodge will develop a fiveyear plan and make these goals come alive in their lodge. By working together, we
can increase the relevance of our fraternity and enhance our member experience.
I’m calling on all Masons and all lodges to include support for the Masonic youth
orders in these plans.
Our youth orders include young ladies of the Rainbow for Girls and Job’s
Daughters, and young men of DeMolay. Our fraternity sponsors these youth. They
may be our sons and daughters, our nieces and nephews, or our grandchildren.
They may be kids in our community who need to be exposed to Masonic values.
They combine with us and form our Masonic family. They are our youth, our
responsibility, and we need to help them become the future leaders of our nation.
We need to treat them with respect not only for who they are today, but also for
who they will become. One of our youth may be the person that finally discovers
the cure for cancer or Alzheimer’s; one might become a Supreme Court Justice
or state Governor. And let’s not forget, they might just become Worthy Grand
Matron or Grand Master.

84

Proceedings of the

As an example for our lodges, I will lead a plan to fully support our youth
orders. They will be featured in every edition of our award-winning magazine. I
want everyone to pick up the California Freemason and read about our youth. We
are not only going to promote them, but we will support their education and develop
their leadership capabilities. I have asked our Foundation to make funding college
scholarships for our Masonic youth a high priority. No DeMolay, Job’s Daughter
or Rainbow Girl should struggle to finance the education they deserve. We will
invest in them. The Foundation has also agreed to fund leadership development
programs for our youth. In 2016, we will offer the first Leadership Experience
2016 or LX 2016.
LX 2016 will take place over consecutive weekends in late July. One
weekend will be in the south and one in the north. Youth will be immersed in a
36-hour experience, focused on applied and practical leadership and life skills.
All Masonic youth are invited at little or no cost. We will raise the money for the
program. Every Mason is encouraged to help our youth participate in LX 2016, so
we all have a stake in their success.
We will build the values and character of our youth. Our society
desperately needs it. Our world cries out for it, and our fraternity must answer the
call. We have within our grasp the ability to become one of the strongest and most
dynamic forces in our world today.
Alone we can do so little, but together we can do so much. The great
principles taught in our lodges must be the foundation we build upon. We are not
known for what we’ve done, but what we do.
Together we can. Together we shall. Together we will Rise and Build.
Thank you.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2016-2017
John R. Heisner, Senior Grand Warden

Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2016 to fund the operations of Grand Lodge fiscal year for the
period of November 1, 2016 through October 31, 2017.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked very
closely with the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand
Lodge staff to develop projections of the income and the necessary expenses for
the 2016/2017 fiscal year. Earlier this year, I was able to share our plans with the
Masters and Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I very much
appreciate the comments and input I received during and following the retreats.
In preparing a draft budget for the 2016/2017 fiscal year, I have
considered the factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that will
reduce any necessary increase.
The major factors that will increase the per capita are:
•
•
•
•
•
•

Membership decline. We project a total loss of 1,779 billable
members. This represents a loss in revenue of $70,270 or $1.47 in
Per Capita.
Reduction of the Nob Hill Dividend. The dividend was reduced by
$45,000 or $0.94 in Per Capita.
Insurance. Premiums for our lodge insurance coverage will increase
by 5.5%. This represents $.15 in Per Capita.
Personnel costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. All other Personnel
costs will increase by an additional 5.3%. Personnel cost increases
represent $0.99 in Per Capita.
Other expenses increase. Fraternal, Appropriations and Programs
increased 2.7 % representing $.064 in Per Capita.
Inflation. Items subject to inflation are expected to increase
by 2% to 3%.

Per Capita would need to increase by $4.19 to cover the effect of all of
these factors discussed here.

88

Proceedings of the

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED
MASONS OF CALIFORNIA

The factors that will help partially offset the per capita increase are
the following:
•
•

Revenue Improvements. Revenue Improvements in Investment and
Other Income offset some of the Per Capita increase.
Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that can be
held at or near last year’s levels. You will notice that the expenses
in many categories are nearly the same as the budget presented by
the Deputy Grand Master. A $50,000 savings that helped reduce
Per Capita was the non-recurring cost of the World Conference of
Regular Grand Lodges to be held in 2015/2016.

These factors allow us to present a balanced budget, with a Per Capita
assessment of 42.50. Although this represents an increase of $3.00 over the
2015/2016 assessment, 80% of the increase relates to the anticipated reduction in
billable members for 2016/2017 and the reduction in the Nob Hill dividend. The
remaining amount represents a modest increase of 1.5% over 2015/2016.
I very much appreciate your feedback on matters that are important to
our Craft and I thank you for your support of this Per Capita proposal.

Revenue Analysis
PER CAPITA

There are several factors that affect Per Capita. Membership levels, Nob Hill Dividend,
insurance, labor costs, and general inflation are all primary factors. Membership
projections show a total loss of 1,779 members which represents $70,270 or $1.47 in
Per Capita increase. The reduction of the Nob Hill Dividend of $45,000 represents a
$0.94 in Per Capita increase. Insurance and labor increases along with inflation of
approximately 2.5% account for the additional Per Capita. All other things being equal,
the Per Capita would have to be increased by $4.19 to cover the effect of all of these
factors discussed here. A $50,000 savings that helped reduce Per Capita was the nonrecurring cost of hosting the World Conference of Regular Grand Lodges in 2015, a
$1.05 reduction in Per Capita. Other improvements in Revenue driven by Investments
and other Income also helped reduce Per Capita. These factors allow us to present a
balanced budget with a Per Capita of $42.50.

93

Report of the Grand Treasurer
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge officers, Members of Boards and
Grand Lodge Committees, Brethren All.
The overall financial condition of your Grand Lodge continues to be
very good due to the hard work and diligent efforts of Grand Lodge officers,
boards and committee members and the efficient Grand Lodge staff.
Grand Lodge budgets continue to be closely monitored by the Grand
Lodge Executive Committee and the Grand Lodge Finance Committee amid
continuing efforts to conserve and curtail spending.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee continues their customary
diligence over the Grand Lodge’s investment portfolio. As a result of their
consideration of the current economic environment, they have made some wellstudied changes in the make-up and allocation of the portfolio in anticipation
of continued volatility in the economy and markets. They are continuing to
consider new asset classes and investment managers to further diversify our
investment portfolio.
The Investment Committee continues to recommend that no more than
4.5% of the Endowment Fund Investments be distributed to the Grand Lodge
operating budget and to the other entities participating in the investment pool.
This will preserve capital in the face of future potential inflation.
In 1992, our Grand Lodge voted to set aside surpluses from future Grand
Lodge budgets into a Grand Lodge endowment fund. This fund has now grown to
$2.378 million at the beginning of this fiscal year. In Deputy Grand Master Perry’s
proposed 2015 – 2016 budget, this distribution from this endowment now adds
$97,088 to our revenue.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee applies their considerable
expertise to the ongoing risk management of the Grand Lodge and our various
entities to keep them well protected at favorable and competitive premium costs.
The Grand Lodge Finance Committee provides advice in the development
of the Grand Lodge operating budgets and the per capita as well as advice to
our lodges.
The Audit Committee determines who will audit our books and records
and provide tax services for the Grand Lodge and its related entities. The Audit
Committee reviews the annual audits and 990 tax returns and provides an
independent report to the boards of each entity. This year, the Audit Committee,
after reviewing the audit work that Moss Adams provides, decided to reappoint
them as auditors of our Grand Lodge and our related entities. The Committee
continues to be impressed by Moss Adams’ diligence and expertise in carrying out
the audits in a cost-efficient manner.

94

95

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

During the past year, we have continued to reinforce the elements of good
financial management for a Lodge at our Secretaries and Treasurers Retreats, our
Masters and Wardens Retreats and at this year’s Inspector Development Academy.

and Covina which are owned by the Masonic Homes of California, the Acacia
Creek community in Union City, the Nob Hill Masonic Center and the California
Masonic Foundation - all separate corporations.

I continue to be very concerned about our Lodges’ financial management.
It is critically important that our Lodges have up-to-date financial statements for
the Lodge and for the Hall Association and promptly file their IRS and Franchise
Tax Board as well as their employment tax returns and payments if applicable.
Our Grand Lodge Finance staff can support both your Lodge and Hall Association
in these important responsibilities.

The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge and related entities were up
3.2% for the 12 months ended July 31, 2015. The annualized return for the prior
three-year period was 9.3% and 8.4% annualized for the prior five-year period.

One way to ensure that your Lodge’s financial statements and tax
filings are done on time is to use Intacct, the accounting system that the Grand
Lodge introduced three years ago. Currently a total of 124 Lodges and 59 Hall
Associations are using Intacct. We have unique resources in our Grand Lodge
finance staff who serves as a dedicated help desk for our users.
Three years ago, legislation was passed that allowed lodges to transfer
their Life Membership Fund to the Grand Lodge for investment. As of the end
of August 22 lodges have transferred their life membership funds to the Grand
Lodge, with a market value as of September 16 totaling $ $583,672.
The dedicated and efficient finance staff in the Grand Lodge office
continues to provide unexcelled service in the management and reporting on the
financial affairs of our organization under the leadership of our Chief Financial
Officer, Thomas Boyer.
You can be very proud of the work that has been done by all those
involved in the financial affairs of our fraternity. The detailed financial information
I am going to give you today is for a nine-month period from the start of this
current fiscal year, November 1, 2014, through July 31, 2015. I will compare that
information to the same period a year earlier. This report is already posted on
the Member Center under Forms/166th Annual Communication. It will continue
to be available to you until the official proceedings of this Communication
are published. Those proceedings will contain the customary audited financial
statements for the entire fiscal year.
It should be noted that this partial-year information has been prepared
internally by our fine finance staff and has not been audited.
As of July 31, 2015, your Grand Lodge had assets of $6,562,974 and
liabilities of $ 2,587,233 for Total Net Assets of $ 3,975,741. Total Net Assets at
the end of July were 3.4% higher than at October 31, 2014 fiscal year.
Keep in mind that most of the assets you might attach to the California
Grand Lodge are not actually owned by the Grand Lodge, itself, and do not
appear in these numbers. I am referring to assets such as this facility, which is
owned by the California Masonic Memorial Temple, our homes in Union City

The annualized return for our investments accounts since the inception
of measurement on January 1, 1995 has been 7.9% compared to an annualized
CPI of 2.3%, which represents a real return of 5.6%
Your Grand Lodge continues to operate in the black on a year-to-year
basis. For the nine months ended July 31, 2015, total income was $1,979,682
while total expenses were $1,821,498. This income was 2.9% higher than the
comparative period last year. Expenses for the nine-month period ended July 31,
2015 were also 2.9% higher.
While the Net Excess of income over expenses is $158,184, it should
be noted that approximately 30% of total year’s expenses are expected to occur
in the last three months of the fiscal year. The current projection, however, is
that the Grand Lodge will end this fiscal year on October 31st with a modest
surplus. This will be the eighth year in a row that Grand Lodge will have ended
the year with a small operating surplus versus the budgets you, my Brothers, have
approved each year.
The 2015 expense budget is divided in the following manner: 29.5%
for fraternal matters (such as this Annual Communication, travel expenses of
elected and appointed Grand Lodge Officers, insurance for the constituent lodges
as well as other miscellaneous fraternal expenses), 15.0% for Appropriations and
Programs (such as Leadership Development programs, various lodge support
committees, the Freemason magazine and other Committees such as Policy,
Jurisprudence, Investment, Ritual and Trial Review), and 55.5 % for General
and Administrative items (such as salaries and benefits, accounting and auditing,
investment management fees, legal fees and general office operations).
These results reflect the concern and diligence that the Grand Lodge
Executive Committee, the Grand Lodge Finance Committee and the Grand Lodge
financial staff bring to the monitoring of actual income and expenses versus the
budget. The numbers are compiled and studied by all parties in great detail as the
year progresses. You should know that any surplus at the end of the fiscal year is
not carried over into the next year, but instead is permanently transferred to the
Grand Lodge Endowment Fund. The result is that each Grand Master starts his
year with a zero balance with only the budget for that year to work with.

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present to you this, my eighth report, as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
Our membership at the beginning of the 2015 fiscal year was 54,973.
We had 2,441 gains and 4,632 losses. The ending membership on June 30, 2015,
was 53,449, which includes 3,439 Entered Apprentice Masons, 1,018 Fellow
Craft Masons and 48,992 Master Masons. Our database also includes 24,070
Masonic widows.
A more detailed report of membership activity, together with a number
of Lodge Bylaw amendments, life memberships, Masonic trials and veteran’s
awards are included in my written report to be distributed in the Proceedings.
Charters and Dispensations
As of today, there are 332 lodges in our jurisdiction, including two lodges
under dispensation and five research lodges. There were three lodge consolidations
this year: Canal Farm Lodge No. 312 in Los Banos and Yosemite Lodge No. 99
in Merced consolidated to form Yosemite Lodge No. 99; Sierra Valley No. 184
in Sierraville and Feather River No. 234 in Beckwourth consolidated to form
Feather River No. 234; and Clovis No. 417 and Las Palmas-Pondersoa No. 366 in
Fresno consolidated to form Las Palmas-Ponderosa No. 366.
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Plumas
Historic Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. Grand Master
Charvonia granted a dispensation to Plumas Historic Lodge on November 10,
2014. In reviewing the records of this Lodge and from information provided by
the Inspector, it has been determined that Plumas Historic Lodge has met the
requirements of the petition.
A motion was made, seconded, and adopted to issue a charter to Plumas
Historic Lodge.
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Green
Dragon Masonic Fellowship Lodgee U.D. in Bakersfield has submitted the lodge
Bylaws, books and records. Grand Master Charvonia granted a dispensation to
Green Dragon Masonic Fellowship Lodge on July 30, 2015. The Lodge has not
operated for sufficient time to petition a Charter, but it prays the Grand Master
will continue the dispensation after the close of the Annual Communication.

100

Proceedings of the
Five Lodges voted to voluntarily surrender their Charters this year:
1. Plumas Lodge No. 60 in Quincy on December 8, 2014;
2. Concord Lodge No. 117 in Sacramento on June 4, 2015;
3. Provident Three Pillars Lodge No. 609 in Sacramento on
June 8, 2015;
4. Santa Clara Valley Daylight Lodge No. 844 in San Jose on
June 25, 2015; and
5. Foothill Lodge No. 305 in Monrovia on August 13, 2015.

It was moved and seconded that the voluntary surrender of the Charters
issued to the Lodges named above be accepted by the Grand Lodge; that the lodges
be dissolved in accordance with the Code; and that the assets thereof, other than
each dissolving lodge’s Life Membership Funds, be held for the establishment of
new lodges. The motion was adopted.
Summary of Accomplishments
We achieved a number of accomplishments this year that I would
like to share with you today, as well as introduce some new programs for the
coming year.
Intacct and Government Returns
About 40 percent of lodges are now using Intacct for financial accounting
and reporting; another 20 percent are ready to implement in 2016. Lodges that use
Intacct can access a number of resources, including system training for secretaries
and treasurers by our Intacct team. Intacct is especially valuable, with increased
government scrutiny of non-profit organizations.
This year, the IRS revoked the tax-exempt status of 39 lodges,
subjecting them to income tax, which can be a prohibitive expense. Our finance
team supported these lodges in applying for reinstatement. So far, 19 have been
reinstated and another six have completed the reinstatement process.
Lodges can avoid losing tax-exempt status by filing required tax
documents on time. Two years ago, we began offering tax services to lodges at
no cost and to hall associations using Intacct for a modest fee. This year, we
offered this service to all lodges; 196 accepted, 122 opted to self-file, and 14 did
not respond. Grand Lodge has successfully filed returns for 181 lodges that opted
in. Those remaining are waiting for their tax-exempt status to be resolved before
filing. We also completed tax returns for 18 hall associations. I wish to thank the
lodge leaders who diligently provided information throughout this process, and
our finance team for their excellent work.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

101

Leadership Development
This year’s Master and Wardens Retreats were the largest ever – over
500 officers attended. About 350 secretaries and treasurers attended their retreats,
10 percent more than last year. In total, 76 percent of lodges were represented at
the retreats. In 2016, there will again be four locations for the Master and Wardens
Retreats, including Monterey, Lake Tahoe, Irvine, and Palm Springs.
Communications
I continue to be very proud of our communications. In addition to
publishing six issues of California Freemason magazine in print and in digital
formats, we publish a monthly e-newsletter, The Leader, to lodge officers as well
as a weekly e-newsletter and annual report to all members. We maintain several
websites, and utilize Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram to communicate
with our members and the public.
Each issue of Freemason magazine is mailed to more than 70,000
subscribers, including nearly 20,000 Masonic widows. The free California
Freemason App, available through iTunes, Google Play, and Amazon, has nearly
40,000 subscribers from 158 countries.
The magazine has won more than 20 national awards since 2004. This
year, the December/January issue, “Civility in an Uncivil Age,” was awarded
the best single topic issue by the Association of Media and Publishing, a trade
organization of more than 1,000 nonprofit membership organizations. The
magazine is also among five finalists for best overall design of a non-profit
association by Folio Awards, the largest association of for-profit and nonprofit
magazine and media executives.
Last year, we published 15 years of articles by our immediate Past
Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother John Cooper, to celebrate his Golden
Anniversary as a Freemason. I’m pleased to announce that Macoy Publishers will
publish this book, “The Questing Mind Is a Salient Characteristic of a Freemason:
A Collection of Writings by John L. Cooper.” This collection is the fruit of years
of deep study and an extensive understanding of Masonry. You can purchase
a copy this weekend at the Southern California Research Lodge booth in the
Exhibition Hall. It will also be available online from Macoy. I think you will
enjoy it immensely!
We are connected with nearly 100,000 people on Facebook. Each week,
our posts reach as many as 120,000 people and about 7,000 on average are
engaged each week liking, commenting, and sharing our posts.
Our YouTube channel has a library of more than 70 videos, including
educational videos, member profiles, charitable reports, and conference programs.
These videos have more than 75,000 views.

102

103

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Recently, I announced the launch of a new app that will enhance lodge
communications. This is a social, mobile, smartphone app that is focused on
engaging members outside the lodge. Its features include: Facebook-like posts
that are shared with all members of the app; photo sharing; a calendar with RSVP
functions and push notification reminders; contact lists to email or call members
directly from the app; and a chat feature, to message individuals or small groups.

Allow me to thank all of the members of our Grand Lodge committees
and boards, who perform essential functions for our fraternity. I especially want
to recognize Worshipful Brother David Ferreria, chairman of the Jurisprudence
Committee, who finishes his nine-year tenure on the committee this year.

The deputy grand master included the app fees within the Grand Lodge
budget, so there is no additional cost to lodges. To learn more about the app or to
try it out, visit the Lodge Resources booth in the lobby.
The Vault
Last year, we launched The Vault, an online system that stores lodge
minutes, applications, bylaws, and other important documents. Over 100 lodges
are already using it, with more joining each month.
Grand Lodge has also been digitizing its historic records: This year we
digitized the Proceedings from 1850 to the present. They will be accessible to
members later this year.
Philanthropy
This year’s fundraising efforts were very successful. California Masons
continue to lead the way in charitable giving. Gifts to the Masonic Homes and the
California Masonic Foundation were higher this year than last. More members
gave and 49 lodges reached 100% officer giving. Nearly $200,000 was donated
to the Firefighters in Safety Education Program. We expanded Masons4Mitts
to include the Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres, in addition to the
San Francisco Giants, and together we raised nearly $160,000, reaching 8,000
underprivileged children. Masons4Mitts is a great community engagement tool:
More than 2,500 Masons and their guests attended Masons Night at the ballparks,
thousands of people attended our check presentations, and we received nearly
10 minutes of television and radio coverage. Thank you to all of the teams and
captains that made this program a huge success.
Planning for the XIV World Conference of Regular Masonic Grand
Lodges has been a high priority during the year. To be held here at our Memorial
Temple November 18-21, 2015, ours will be the largest World Conference ever.
Nearly 1,000 Masons will be in attendance from 100 Grand Lodges from around
the globe. It’s not too late to register if you want to be a part of this historic event.
To conclude my report, I wish to extend my appreciation to our lodge
secretaries and assistant secretaries whose dedicated work is the backbone of both
our lodges and our Grand Lodge. I also wish to thank our assistant grand lecturers
and district inspectors who, in addition to their ritual duties, manage a number of
administrative matters. Worshipful Brother Roy Pool is retiring as assistant grand
lecturer. I’d like to thank him for his assistance to me over the years.

Our Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Brother Ray Schmalz, has
decided to retire. Thank you, Brother Ray, for your outstanding work on behalf
of our Grand Lodge, our lodges, our committees, and boards. It has truly been a
pleasure to serve with you.
In May, I announced the retirement of our Assistant Grand Secretary,
Worshipful Brother James Banta, who was selected to be the executive director
of Northern California DeMolay, a key leadership position. This is such an honor
for James and for our Grand Lodge. I could not be more proud of him or more
excited for the future of DeMolay. James, on behalf of your colleagues at the
Grand Lodge and all the Masons of California, I’d like to present you with this
framed apron recognizing your service as assistant grand secretary from 20092015. Please join me in thanking Brother James.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother Russ
Charvonia, for his service. And I thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to
serve and work with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary
