Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Our Code requires the Grand Lecturer to render to Grand Lodge, at each
Annual Communication, a full and detailed account of his services during the
year, and to set forth, with respect to ritual, the condition of the Lodges. Therefore,
I am pleased to present to you my fourth report to you as your Grand Lecturer.
Account of Services
This year I met with the Ritual Committee monthly to discuss the various
matters of ritual and administration concerns; including the tracking of Inspector
vacancies, updating of the Book of Ceremonies, the Funeral Ritual, the Monitor
and Officers’ Manual, the Installation Ritual, and the Handbook for Candidate’s
Coaches (which had not been updated since 1992). During each meeting I posted
a comparison chart that monitored our expenses for each budgeted category.
I continued to meet with the Grand Master’s special Task Force on Ritual
in order to identify innovative ways to improve the ritual experience.
With the assistance of Worshipful Brother Ricky Lawler, Assistant Grand
Lecturer to Division 4, we created an Officer’s Coaches training course consisting
of 12 modules. This course will be presented to the Inspectors at the 2016
Inspector’s ritual conferences where they will be instructed how to implement the
program for current and prospective officers’ coaches.
I held six Master Masons schools that covered all three degrees in a
continuing effort to present ritual in such a manner as to produce a very positive
response by all present.
I held two ritual conferences for all Inspectors; one in the northern
California and one in southern California. These conferences covered all three
degrees as well as the funeral ritual.
I activated the final version of the Ritual Floor Work Manual and made
it available to all Inspectors via the Member Center. It is hoped that this manual
will serve as a resource to help Inspectors resolve ritual misunderstandings.
This manual should become available to all officers’ coaches before the end
of this year.
At the request of the Grand Master, the Assistant Grand Lecturers of
Divisions 3, 4, 5 and 7 coordinated a demonstration of a “Brotherhood Degree”
where the words spoken by each officer in the selected degree was of a different
language. Although it was understood that this special demonstration was not a
representation of the manner in which we currently confer our degrees, which is

132

133

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

to start and end the degree conferral in the same previously–approved language,
it was to demonstrate that our fraternity was made up of men from many cultures
and languages who were able to work together in peace and harmony. Before or
after each event, the brethren enjoyed a meal consisting of foods from the several
representative cultures.

I would like to express my sincere appreciation to Worshipful Ricky
Lawler for all the work he and his team did to develop the Officers’ Coaches
training program. Your work in support of our Officers Coaches will ease their
work as well as that of their Inspectors.

Ritual competitions were held within each Division to identify
the best ritual performance in the Second Section of the Third Degree. I was
slightly disappointed in the fact that in two Divisions not a single team desired
to participate. As a result the following teams were selected as the Guardians
of Ritual Consistency in the Second Section of the Third Degree for their
respective Divisions:
Division 1 – (No participating teams)

For next year, the ritual competition will consist of two opportunities:
One for the individual and the other for a ritual team. The team competition will
be the 2nd Section of the 3rd Degree and the individual competition will be the
Senior Deacon’s work of the Middle Chamber lecture. The formal announcement
will come out soon along with the registration form. The deadline for submitting
your individual and team registration form will be February 1, 2016 so
don’t delay.
We prepared this year’s Masters and Wardens Questions for Advancement
to include, for the first time, essay questions governing civility.
We developed a Best Practices Library of various ways Inspectors could
conduct District Officer Schools of Instruction. This library is now accessible to
each Inspector via the Member Center.
My Appreciation
First I wish to thank each of the Assistant Grand Lecturers, the Inspectors
and, especially, the Officers’ Coaches for their outstanding commitment to our
Craft and for their continuing efforts to preserve our ritual. A special thank you
goes to the fine work by Worshipful Roy Pool who steps down as an AGL only
to accept a new position as Assistant Grand Tiler. I know your experience as an
Assistant Grand Lecturer will greatly assist you in your new role.

Lastly, I wish to thank former Assistant Grand Lecturer Franklin Lee,
who, along with his committee of dedicated and committed Masons, continues
to assist the Fraternity by completing the cornerstone training DVD without the
use of any Grand Lodge funds or Grand Lodge staff. The commitment shown by
Frank in the completion of this very complex project demonstrated his excellent
leadership skills in general as well as his unfaltering love of this Craft in particular.
This DVD will be available to you in the Resources and Publications section of
the Members Center in the Ceremonies folder. Additionally, a shortened version
will soon be available on the Member Center for public viewing.
Ritual Conditions of the Lodge
For your information, as of August 1, 2015, California has 333 lodges
and 53,449 Masons. 44% of the Masters of our lodges are Past Masters with
an average age of 56 years and with an average of 16 years of experience (7%
of the lodge Masters have less than 5 years of experience); the oldest is 84 and
youngest is 25.
43% of our Senior Wardens are Past Masters with an average age of
55 years and with an average of 15 years of experience; the oldest is 92 and the
youngest is 26.
34% of our Junior Wardens are Past Masters with an average age of 55
and with an average of 14 years of experience; the oldest is 88 and youngest is 24.
20% of our Senior Deacons are Past Masters with an average age of
50 years and with an average of 9 years of experience; the oldest is 87 and
youngest is 20.
4% of our Junior Deacons are Past Masters with an average age of
49 years and with an average of 7 years of experience; the oldest is 86 and
youngest is 22.
Throughout this year the Ritual Committee worked in support of two
of the Fraternities four strategic priorities: The conferral of meaningful degree
conferrals and ensuring a rewarding membership experience.
Most of our lodges perform quality ritual and confer meaningful degrees,
which go a long way towards improving membership experience for all involved;
however, there are a significant number of lodges where ritual performance is in
need of improvement.

134

135

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Overall, the quality of our membership experience as well as the
performance of our ritual is in direct proportion to the degree of harmony
exhibited within the lodge as well as the effectiveness of its administration. When
lodges operate effectively and harmoniously, with a culture of continued Masonic
education, the ritual is better and portrayed with meaning. What concerns me are
the number of lodges where the ritual of our stated meetings, not to mention our
degree conferrals, is spoken without feeling and performed as if the ritual work
was more a chore rather than a cheerful opportunity. So I asked myself, as many
other Grand Lecturers have done in the past, what can we do to improve the
quality in the ritual and membership experience within our lodges?

On the officer level, though unintended, some lodges have lost the power
of brotherhood that comes from struggling together to master our ritual as a team
of brothers working together.

A possible solution came to me when I heard the recent remarks of a
Golden Veteran Award recipient, Worshipful Max H. Rush, Inspector to the 1018th
District, who summed up his 50 years as a freemason in five words --- Good
intentions with unintended consequences.
In summary, what Worshipful Max observed was that in 1965 between
the conferral of each degree a significant amount of time was spent with his coach.
Less than 25% of the time was devoted to Masonic catechism while 75% of the
time was devoted to discussions about the lodge, its officers, its members and the
history of freemasonry in general. Max learned his ritual, as well as our history,
from mouth to ear.
Later Max was exposed to the use of an unofficial Cipher as an aid to
the memory and the book served him well. Some 20 years later, the Cipher was
adopted by our Craft and in the years that followed unintended consequences
diminished the good intentions of the cipher’s use.
Over simplifying a little, the sub-title of the Cipher --- A Valuable Aid
to Memory --- became too quickly ignored. The initial supporters never intended
that a cipher would, over time, become a substitute for much of the candidates’
coaches’, and to a lesser extent the officers’ coaches’, role by becoming the
primary teaching tool for learning our work.
The tradition of teaching from mouth-to-ear remains extremely valuable
and the cipher becomes a valuable aid to the memory during practice times when
the coach was not readily available. However, the mentor’s value is reinforced
when he routinely examines the student’s memory proficiency to ensure every
word is correct and he understood their meaning and history.
The cipher, used as an aid to the memory and not as a primary teaching
tool, reinforces and improves ritual as it was intended to do. The downside has been
our inability to recognize, manage and minimize the unintended consequences of
its use. Through inattention we have allowed the cipher to displace the importance
of well-trained and supported coaches.
On the candidate level some lodges have lost the hidden power of trained
candidates’ coaches who somehow had the ability to inspire true brotherhood
between two men who otherwise would have remained at a perpetual distance.

While there are exceptions here and there, the fact is, in too many lodges
the art of coaching (candidates and officers) has been lost.
Weakness is not the fault of the Cipher. The weakness comes from failing
to recognize, or just ignoring, the unintended consequences of the good intentions
of the cipher movement.
Worshipful Max’s comment reminded me of the words of Brother
Joseph Fort Newton, Past Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge of Iowa in 1911,
who reminds us that, “The ‘secret’ in Masonry is the method of its teaching, the
atmosphere it creates, the spirit it breathes into our hearts, and the tie it spins
and weaves between man and man; in other words, the lodge and its ceremonies
and obligations, its signs, tokens and words - its power to evoke what is most
secret and hidden in the hearts of men. No one can explain how this is done. We
only know that it is done, and guard as a priceless treasure the method by which
it is wrought.”
As we go forward into the future of Freemasonry and find it necessary
to adapt our traditions to become more relevant, we must concurrently recognize
the importance of managing any unintended consequences so we may never lose
that priceless treasure, the method by which Masons are taught, so the good that
is created is not erased by the unintended consequences.
So what do we do now? We need to restore our ancient mentoring
culture; we must return to the basics that formed the foundation upon which this
wonderful Craft was built: The Masonic Mentor!
Candidate coaching lays the foundation for the way in which a candidate
will engage in the Lodge once he becomes a Master Mason. Ineffective candidate
preparation and coaching causes candidates to feel unwanted and leads to
confusion, misunderstanding and a lack of interest or commitment. When these
candidates fail to advance, they usually feel cheated and they do not act in a way
that promotes our Craft. However, a well prepared candidate, one who participates
in an effective mentoring program, will represent our Craft well and will engage
in the continuance of the lodge culture that not only welcomed him into the
Fraternity but also gave him the lessons to make others feel equally welcomed.
It is my opinion that the executive committee of every lodge, under the
management of the lodge Master, needs to establish a continuing lodge culture
relative to reinforcing their candidate’s education as well as their supporting the
officer coaching program.
We need to manage the unintended consequences of the past changes.
First we must reverse the trend to use our Cipher as a primary training tool
by creating pools of well-trained and properly supported candidate and
officer coaches.

136

Proceedings of the

Starting with each prospective candidate, each lodge needs to renew
its commitment to mentoring and create a culture where mentoring is supreme.
We must remind ourselves of the content of our current candidate mentoring
guidelines found in the Lodge Manual, the Handbook for Candidate’s Coaches
and the Inspector’s Manual so we can strengthen our resolve to provide each
candidate with a well-trained and supported coach and thus, reverse the unintended
consequence of inappropriate reliance on the cipher.
Once the candidate is properly coached and becomes a Master Mason,
the foundation is formed to allow him to coach others in the same manner he was
coached. Over time a well-trained and supported candidate coaching program will
provide a sufficient pool of candidates from which to select future officers, as well
as officer coaches with a similar mentoring commitment.
I propose we return to the basics of the past in support of that special
secret that was mentioned by Very Reverend Newton when he observed that
mentoring is the method of teaching that creates an atmosphere that breathes a
special spirit into our hearts and spins and weaves a tie between the coach and his
student; be it a candidate striving to become a Master Mason or an officer striving
to become Master of his lodge, that allows each to be better men and leaders.
Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Gary C. Silverman
The internal dialogue that affects our self-esteem.
Good Morning, What a glorious way to spend a Sunday Morning together
talking about our favorite subject. US! More specifically our attitude and how the
words we use influence our self-esteem and subsequently our actions.
One of my favorite sayings is Attitude more than Aptitude determines
Altitude. Our Grand Master this year inspired us to Repair the World by
improving ourselves and what better way to accomplish this than by elevating our
Self Esteem and aligning it with our internal dialogue.
You see Self Esteem is the SILVER BULLET to a positive Mental
Attitude and creates a sense of Happiness. Has anyone ever asked you - What
does happiness mean to you?
Most people I talk to give me some variation of feeling good either by
deeds; acts or relationships.
If our Primary goal is to feel good; then what stands in our way of that
Feel Good or Positive Mental Attitude? Perhaps it is that internal dialogue we’re
constantly hearing putting up speed bumps.
Let me ask you;
1. Have you ever done something you didn’t want to do?
2. Does anyone have the ability to make you feel upset or angry?
3. Do you ever feel guilty about some indulgent or selfish behavior?
If you answered yes to any of these you’re in good company and in the
majority. According to the Barksdale Foundation studies, most people’s selftalk (that internal dialogue we all have with ourselves) is compromising our self
Esteem by making us feel we’re not in control of our lives.
The reality is, the answer to all three of those question is NO! It’s an
inside job and we are doing it to ourselves. Don’t surrender to the GIGO (Garbage
in Garbage Out) programing of our youth when the action was tied to the person
doing the action.
Since our time is limited this morning, I’d like to share with you 4 simple
concepts that can help us rephrase that internal voice to make an impact on our
future attitudes.
Eliminate I’ll Try from your vocabulary
It was that great Sage of mythical Masonic lore Master Yoda who said it
best “Do or do not - there is no try”

140

141

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Try implies that we probably won’t do it or be successful. If we intend to
do something, do it! If we have no intention of doing it, then let’s own that; it will
help us to recognize more clearly what we want to do in our life.

The businessman thinks for a minute and says, did your research show
you that my mother is dying after a long, painful illness with huge medical bills
beyond her ability to pay?’ Embarrassed, the volunteer mumbled, ‘Uh... no, I
didn’t know that.’

Eliminate Would’a; Could’a; Should’a
They simply don’t imply positive actions; but instead passive
intentions. Just like I’ll try is not productive and leads to Guilt, one of the most
destructive emotions.
Use a little word that packs a knockout punch YET.
This little word tacked on to the end of any shortcoming transforms it
from a challenge to an aspiration. For example “I don’t know how to lose weight”
YET; I can’t learn Italian YET; or my personal favorite I’m not ready to get
married YET! With these 3 little letters you can turn a hopeless statement into
a future goal. After all, if Martin Luther King can have a dream why can’t we?
Lastly Never Feel Ashamed To Ask For Help
We talk about our tenets of Brotherly love Relief & Truth; but when we
think about relief it’s usually of the giving nature.

‘Secondly,’ did it show that my brother, a disabled veteran, is blind and
confined to a wheelchair and is unable to support his wife and six children?
Again the volunteer stammered an apology.
Lastly, did your research also show you that my sister’s husband died in
a dreadful car accident, leaving her penniless with a mortgage and three children,
requiring an array of private tutors?
The humiliated volunteer feeling completely beaten up, says, ‘I’m so
sorry I had no idea.’

Nobody is a genius from day one, Successful people never make the
mistake of not asking for help when needed. It is a sign of strength not weakness
to seek assistance when in need.

And the businessman says, ‘So, if I didn’t give any money to them, what
makes you think I’d give any to you?’

Along those lines as Grand Chaplain I have been fortunate to travel the
State visiting so many of the fabulous communities which make up our Grand
Lodge. To share in the many celebrations of Life; Lodges and locales. None more
fulfilling than visiting our Masonic Homes here in Union City and Covina.

Words you see paint a powerful picture and send strong messages
however conveyed. To prove this point I offer the following as an example;

Occasionally I’ve been asked to assist the Philanthropy department in
its laudable goals of bolstering its endowment to provide the highest level of
care for our residents. Being one who encourages the teaching of the great sage
Maimonides and his 8 levels of Tzedakah (charity) the highest being to help
sustain a person before they become impoverished by offering assistance in a
dignified manner. I’m a firm believer that each person’s relationship with his
philanthropic goals is private and for me always anonymous.
It always reminds me of a humorous story about a prominent nonprofit
organization’s volunteer who was dispatched to pay a visit to the most prominent
businessman in the community at his lavish office.
The volunteer opened by saying, ‘Our research shows that even though
your annual income is over two million dollars, you don’t give a penny to
charity. Wouldn’t you like to give something back to your community through
our 501 C3?’

Play video clip I can’t see
https://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=player_detailpage&v=HX5aRzXUzJo
Powerful words and images touch our hearts and souls. Let us commit
NOW to bring our self-esteem in line with our internal dialogue achieving the
altitude our attitude deserves.
Thank you for being a part of our Masonic family and I wish you G-d’s
blessing on your journey of Repairing the World by Improving ourselves so we
can Rise & Build for the future.

Grand Oration
Remember
A little bit of light dispels much darkness.
My brothers, let’s go back to a critical moment in the Masonic journey
when we were first about to see the light of Freemasonry. Before the light, there
was a sound that commanded.
“In the beginning G-d created the heavens and the earth, and the earth
was void and without form, and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
And G-d said Let there be light! And there was light.”
That moment is powerful. The words have purpose; there is a message
and lesson to be learned. We were at that time, like the universe at the beginning,
in a state of darkness. The first injunction upon all creation and on us as newly
initiated Masons? “Let there be light!” Think about it: we are talking about big
bang, creation, the beginning of being a Freemason. Let there be light.
Brethren, I submit to you that these words are the purpose of life and the
foundation of all we are meant to do as men and Masons. Our mission is to bring
as much light as we can into the world. After all it is either light or darkness.
In 2002 I left behind my family, friends and business, and followed my
dream and moved to Israel. It was a tempestuous time in the country. One day, I
was on the phone with my friend David back in Los Angeles. He made a request
that left me feeling unsure.
David and I had become friends in an online video game and eventually
real life friends, too. He is Catholic. He asked me to purchase two rosaries and
have them blessed for him and his mom and to send them to L.A.
As an observant Jew, it wasn’t a request I felt comfortable with, but at
the same time, I didn’t know how I could possibly deny such a favor. I blurted out
yes and so began one of my fondest life quests.
The Old City of Jerusalem is a giant maze winding streets where it’s easy
to get lost.
I was dressed like a cross between an orthodox Jew and a thug.
Of course, this was how I normally dressed. I was about to walk through
the Muslim quarter in an attempt to find the Christian quarter to which I had never
been, then to find rosaries and somehow get them blessed.
I had no clue what I was doing and I wasn’t rolling onto the friendliest
turf. At the time, walking alone in the wrong areas wasn’t the safest endeavor.

146

Proceedings of the

I spent quite a bit of time wandering around. You should have seen the
way people were staring at me: confused, apprehensive, even nervous; like the
scene was off. Finally, I spied a little corner shop filled with rosaries.
Before I went in, I reminded myself that this was to make a friend happy
and give him something he considered sacred. It didn’t detract from my faith and
observance, but would bring another human being joy.
I walked in and explained the situation to this wary shopkeeper who eyed
me suspiciously. He recommended olive wood rosaries.
Great! I bought two and ask him to double bag it. Then I asked him for
just one more bag for good measure.
Achievement unlocked!
Now - to get them blessed: I assumed this required a Catholic priest. I
left the store and began looking at the signs on various buildings. Eventually one
read something about the Vatican and I knew that was it.
The parking gate was open; several fancy black Mercedes with Vatican
flags were parked in front. The building was a very large villa. I walked right
through the gate and as I approached the front door, my mind was scrambling:
“What am I thinking? What the hell am I gonna’ say when they open the door?”
Just then, like out of a movie scene, the front door opened and a man in a
red yarmulke and a black cassock strode out flanked by another man. The two of
us locked eyes, and he drew back. I put on my best I’m-not-a-terrorist-smile, and
said “Excuse me.” He thought he was about to meet his maker. “Yes?” he asked.
“Can you please bless these rosaries for me?”
“You want me to bless rosaries for you?”
“Well not for me. They’re for a friend….”
“Uhuh. And where is your friend?”
“Los Angeles.”
“Is he Catholic?”
“Yes.”
“How did you get in here?”
“The gate was open.”

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

147

I’m telling you he gave me the third degree!
After all his questions were satisfactorily answered, he cautiously took
the bag and opened it, whereupon he found another bag, and on opening that, eyed
yet another bag. “That’s a lot of bags,” he said. When he saw there actually were
rosaries in the bag and not a weapon, he performed a blessing on them. I thanked
him and left to mail them.
The package arrived and David called to thank me. When I told him the
story, there was a pause on the other end, “red beanie and black outfit?”
“Yeah.”
“You mean to tell me these are rosaries made of olive wood from
Jerusalem blessed by a cardinal!? Wait until my mom hears this!” David and his
mother were delighted. Those rosaries meant so much. They treasured them; and
they’ve thanked me numerous times. When David’s brother died unexpectedly
some years ago, they buried him with one of the rosaries, and his mom told
me it gave her much comfort knowing her son was buried with such a special
object. David’s grandmother passed a couple years ago. She was buried with the s
econd rosary.
“Let there be light.” One act of kindness can change someone’s life. We
never know how great an impact our actions can have.
David and I were friends before the rosary quest, after - we became
brothers. We may not be blood, we may not be of the same tribe, and he is not
a Mason, yet we are brothers nonetheless; brothers who respect one another and
appreciate our differences. This act meant so much to David, and to me, that it
brought us much closer as sincere friends.
I say this was my first truly Masonic act.
It was not long after I knocked on the door of Freemasonry.
This story is a small example of what Grand Master Charvonia has
enjoined us to do this year:
To repair the world, by improving ourselves. If we want to bring greater
light into this world, if we want to make it a better place, if these words are not
just grand lip service, first make yourself a better man, and then go out and change
the world for the good.

148

149

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I was confronted with a situation which caused me to stop and ask myself
seriously, “Who am I? Who do I want to be in this situation? What message will
my actions convey?” I chose to go out of my comfort zone to help a friend, and as
a result, I improved from the experience.

The first of my two most memorable moments came when we initiated
an Arab Christian man into our fraternity inside Solomon’s Quarries. This
degree saw both the Grand Lodges of Israel and California participating in the
ritual together, and which was attended by brothers from all over the world. It
was deeply moving and a memory I will always cherish. It was Freemasonry
at its best.

For real personal growth to take place, we all have to go out of our
comfort zones.
Masonry should make us uncomfortable at times; otherwise we may not
be working hard enough.
Moses stood at the burning bush and was commanded to lead the
Israelites out of Egypt, and he asked, “Who am I?” On the surface, it’s a statement
of humility. But there is also an existential question here, a deeper level.
When Moses says “Who am I?” he is asking: Am I a prince of Egypt?
Am I a simple shepherd of Midian? Or am I an Israelite whose destiny is to lead
his people out of bondage? Moses was asked to go way out of his comfort zone.
But he accepted the challenge and he grew into one of the greatest figures in
history. He didn’t just change the world, he rocked the world.
When we face our own burning bush, and ask, “Who am I?” What path
will we choose?
The one that requires little effort bears little fruit. The one that makes us
sweat, toil, and be uncomfortable, will cause us to grow into men who can make
a real difference.
Just being good is not good enough for Masons. We agreed to rise to a
call when we became brothers of this great order. We agreed to become builders of
ourselves and society. We agreed to be men who use the teachings of our fraternity
to heal our fractured world. We agreed to let there be light.
This past May, I participated in this Grand Lodge’s amazing journey to
Israel. On a couple occasions, I was out of my comfort zone.
Oddly, my most uncomfortable moment came during a Jewish ceremony,
because that ceremony broke with many of my own traditions. One could say it
was “un-orthodox.” Fortunately there was a brother who whispered good counsel
in my ear and told me that growth is uncomfortable.
Going into a church was something that also made me uncomfortable.
Up to that point I had been in only one church in my life and we were scheduled
to visit a bunch.
Before the trip I had to ask “Who am I?” Would a true Mason stand
outside buildings holy to his fellow brothers rather than learn to appreciate that
which they hold sacred? I chose to visit all the sites and am glad I did. It was both
educational and stirring to share in my friends’ experiences.

Would you believe me if I told you that my other favorite moment was
watching friends being baptized in the River Jordan?
By this point I had learned how to share in the happiness and joy of my
brothers, like Freemasonry teaches, and it felt great! I grew on that trip and it was
life-changing. A highlight of the year.
Jerusalem was where I first set foot in a lodge. Upon first entering Holy
City Lodge #4, I saw Muslims, Jews, Christians, Armenians, Arabs, Englishmen
- men of multiple faiths and backgrounds - seated around a table eating, laughing,
and asking how each other and their families were doing.
While this may seem ordinary, given the context of what was happening
at the time in the country, it was nothing short of extraordinary. Outside was
chaos, inside - harmony and light.
It blew my mind, and was the impetus for my wanting to join the craft.
If Freemasonry can bring together men of every background while war is being
fought outside its doors, Freemasons can help to bring together all mankind. We
have a lot of light to share.
Look around. You men who are gathered here are leaders of your
respective lodges, jurisdictions, concordant bodies and let’s not forget, families
and communities. Brethren, in this room there are literally millions upon millions
of hours dedicated to our beloved craft.
If we are not here to change the world and make it better, if we are not
here to make ourselves the best men we can possibly be, if we are not here to let
there be light, then we are wasting all that precious time! Those millions of hours
must count!
The 13th century Persian poet, Rumi, said, “The wound is the place
where the Light enters you.” Part of improving yourself is to identify that which
is broken inside. The process of healing our wounds and imperfections is how we
grow and receive further light.
One of the most influential rabbis of the past few centuries, the
Lubavitcher Rebbe, said “If you see what needs to be repaired and how to repair
it, then you have found a piece of the world that G-d has left for you to complete.
But if you only see what is wrong and what is ugly in the world, then it is you
yourself that needs repair.”

Each of us is given a unique mission. There is a light only you can shine.
Let us rise to that challenge and build a better society.

I, you, we, must continue to build a better self. We must be the bridge-builders
between and among men because we have those tools. I may never fully get there,
but I will always be traveling to the east because:

I have three quick and easy tips, derived from our three degrees, I wish to
share with you. They are my cheat sheet for character improvement:

“Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot

Entered Apprentice: Keep your mouth shut!
In all the various ways this means. Not just keeping secrets, which is very
important, but also gossiping about another, badmouthing, falsehood,
deceit, and lies. Learning when and how to keep quiet is a key to wisdom
and self-improvement.
Fellow Craft: Never stop learning!
Learn, read, educate yourself, ask questions, explore the wonders of the
universe, expand and improve your mind. Enlighten yourself.

The third degree teaches me to remember that our time is limited; to

Memento Mori. Remember that we must die. Look what becomes of all

I know that was dramatic, but I believe it is the most important lesson
to learn from the three degrees. Every time I witness that scene, it causes me to
tremble inside and reassess my life and ask, “Am I living to my fullest potential?”
When confronted with mortality, suddenly many things we consider important
turn out to be trivial and vice versa. When our time is up, there will be no more
repairing, building or improving. So if not now, then when? Let there be light!
Brother Albert Pike said, “What we have done for ourselves alone
dies with us; what we have done for others and the world remains and is
immortal.” If you spark another soul, your light will continue to shine even past
death. Remember.
Soon, my Masonic journey will come full circle and I will move back to
the Holy Land to live my dream.
If I told you that all of the hatred has been removed from my heart, if I
told you that I have fought off all the darkness within me and really polished my
ashlar, I would be a liar.
Loving one’s fellow man can be incredibly difficult in the Middle-East
and on that road I have many miles left to travel. “Who am I?” I am a Mason.

Brethren, Freemasonry is not my faith, but I have faith in Freemasonry!
And so when we leave this Grand Lodge in a few days and go back to our
respective communities, lodges and families –
Remember, my brothers! Remember that even a little bit of light we
shine, can dispel much darkness. Remember that the point of all of this existence,
the point of all we do in Freemasonry, are those four pure and pristine words - let
there be light!
be light!

The titles, the honors, the rings, the bling- they mean nothing! Instead:

Use the precious time you have been given to be a mentor to someone,

Remember! Remember from whence you came and to where you are
going, and in that blink of an eye - while we get to have a part in this perfectlyimperfect miracle that we call life, let there be light my brothers, Let there

Thank you and G-d bless you.

Grand Master’s Decision
Grand Master Charvonia’s Decision No. 1
Master’s Authority to Refuse to Admit or to Exclude a Member
On several occasions in recent years, Grand Masters have been asked
about the Master’s authority to refuse to admit or to exclude a member from
Lodge meetings and events because the member has exhibited poor behavior and
has caused disharmony in the Lodge.
Under California Masonic Code Section 804.815, a member has the
right to be present and participate in his Lodge’s proceedings, which are the
Lodge’s Stated Meetings and Special Meetings, while he conducts himself
with due order and propriety. This member’s right notwithstanding, California
Masonic Code Section 804.815 gives the Master the authority to refuse to admit
or to exclude a member from the proceedings of a Lodge for a breach of propriety
and it recommends that the Master do so if the member presents himself in a state
of intoxication.
This Decision clarifies that the Master may refuse to admit or may
exclude a member from Lodge proceedings at which the breach of propriety
occurred as well as from future proceedings for a reasonable time thereafter if the
Master reasonably believes the refusal or exclusion is necessary to preserve the
peace and harmony of the Lodge.
The Code does not give a member the right to attend any Lodge event
other than the Lodge’s proceedings. As the Master may refuse to admit or may
exclude a member for a breach of propriety from Lodge proceedings at which
the member has the right to attend, the Master has the inherent power to exclude
that member from Lodge events at which the member has no affirmative right to
attend. This Decision also clarifies that the Master has such power.
Maintaining the peace and harmony of the Lodge is a primary duty of
the Master. The Master must have the authority that is intended by this section
of our law. Without it, he is powerless to prevent a poorly behaved brother from
causing unnecessary dissention and disharmony in the Lodge. The Code already
provides remedies if the Master is ever to abuse any of his powers. Adopting this
Decision will provide much needed clarity to future Masters and the brothers of
our Lodges.
If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added
to the appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s
interpretative decisions are recorded:

Grand Master’s Recommendations

Master’s Authority to Refuse to Admit or to Exclude a Member

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 1
Permits All Forms of Electronic Voting

The proceedings of a Lodge are the Lodge’s Stated Meetings and Special
Meetings. For a breach of propriety, the Master may refuse to admit or may exclude
a member from Lodge proceedings at which the breach of propriety occurred
as well as from future Lodge proceedings for a reasonable time thereafter if the
Master reasonably believes the refusal or exclusion is necessary to preserve the
peace and harmony of the Lodge. The Code does not give a member the right
to attend any Lodge event other than the Lodge’s proceedings. Accordingly, the
Master may refuse to admit or may exclude a member for a breach of propriety
from any Lodge event at which the member has no affirmative right to attend. The
Master may also refuse to admit or may exclude a member from future Lodge
events at which the member has no affirmative right to attend for a reasonable
time after the occurrence of such breach of propriety if the Master reasonably
believes the refusal or exclusion is necessary to preserve the peace and harmony
of the Lodge.

Grand Lodge has used the same computer punch card electronic voting
system for many years at its Annual Communication. In that time, significant
improvements have been made in electronic voting systems, particularly those
that utilize computer network technology. Our Grand Lodge would benefit from
the use of a modern electronic voting system at its Annual Communication. The
voting process would be more efficient and accurate. There would no longer be
any risk of a paper or computer punch card ballot being lost or a vote being read
incorrectly as a result of a “hanging chad” or “overvoting” (e.g., where punch card
has both a “yes” and “no” vote indicated). Voting results would be reported to the
membership more quickly. In addition, other Grand Lodge jurisdictions, such as
Oregon and Alaska, have already begun using modern electronic voting systems
and have found the systems to be reliable and secure.

Report from Legislative Analysis Committee
The Master of a Lodge has a primary duty to maintain an atmosphere
of peace and harmony during Lodge proceedings. The California Masonic Code
explicitly empowers the Master to refuse to admit or to eject a member from
Lodge proceedings if that member commits a breach of propriety. The CMC
further recommends that the Master of a Lodge deny admission to a member in an
obvious state of intoxication. The CMC does not state whether the Lodge Master
can bar a member from future Lodge proceedings based on past behavior and does
not address other types of events.

It is therefore my recommendation that our Code be modified to permit
the use of modern electronic voting systems that do not rely upon computer
punch cards.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the Code. Section 100.010 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§100.010. BALLOT:
A secret vote by balls and cubes or in writing (which in a Communication
of the Grand Lodge includes a computer punch card, any other form of electronic
ballot used by a direct-recording electronic voting machine, a computer network
voting system or any other means of electronic vote tabulation system). Ballots
should be in writing unless the context requires balls and cubes.

This Decision clarifies the CMC to authorize the Master to exclude a
member from future Lodge proceedings if the Master believes that the member
will be disruptive or behave improperly. Lodge proceedings are defined as Stated
Meetings and Special Meetings.

In addition, Section 403.065 of the Code would be amended to read
as marked:

Furthermore, this Decision clarifies that a member can be excluded by
the Master from future Lodge events that are not Lodge proceedings, such as
social events, for similar reasons.

All questions in Grand Lodge, except election of officers, shall be decided
either by voice, hand, a rising vote or by written ballot, as the Grand Master shall
direct, unless, before the announcement of the result thereof, three members shall
demand that the vote be taken by written ballot. At least one member demanding
the written ballot must have the authority to speak for the others joining with
him in the request, and this shall be so stated in the request for the written ballot.
At least one designated spokesman must be present in Grand Lodge at all times
that a written ballot is to be taken pursuant to the demand. If no spokesman is
present, the Grand Master may in his discretion proceed as though no demand had
been made.

Should a Lodge Master abuse this power, the CMC provides remedies
and avenues of appeal.
If this Decision is adopted, the powers of a Lodge Master to preserve the
peace and harmony of the Lodge will be clarified.

§403.065. MANNER OF VOTING.

158

Proceedings of the

A written ballot is defined as one inscribed upon a slip of paper, or a
computer punch card provided by the Grand Secretary, and distributed, collected
and counted by appointed Grand Lodge tellers, or any other form of electronic
ballot used by a direct-recording electronic voting machine, a computer network
voting system or any other electronic vote tabulation system.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
Most Worshipful Charvonia’s recommendation 15-01 seeks to
authorize the use of electronic voting during the Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge.
In 1989, this body approved the use of electronic punch cards to be
used in place of a written ballot. At that time, punch cards were considered more
accurate and more efficient than written ballots. However improved this process
has been, there have still been problems with it. Each time the cards are run
through the electronic scanner, the paper degrades slightly increasing the risk of
a miscount. Also, if a delegate wishes to change a vote on an issue after they
have punched the card, the only way to do so is to punch the opposite chad thus
negating their vote entirely.
New voting technologies have been developing for years and several
other Grand Lodges have been using these systems with a high degree of success.
They are more accurate, more reliable and have less chance for human error.
Also, if a member wishes to change a vote, they can do so, provided the voting is
still open. Additionally, using these systems will make it easier to assure that the
proper number of ballots are given to any particular delegate.
With most electronic voting systems, the delegate will need to be present
in the auditorium at the time the vote is called, and the voting on a particular piece
of legislation will only remain open for an allotted amount of time. This will make
it so members cannot pre-mark their ballots or miss the session altogether and turn
in their ballot at the end of the session. It could also mean that someone could miss
a vote if they step out of the auditorium.
It should be noted that this recommendation seeks to authorize
electronic balloting in general. The specific system will be determined by the
Executive Committee.
As with any new technology, there is bound to be a learning curve.
However, once this new technology is functioning, the evidence points to it being
a cleaner more accurate process than what is currently in place, with the potential
for results being available immediately after balloting.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

159

Report from the Finance Committee
The Committee was provided information about the costs of an
electronic voting system from the Grand Secretary based on quotes received for
our own purposes, and also using information collected from the Grand Lodge
of Washington and the Grand Lodge of Oregon who have already implemented
electronic voting.
If electronic voting is implemented, the costs to our Grand Lodge will
include the one-time and ongoing purchase and replacement of equipment and
one-time and ongoing software development. The necessary additional equipment
includes hand-held devices that are used for electronic voting and the receivers
that transmit the information. The software development includes changes to
our current registration software to interface with the voting software that comes
with the purchase of the equipment. The one-time cost is approximately $48,000
and the annual recurring costs would be approximately $1,500. The cost of the
current punch card printing and tabulation is approximately $7,000 annually. So
while the electronic voting would have an upfront cost, the annual cost would be
much lower.
The Grand Master has mentioned that it might be possible to share the
upfront cost with other jurisdictions that also seek to implement electronic voting.
This of course, would reduce these approximate costs.
Recommendation APPROVED.
Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 2
Permits a Flag Tribute to be Performed During
the Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges
Some Masonic Organizations, Masonic Youth Orders, fraternal groups,
service clubs and youth organizations have a ceremony that pays tribute to the
Flag of the United States of America. Some of our Lodges have allowed Masonic
Organizations, Masonic Youth Orders, fraternal groups, service clubs, and
youth organizations, to perform their flag tribute ceremonies during the Lodge’s
installation of officers. However, the Installation Ceremony for Constituent
Lodges is part of the Ritual, and Grand Lodge alone has the power to authorize
changes in the Ritual. See California Masonic Code Sections 100.085, 402.020.
In my view, such displays of honor, respect and support for the Flag of our country
should be encouraged.
It is therefore my recommendation that this Grand Lodge modify the
Installation Ceremony of Constituent Lodges to give each Lodge the option
to have a flag tribute performed by a Masonic Organization, Masonic Youth
Order, fraternal group, service club or youth organization, during its installation
of officers.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
This Grand Master’s recommendation, if adopted, would modify the
Installation Ceremony of Constituent Lodges. This would give Lodges the option
to have a flag tribute performed by a Masonic Organization, Masonic Youth Order,
fraternal group, service club or youth organization.
It has been the practice of many Lodges to have a flag tribute performed
during their installations. Until now, those tributes have been in violation of
accepted ritual of this Grand Lodge. Tributes to the flag of our country should
not be discouraged. This recommendation would allow these tributes to continue
without violating our ritual.
Report from the Ritual Committee
Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 2 seeks to allow
Masonic groups or other organizations to offer a tribute to the Flag of the United
States of America during the public lodge installation ceremony. Tributes to our
flag are often offered by our Masonic Youth Orders at their public ceremonies and
also by scout troops and other civic and patriotic organizations.
California Masonic Code Section 1300.020 allows a lodge to invite a
Masonic Youth Order to exemplify, before the Lodge, at any public meeting, all
or any portion of the public ceremonies or non-secret ritualistic work of such
youth order. However, California Masonic Code Section 100.085 identifies the
Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges as Ritual and Section 402.020
states that Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize any changes in the Ritual.
The current Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges does not provide for
the inclusion of additional ritual or ceremony by any Masonic group or any other
organization.
The Ritual Committee supports this recommendation and, if adopted,
stands ready to amend the Installation ritual for public ceremonies to allow
members of a Masonic group or other organization to offer a tribute to our
American Flag.
Recommendation APPROVED.

Some Masonic Organizations, Masonic Youth Orders, fraternal groups,
service clubs, and youth organizations have a ceremony known as the “Arch of
Steel,” which is used to formally receive dignitaries. The Arch of Steel is formed
by two rows of individuals, who face each other while holding swords, and upon
command of their presiding officer, raise or cross their swords overhead to form
an archway of respect and honor, under which the person(s) being honored passes.
Some of our Lodges have allowed Masonic Organizations, Masonic Youth
Orders, fraternal groups, service clubs and youth organizations to perform an
“Arch of Steel” ceremony during the Lodge’s installation of officers. However,
the Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges is part of the Ritual, and only
Grand Lodge may authorize changes in the Ritual. See California Masonic Code
Sections 100.085, Section 402.020.
We should strive to maintain unity throughout the Masonic family.
We should encourage the members of the Masonic family to participate in each
other’s events and create opportunities for closer bonds to be formed between our
Blue Lodges, on the one hand, and Masonic Organizations and Masonic Youth
Orders, on the other. Likewise, we should welcome other community groups to
our Lodges’ public events, so that we may become better acquainted with each
other, and thereby strengthen the relationships between local Lodges and their
communities at large. In addition, displays of honor, respect and support of our
Blue Lodges should be received in the same manner in which they were offered.
It is therefore my recommendation that this Grand Lodge modify the
Installation Ceremony of Constituent Lodges to give each Lodge the option
to have an “Arch of Steel” ceremony performed by a Masonic Organization,
Masonic Youth Order, fraternal group, service club or youth organization during
its installation of officers.

It has been the practice of many Lodges to have an Arch of Steel
performed during their installations. Until now, those tributes have been in
violation of accepted ritual of this Grand Lodge. This option would allow
additional opportunities to bring other members of our Masonic family, as well
as civic groups, to participate in our installations. This recommendation would
allow these honors to continue without violating our ritual.
Report from the Ritual Committee
Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 3 seeks to allow
Masonic groups or other organizations to form an “Arch of Steel” to receive
and honor the officers about to be installed during the public lodge installation
ceremony. The arch of steel is formed by two rows of individuals each holding a

California Masonic Code Section 1300.020 allows a lodge to invite a
Masonic Youth Order to exemplify, before the Lodge, at any public meeting, all
or any portion of the public ceremonies or non-secret ritualistic work of such
youth order. However, California Masonic Code Section 100.085 identifies the
Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges as Ritual and Section 402.020
states that Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize any changes in the Ritual.
The current Installation Ceremony for Constituent Lodges does not provide for
the inclusion of additional ritual or ceremony by any Masonic group or any other
organization.
The Ritual Committee supports this recommendation and, if adopted,
stands ready to amend the Installation ritual for public ceremonies to allow
members of a Masonic group or other organization to form two lines of their
members starting just east of the two pillars in order to honor those about to be
installed as they enter the lodge room.
Recommendation APPROVED.
Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 4
Updates the Masonic Funeral Service
It has been brought to my attention that our Funeral Service needs to be
updated to reflect current code sections and modified to clarify portions and to
correct grammatical errors.
In addition, it has been brought to my attention that several non-Christian
families of our departed brethren opted to not have a Masonic Funeral Service for
a departed Brother because of the use of the word “resurrection” in our Funeral
Service. Although the phrase “So, in the bright morning of the resurrection,”
refers to the awakening of our ever-living spirit and its return to God in Heaven
from whence we all came, some families have confused its use with the Christian
resurrection. As a Brotherhood comprised of men of different faiths, we should
address this issue. I sought advice from several brethren, including those of the
Ritual Committee and Grand Master’s Special Task Force, and could not identify
a more suitable replacement word. Consequently, I believe we should update our
Funeral Service to better reflect Freemasonry’s religious inclusiveness by making
the reference to the resurrection optional, which is in keeping with the instructions
of our Funeral Service that recommend “complying to any reasonable request of
the family that is not inconsistent with our established customs and instructions,”
and would increase the use of the Masonic Funeral Service by non-Christian
families of our departed brethren.

166

Proceedings of the

It is therefore my recommendation that the Funeral Service be amended
to reflect current code sections, make clarifications, correct grammatical errors,
and make the reference to the resurrection optional based upon the preference of
the departed Brother’s family.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Funeral Service will be amended

MASTER:—Brethren and Friends: It has been a custom among the
Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons from time immemorial, at the request of
a departed brother or his family, to assemble in the character of Masons and with
the solemn formalities of the Craft, to offer up to his memory, before the world,
the last tribute of our affection.
Our brother has reached the end of his earthly toils. The brittle thread
which bound him to earth has been severed and the liberated spirit has winged
its flight to the unknown world. The silver cord is loosed; the golden bowl is
broken; the pitcher is broken at the fountain; and the wheel is broken at the cistern.
The dust has returned to the earth as it was, and the spirit has returned to God
who gave it.

The Great Creator having in His infinite wisdom, removed our brother
from the cares and troubles of this earthly life, thus severing another link in the
fraternal chain by which we are bound together, let us who survive him be yet
more strongly cemented by the ties of brotherly love; that during the brief space
allotted to us here, we may wisely and usefully employ our time, and, in the
mutual exchange of kind and friendly acts, promote the welfare and happiness of
each other.

the God who spake them into existence. “Man that is born of a woman is of a few
days, and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down; he fleeth
also as a shadow, and continueth not.” The almighty fiat has gone forth—“Dust
thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return;” and that we are all subject to that decree,
the daily observation of our lives furnished furnishes evidence not to be forgotten.

(No further change until the following paragraph:)
In advance of the Service, the Lodge is opened on the Third First Degree
of Masonry “for the purpose or of conducting the funeral of our late Brother
___________,” and in regular form is called from labor to refreshment for that
purpose. The jewels are “broken” and the columns changed. Thereafter, and
before visitors are admitted to the room, the casket, or table, is placed in usual
position west of the Altar, head to the west. The casket may be open or closed,
according to the wishes of the family.
A reasonable time before the commencement of the Service, visitors
should be admitted to the Lodge Room, and ushers should be provided to escort
them to seats. The Master personally should meet the members of the family
at the entrance to the Lodge Room or ante-room and conduct them to seats in
the candidates’ room or other “screened off” location. All officers’ stations are
vacant and officers are outside the Lodge Room. When time for commencement of

this fleeting world will pall upon the senses, and the recollection of a virtuous and
well-spent life will yield the only comfort and consolation. Thus we shall not be
unprepared to enter into the presence of the one all-wise and powerful Judge, to
whom the secrets of all hearts are known; and on the great day of reckoning we
shall be ready to give a good account of our stewardship while here on earth.
With becoming reverence let us supplicate the Divine Grace, whose
goodness and power know no bounds, that, on the arrival of the momentous hour,
our Faith may remove the clouds of doubt, draw aside the sable curtains of the
hidden world beyond, and bid Hope sustain and cheer the departing spirit.

FOREWORD
FOR MEMORIAL SERVICE
OTHER THAN LODGE ROOM MEMORIAL SERVICE
The Memorial Service may be held entirely in a chapel, home, church,
synagogue, or temple.
The Service may also be rendered in a hall, room, or other facility, in
keeping with the solemnity of the occasion.
The language of the Service is ritual and shall not be deviated from
(except for movement options), nor are interpolations to be permitted except that
a eulogy may be delivered at the place indicated in the Service.
All Masons including Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts may be
accorded the Masonic Memorial Service at the request of the deceased Brother’s
family. Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts cannot take part in the Ceremony
but may attend the Masonic Memorial Service, participate in the processions
thereof, and wear the white apron in the manner appropriate to their degree..
All Brethren in the Procession including the Master and Chaplain
should be dressed in dark clothes with white aprons worn on the outside of the
coat. Regalia of concordant and appendant bodies shall not be worn. The Master
wears an Evergreen and is without hat or gravel gavel.
There is no Masonic Funeral street procession.
A table, measuring not less then than 15” x 24” x 30” high, shall be
provided and placed at the right hand side of the podium, lectern or designated
position from which the Service is to be rendered in the chapel, hall, or other
facility. This table is covered with a white cloth upon which will be placed an Urn
(if desired). The Sacred Roll, the Lambskin Apron, and the Evergreen shall be
placed upon the table when and where indicated in the Service.

MASTER:—Brethren and Friends: It has been a custom among the
Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons from time immemorial, at the request of
a departed brother or his family, to assemble in the character of Masons and, with
the solemn formalities of the Craft, to offer up to his memory, before the world,
the last tribute of our affection.
Our brother has reached the end of his earthly toils. The brittle thread
which bound him to earth has been severed and the liberated spirit has winged
its flight to the unknown world. The silver cord is loosed:; the golden bowl is
broken; the pitcher is broken at the fountain; and the wheel is broken at the cistern.
The dust has returned to the earth as it was, and the spirit has returned to God
who gave it.

——0——
The Great Creator having in His infinite wisdom, removed our brother
from the cares and troubles of this earthly life, thus severing another link in the
fraternal chain by which we are bound together, let us who survive him be yet
more strongly cemented by the ties of brotherly love; that during the brief space
allotted to us here, we may wisely and usefully employ our time, and, in the
mutual exchange of kind and friendly acts, promote the welfare and happiness of
each other.
While we pay this fraternal tribute to his memory, let us not forget, my
brethren, that we, too, are mortal; and that our spirits, too, must return to the God
who spake them into existence. “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and
full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down; he fleeth also as a
shadow, and continueth not.” The almighty fiat has gone forth—“Dust thou art,
and unto dust shalt thou return;” and that we are all subject to that decree, the daily
observation of our lives furnishes evidence not to be forgotten.
Seeing then, my brethren, that life is so uncertain, and that all material
pursuits are vain, let us no longer postpone the all-important concern of preparing
for eternity; but let us embrace the present moment, while time and opportunity
are offered, to provide for the that great change when all the pomp and pleasure
of this fleeting world will pall upon the senses, and the recollection of a virtuous
and well-spent life will yield the only comfort and consolation. Thus we shall not
be unprepared to enter into the presence of the one all-wise and powerful Judge,
to whom the secrets of all hearts are known; and on the great day of reckoning
we shall be ready to give a good account of our stewardship while here on earth.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The Grand Master has observed that it has been many years since our
Funeral Service has been updated. During that time, a number of typographical
and grammatical errors have been perpetuated. In addition, the practices of society

186

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

and our Grand Lodge have changed, with resultant discordances with the more
antiquated funeral services. As a result, the Grand Master has recommended that
a series of changes be introduced. In summary, these include the following:

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 5
Adds a Resident Member to the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees
In Accordance with California State Law

The grammatical and typographical problems have been cleaned up.
The proposed Funeral Service takes into account the fact that we have allowed
increased participation of Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts, so the text has
been amended to indicate that, while such men are permitted to participate in
funerals with regard to being included in the procession, only Master Masons
can conduct the service. The certification process has been delegated to the local
Inspector and an action by Grand Lodge is no longer required, not even to provide
qualified Master Masons with certificates. The procession has been modified
such that, in locations where a procession is physically difficult to accomplish, it
need not be done. Furthermore, it provides an individual brother with the option
of sitting with his family during the service, rather than being seated with the
other Masons in attendance. A reminder has been added to inform the audience
to turn off cell phones and other communication devices that can produce
distracting noises.
Perhaps the change that will generate the most discussion is making the
use of the word “resurrection” optional. While it was not the intent of the framers
of this service to introduce a word that happens to have a Christian meaning, it
does appear that some non-Christian Masons have objected to the word, even to
the point of declining a Masonic funeral service. If the departed Mason, or his
family, has no objection to that word, it will continue to be used.
Over the years, our fraternity and our outside society have continued to
evolve. While we should not alter our ritual just for modernity, it is appropriate to
make our messages clearer and more relevant to our brethren and their families.
Over the years, our fraternity and our outside society have continued to
evolve. While we should not alter our ritual just for modernity, it is appropriate to
make our messages clearer and more relevant to our brethren and their families.

Last year, the California legislature amended California Health & Safety
Code Section 1771.8 to require that all boards of Continuing Care Residential
Communities (CCRC) in California have one resident appointed as a voting
member to their governing board. The resident association or a committee of
residents must nominate that voting member. The Masonic Homes of California
is a CCRC and must comply with this law.
This requires a change in our Code. I recommend that the Code be
amended to add one resident member to the board of trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California as required by law and according to policies and procedures
established the board of trustees.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 500.030 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§500.030. COMPOSITION OF BOARD.

in number.

until the close of the next Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge; .

of three, three and four Trustees each. The terms of at least
three of the appointed such Trustees shall expire at the close

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 6
Defines Lodge and Grand Lodge Volunteers so They are
Covered by Workers’ Compensation Insurance
The Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges maintain Workers’
Compensation insurance to provide coverage for members who work for the Grand
Lodge or Lodge. This includes members who volunteer their time. The California
Labor Code permits volunteers of a private, non-profit organization to be deemed
employees of the organization solely for the purpose of being covered under its
Workers’ Compensation coverage provided that the organization has adopted a
resolution stating such. Thus, this Recommendation is necessary to continue this
coverage. It is important to note that volunteer members are considered employees
solely for the purpose of the Workers’ Compensation and are not subject to any
other employment conditions as a result of this Recommendation. Workers’
Compensation does not cover non-member volunteers.
It is therefore my recommendation that this Grand Lodge adopt the
following standing resolution:
WHEREAS, volunteers provide various types of services for this
Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges and receive no remuneration for such
services other than possibly meals, transportation, lodging or reimbursement for
incidental expenses;
WHEREAS, California Labor Code Section 3363.6 provides that
a private, nonprofit organization may declare its volunteers as employees for
workers’ compensation insurance purposes by adopting a resolution authorizing
such coverage;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that any member of the
Grand Lodge or a lodge chartered by or under dispensation from the Grand Lodge
(“Constituent Lodge(s)”) who performs voluntary service without pay for the
Grand Lodge or a Constituent Lodge (“Volunteers”) is deemed an employee of
the Grand Lodge or the Constituent Lodge for which the Volunteer performs such
service, as applicable, solely for purposes of Workers’ Compensation insurance
coverage while performing such service, pursuant to Section 3363.6 of the
California Labor Code. For the purpose of this resolution, “voluntary service
without pay” includes the performance of services by a Volunteer who receives
no remuneration other than meals, transportation, lodging, or reimbursement for
incidental expenses.

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 7
Sets the Number of Trustees for the California Masonic Foundation
at not less than Nine nor more than Twenty-one
The California Masonic Code provides that the number of trustees for
the California Masonic Foundation shall be nine in number. It might be desirable
and necessary to increase the number of trustees in order to meet the needs of the
Foundation and the fraternity over time. I recommend that Section 700.030 of
the California Masonic Code be amended to provide that the number of trustees
shall be not less than nine nor more than twenty-one in number. This allows for
the flexibility to increase the number of trustees if necessary. I am confident that,
should the need arise, there are qualified brothers throughout the state to fill these
additional positions.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The California Masonic Code provides that the number of Trustees for
the California Masonic Foundation be nine in number. This sets the maximum

may not necessarily provide for the needs of the Fraternity and/or Foundation.

scientific purposes.

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 8
Changes the 12-month Residency Requirement for
Eligibility to Apply for Degrees
The three most fundamental requirements of an applicant for the degrees
of Masonry are that he is (1) a man (2) of lawful age (3) who believes in a Supreme
Being. These are part of the Landmarks of Freemasonry. Over the centuries,
certain Grand Lodges have imposed additional requirements of applicants. Since
1850, the Grand Lodge of California has imposed certain residency requirements.
Initially, and for at least a century, an applicant for the degrees was
required to be a resident within the jurisdiction of California during the twelve
months and within the jurisdiction of the particular lodge during the three to six
months preceding the date of his application. An applicant was in the jurisdiction
of a lodge if he resided nearer to the meeting place of the lodge than to that of any
other lodge. The requirement to be a resident within the jurisdiction of the lodge
was removed decades ago when the members of Grand Lodge concluded that it
was no longer necessary. The requirement to be a California resident for twelve
months has remained.
I believe it is time to consider whether this requirement serves any
useful purpose in today’s world. While I could not find a reason for the residency
requirement published in any number of well-known Masonic authorities, I can
imagine that the residency requirement was once necessary in order to evaluate
the character of an applicant. In those days, most people were not as mobile as
they are today. A man would move into town and develop his reputation there.
Towns were smaller, and a man could become well-known and trusted. As the
world has changed, this requirement is no longer relevant. Simply knowing that a
man has been a resident in California for twelve months, with no insight into his
character, does not provide the brethren with any useful means of evaluating his
worthiness. We have other effective ways to accomplish this purpose - namely the
character investigation procedure, which was recently updated, and the criminal
background check procedures that were implemented in 2012.

I recommend that the Code be amended to require that an applicant for
the degrees be a resident of California, without any time requirement. I further
recommend that if an applicant is not a California resident, a lodge may receive
and act upon his application if his application is accompanied by a Waiver of
Jurisdiction from the Grand Lodge with jurisdiction over him. If an applicant who
is not a California resident but resides in a state, province, territory or country
where no recognized Grand Lodge exists, a lodge may receive and act upon his
application with the approval of the Grand Master. I note that no Landmark nor
written law in the Ancient Constitutions forbids the initiation of non-residents.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 804.225 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§804.225. RESIDENCY.
A.

Except as otherwise provided in Section 804.270.B of this Code, Aan
applicant for the degrees must be have been a resident of within this
Jurisdiction during 12 months next preceding the date of his application;

B.

A member of any uniformed service of the United States, whose duty
station is at a facility or on a vessel having an officially designated home

Grand Master Charvonia’s Recommendation No. 9
Provides Membership Continuity for Members of the Uniformed Services
While on Active Military Combat Duty

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
California Masonic Code section 804.225 provides that an applicant
for the Degrees of Masonry must have been a resident within this Jurisdiction
during the last 12 months next preceding the date of his application. The Grand
Master’s Recommendation 15-08 would eliminate the residency requirement in
its entirety prior to his application. The Grand Master, through this Resolution,
would also permit a man in another Jurisdiction to apply for membership in a
Lodge in California providing that the application be accompanied by a Waiver of
Jurisdiction from the Grand Lodge who has jurisdiction over him thus providing
the initiation of non-residents.
From time immemorial, there has been a residency provision in the
California Masonic Code. In 1957, a Resolution was presented to lower the
requirement to 6 months which was defeated. Also, in 2006, Grand Master’s
Recommendation 06-04 which provided that a man whose spouse was a member
of any uniformed service of the United States whose duty station or on a vessel
having officially designated home port in California, could apply for membership
without regard to the 12 month residency requirement was passed.
The Grand Master has asked that we determine if this requirement has
any relevancy in today’s world as we tend to be more mobile than in the past.
It may have been necessary when our communities were smaller and it was
necessary for a man to “prove” himself. The Grand Master has also indicated that
residency alone does not provide the means of evaluating his worthiness to belong
to our Fraternity and that our ability to more easily investigate a man’s character
has recently been adopted by our Grand Lodge.
If this Recommendation is adopted, then the 12-month residency
requirement would be eliminated and the other provisions of the California
Masonic Code would provide the necessary investigative tools for checking on
a man’s character.
One consequence of this legislation would be that an applicant who has been in
California only a short time may prove difficult to investigate. If the applicant is
not a resident of California, then an investigation may pose additional problems,
such as checking references. If the applicant is a resident of another country, then
a criminal background investigation may be incomplete. Also, the definition of
“residency” should be determined by the Committee on Jurisprudence.

197

We have learned that certain brothers have been suspended for nonpayment of dues while serving in active military combat duty in Afghanistan and
Iraq. All Masons are required to pay their dues in a timely manner. This is a
basic Masonic principle. That being said, it seems contrary to our greater Masonic
ideals to suspend a brother while he is called to combat on behalf our country.
It is therefore my recommendation that a Mason of a California lodge
be exempt from suspension for non-payment of dues if he has been on active
military combat duty anytime in the previous 24 months. Active military combat
duty means having been active military personnel assigned to a combat zone for
a named United States conflict. A combat zone for a named United States conflict
means any area the President of the United States designates or has designated as
an area in which U.S. Armed Forces are engaging or have engaged in conflict. I
also recommend that if a lodge finds that a brother was on active military combat
duty during the 24 months preceding a previous suspension, the lodge shall
remove the suspension from his record as if it did not occur. I further recommend
that a brother have the right to request his lodge to remove a suspension from his
record as if it did not occur if he was on active military combat duty anytime in the
24 months prior to such suspension, and that his lodge be required to remove such
suspension from his record as if it had not occurred if the lodge then finds that he
was on active military combat duty at any time during such 24 months.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 809.370 of the California
Masonic Code would be amended to read as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
A.

If a Mason has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the
Secretary shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment
of dues unless at the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have
been paid or sickness or inability to pay is shown as the cause for the
failure to pay. The notice shall be given either by certified mail, return
receipt requested, postage prepaid, addressed to his last known address,
or by actual service of notice, duly certified by the Tiler. If all dues due
and payable have not been paid by the time of the Lodge’s next Stated
Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless for special
reasons shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him further time
for payment.

B.

No worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended for
non-payment of dues.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
This Grand Master’s recommendation, if adopted, would protect a
California Mason who is serving on active combat duty or has served in the past
twenty-four months in a combat zone from being suspended from his Lodge
for non-payment of dues. It would also permit an eligible Mason who has been
suspended for non-payment of dues while serving in a combat zone to have his
suspension removed from his record.
This recommendation would apply specifically to a Mason serving in the
armed forces on active duty, reserves, or National Guard in a combat zone for a
named U.S. military conflict as designated by the President. It would not apply to
a Mason working in a combat zone as a U.S. government civilian, a contractor, or
military personnel supporting combat operations remotely.
Prompt delivery of a dues notice to a Mason serving on active combat
duty in a war zone may be difficult, as well as his mailing a check for dues back
to the Lodge. Sending a certified letter notifying such a Mason of his suspension
may be equally impractical.
Once an eligible Mason has returned from service in a combat zone, he
has twenty-four months to pay his dues, including those incurred while he was on
duty. If he fails to do so he may then be suspended as per the California Masonic
Code Section 809.370.
While it is an important principle of Freemasonry that a Mason pay his
dues in a timely fashion, it is also an important principle that a Mason serve his
country to the best of his ability. This Recommendation seeks to reconcile these
principles and avoid penalizing a Mason serving in combat.
