§805.410. ELECTED OFFICERS.
Before a member may be nominated for the office of Master, Senior
Warden or Junior Warden, there shall be presented to the Lodge Secretary a
Certificate to Allow Nomination from the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand
Lecturer of the division in which his Lodge is situated, or the Inspector of the
district in which his Lodge is situated, certifying that he has met the requirements
of paragraph A of Section 805.520, Section 805.530 or Section 805.540 of this
Code, as applicable.
Should an emergent situation require an immediate election to fill
a vacancy in the office of Master, Senior Warden or Junior Warden, a member
not in compliance with the foregoing may be nominated and elected without the
required certificate, if the Inspector certifies to the Grand Master that such an
emergent situation exists and if the Grand Master agrees. In that event, such
member shall have a 90 day extension for qualification after election.
The Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary of each Lodge shall be
elected annually at the Stated Meeting in November each year. The election shall
be by ballot. A majority of all votes cast shall be necessary for an election. A blank
ballot shall not constitute a vote cast. The Lodge, by unanimous consent, may
permit any designated officer to cast the ballot for the Lodge.
If an eligible candidate fails to receive a majority of the votes cast,
and the candidate receiving a majority is ineligible, there is no election. When
a candidate for office is ineligible because he is delinquent in his dues, but his
dues are paid before a second ballot, and he receives a majority of the votes cast a
second time, he is properly elected.
All members of the Lodge in good standing shall be entitled to vote at an
election of Lodge officers.
An annual election held contrary to the provision of this section
shall be void.

A brief nominating speech is proper but not required. A nomination is not
a proper motion and does not therefore, require a second.
Upon receiving the nomination the Master shall verify with the Lodge
Secretary that the nominated Brother has presented a valid “Certificate to Allow
Nomination” before proceeding. Should the member have failed to present such a
certificate, the Master shall rule the nomination out of order and solicit another
nomination by saying, “Are there any other nominations?”
Upon receiving a valid nomination, the Master shall repeat the following
question three times.
Are there any other nominations?
If there are no other nominations, the Brother who made the nomination
(or another Brother) shall then rise and make the following motion:
Member - Worshipful Master, I move that the Secretary (or another
Brother) be instructed to cast the unanimous ballot of this Lodge for Brother
............. to serve as Master for the ensuing Masonic year.
The foregoing is a proper motion and requires a second.
Member - Worshipful Master, I second this motion.
Brethren it has been regularly moved and seconded that the Secretary
(or another Brother) be instructed to cast the unanimous ballot of this Lodge for
Brother. ..........to serve as Master for the ensuing Masonic year. Are you ready for
the question? (The question is called.) All those in favor of the motion say “aye.”
Response. Those opposed, “no.” Response.
If the vote is unanimous the Master shall state:
The vote is unanimous, the motion is carried. Brother Secretary
(or another Brother), you will cast the unanimous ballot of this Lodge for
Brother.............to serve as Master for the ensuing Masonic year.
The Secretary will then write out the ballot and present it to the tellers.
Teller - Worshipful Master, the unanimous ballot of this Lodge has been
cast for Brother...............to serve as Master for the ensuing Masonic··year.
If the vote is not unanimous, election shall be by written ballot with a
majority of all votes cast necessary for election. One teller should count the votes
with his count verified by another teller. The third teller shall then report the
actual count to the Master.

MULTIPLE NOMINATIONS
In the event that more than one name should be placed in nomination
for any elective Office after determining that there are no other nominations, the
Master shall then instruct Brethren to mark their ballots with the name of their
choice and fold the ballot. The tellers will then collect all ballots and conduct
the count. A brother must receive a majority vote to be elected. One teller should
count the votes with his count verified by another teller. The third teller shall then
report the actual count to the Master. The Master shall report the ballot count
to the Brethren and then ask the Brother who received the majority of the vote
if he will serve. If the Brother answers in the affirmative, the Master shall then
declare him elected and sound the gavel. If the Brother answers in the negative,
the balloting should be repeated until someone is selected who is willing to serve.

301

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to amend Section 805.410 of the
California Masonic Code and modify the Monitor and Officers’ Manual to require
that anyone nominated for the office of Master, Senior Warden, or Junior Warden
in a constituent Lodge must have already received a certificate of qualification in
the ritual of that office.
If adopted, any Master Mason wishing to be nominated for Master,
Senior Warden, or Junior Warden would be required to qualify in the ritual of that
office prior to the election, as per Paragraph A, Section 805.520, Section 805.530,
or Section 805.540, as applicable. It would not eliminate the requirement that a
line officer also be qualified in the duties of their office and in the government
of a Lodge but would add the requirement that ritual qualification occur prior to
the election. Any nominations not in compliance with this requirement would be
ruled out of order by the Master.
This would eliminate the situation of a brother being elected to an office
and then being unable or unwilling to qualify in the ritual, thus necessitating a
new election and postponing the annual installation of officers. It would require
Lodge Inspectors to qualify prospective line officers no later than October, in
order to support a November election. Lodges would need to address issues in
their officers’ line well in advance of the November election.
However, this resolution would also tend to limit the pool of available
candidates, since anyone eligible to be nominated would have had to qualify in
advance of the election. The situation could arise in which no candidates had
qualified for a given office by November. Unlike the current election rules, a
Past Master could not be elected to fill that office unless he had qualified in the
preceding year specifically for that office. In such an event a subsequent election
for that office would have to be conducted.
In the event of an emergent situation, such as a sudden or unexpected
vacancy in an office, this requirement could be waived by the Grand Master to
permit an election, with the new officer having 90 days to qualify after the election.
This resolution would be implemented by the creation of a new
“Certificate to Allow Nomination” by the Grand Secretary’s Office. This new
certificate would be issued by the Grand Lecturer, Assistant Grand Lecturer of
the appropriate division, or District Inspector and given to the Lodge Secretary in
advance of the annual election of officers and not sent to Grand Lodge. It would
not replace the Certificate of Qualification, which would still be required prior
to Installation.
The new certificate would be valid until the next Installation. If adopted,
this legislation would not go into effect until the date which is eighteen months
following the close of the Annual Communication at which it is adopted.

302

Proceedings of the

Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents of this resolution seek to require that a member be
qualified in the ritual before he may be nominated for the office of Master, Senior
Warden, or Junior Warden.
Resolution 15-08 clarifies the best ritual practices of the lodge in the
advancement and qualification of the Master and Wardens of their lodge. The
original intent of the predecessor to Section 805.560 of the California Masonic
Code to allow ritual qualifications 60 days after the election of a Master or Warden
was to give an opportunity for the lodge to elect and install a Master or Warden
that may have been required on an emergency basis because the progressive line
of their lodge was interrupted. In 2006, it was found that this emergency exception
was too short and the 60-day period was increased to 90 days. Unfortunately, over
time, a literal reading of Section 805.560 has been used to extend the period for
qualification even when there was no unexpected interruption or change to the
progressive line advancement.
Resolution 15-08, as amended, still provides each elected officer of the
progressive line of the lodge a full year to learn, understand, deliver, and qualify
for advancement. Under this proposal, progressing officers, do not face the
burden of a 90-day deadline for qualification, which often can delay installations,
and in some cases require a new election for a specific office. Furthermore,
the progressing officer is relieved of the burden and anxiety to learn the work
in 90 days.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code protects the right of any
candidate to take his obligation on the book which is sacred in his particular
religion; and
WHEREAS, Section 402.060, Paragraph E of the California Masonic
Code requires that if a candidate takes his obligation on a sacred book other than
the Holy Bible, a small Holy Bible must also be present upon the altar; and
WHEREAS, requiring the presence of the Holy Bible in addition to a
candidate’s choice of sacred book implies the superiority of the Holy Bible over
the candidate’s chosen book, an implication incompatible with the universality
of Freemasonry.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 402.060 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as follows:
§402.060. ALTERNATE HOLY WRITINGS.
A candidate for a degree in Masonry may select an alternate Holy Writings
on which he will be obligated, but only under the following circumstances:
A.

If the candidate does not wish to be obligated on the Holy Bible, he must
select an alternate Holy Writings in book form from a list promulgated
from time to time by the Grand Master of the Holy Writings of those
recognized religions whose theology is not inconsistent with a belief
in a Supreme Being and a future existence. The Grand Master’s list
shall at all times include the al-Kitab al-Aqdas of Bahaism, the Tripitaka
of Buddhism, the Analects of Confucianism, the Vedas of Hinduism,
the Koran of Islam, the Tanach of Judaism, the Koji-ki of Shintoism,
the Adi Granth of Sikhism, the Tao-te Ching of Taoism and the Zend
Avesta of Zoroastrianism. In selecting an alternate Holy Writings, the
candidate must state that the book chosen is the Holy Writings of his
religious faith;

B.

The particular book selected for use on the altar during the ceremonies
of a candidate’s degrees must be of a suitable size as determined by the
Ritual Committee;

C.

Grand Lodge shall make available all books on the list. Grand Lodge
shall loan any book on the list upon request to a Lodge which requires it
for a degree;

D.

The book selected shall remain on the altar throughout the meeting
during which it is used for a candidate’s degree, unless the Lodge
schedules more than one candidate to receive a degree at a meeting and
all candidates receiving a degree on that occasion will not be obligated
on the same book of Holy Writings. In that event, the book shall be
changed when the Lodge is at refreshment between the degrees; and

The “Certificate to Allow Nomination” will be created; The Balloting
procedures are enumerated; and the effective date is 18 months from the date to
which Resolution 15-08 passes, thereby not creating a substantial burden on the
current Wardens.
The Ritual Committee is in favor of Resolution 15-08.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

305

In 1997 and 2001 the Ritual Committee supported similar resolutions
to allow only one Holy Writing on the Altar during degree conferrals. Each year
the proposal failed. It is now time to demonstrate our commitment to religious
tolerance by allowing only one Holy Writing on the Altar for degree conferrals.
This simple act reinforces our ritual where the Craft, standing about the altar,
witnessing the candidate’s oath, in a collective demonstration of religious
tolerance, accepts the candidate’s oath as binding, and welcomes him into the
Craft with the open arms of Brotherly love.

The Proponents of this Resolution want to eliminate the need to have
a closed Holy Bible on the altar if a candidate wishes to take his obligation for
membership in our Fraternity on a Book of Holy Writings of his Faith. This is the
only change for the conditions upon which an alternate book of Holy Writings is
used during the Ceremony.

Resolution FAILED

The subject of alternate Holy Writings for a candidate’s obligation has
been before our Grand Lodge for the last several decades. Prior issues have been
defeated until 1992 when then Grand Master MW R. Stephen Doan presented
Recommendation No. 5 which provided that every man be given the right to
select alternate Holy Writings on which he is to be obligated, but under certain
circumstances. There was also some concern that if an alternate Book of Holy
Writings were approved by our Grand Lodge that it might jeopardize relations
and/or recognition by other Grand Lodges. It now appears that after more than 20
years of practice, that no longer seems likely. This Resolution garnered sufficient
votes to be Carried-Over until the 1994 Annual Communication where it
was approved.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore Antranik “Andy”
Jabourian to membership in Masonry.

In 2001, Resolution 01-05 was introduced at Grand Lodge to require
only one Volume of the Sacred Law at a time be on the Altar for the Obligation.
This was carried-over to the 2002 Annual Communication and was defeated.
Passage of this Resolution would require the Ritual Committee to
review for consistency our Ritual. Also, this resolution is a logical progression in
accommodating our Brethren of different faiths.
Report from the Ritual Committee
The proponents wish to eliminate the requirement to have a closed Holy
Bible on the altar along with the Candidate’s Holy Book of choice.
The Ritual Committee supports this resolution. At the 144th Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge you adopted a resolution to allow candidates
to use an alternate Holy Writing during their degree conferral so long as a closed
Holy Bible was also present on the Altar. The Ritual Committee was advised that
the purpose of having the closed Holy Bible on the Altar was in an abundance of
caution so as to not offend other Masonic jurisdictions. Over the past 22 years
religious tolerance among Masons has improved significantly to the point that this
concern and legal requirement is no longer necessary.

in order they might wisely and knowledgably vote on the desirability of a man to

Guidance for the granting a restoration of membership to an expelled
brother is found in 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 3. The decision states that
when the suspension or expulsion is based on criminal activity, we should look
for evidence of rehabilitation, and one cannot just add up those criteria that have
been met and those that have not in order to determine whether a person has been
rehabilitated. Meeting these criteria does not excuse a person from responsibility
for his prior criminal conduct nor entitle him to restoration. In other words,
evidence must be presented of a state of mind and a state of facts showing he has
been rehabilitated. A state of mind demonstrating rehabilitation is one showing
remorse. Acceptance of responsibility is a necessary prerequisite to establishing
rehabilitation. Nothing in the resolution presents any facts of what Mr. Jabourian
has done since his expulsion to “help and assist the needs of the lodge and its
members” or what he has done to help and assist any public activities of San
Marino Ledge No. 408 and Ararat Lodge No. 848. Opinion without substantiation
is not enough.
Because of the foregoing the Committee cannot support this resolution
and recommends a no vote.
Resolution FAILED.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee

Report from the Ritual Committee

The proponents of this resolution seek to allow the long form of the First
Degree lecture to be delivered by two separate individuals.

To save time, this report will address both Resolutions 2015-11 and
2015-12. The proponents of both resolutions want to allow two qualified brethren
the discretion to divide the full-form Master’s lectures of the 1st and 3rd degrees
in half and then deliver each of them separately.

The passage of this resolution would mark a significant change to how
our lectures have traditionally been delivered. Never in our history has it been
authorized for the same lecture to be delivered by more than one individual.
The pros and cons to this resolution can be categorized into the emotional
impact it will have on the membership and how this change will actually affect the
delivery of degrees.
There are legitimate concerns that if the transition between lecturers
is not done properly, it could be distracting or confusing to a candidate. Those
concerns apply when any ritual is delivered improperly, whether by a single
brother or multiple brothers. Ritual that is not practiced well, or is ill prepared for,
often results in candidates not understanding the intent of the ritual and can even
deter them from returning to the Lodge.
If passed however, individual brothers would have the opportunity to
concentrate more energy on their respective portions and thus potentially result
in a higher quality lecture. Having two different lecturers may even break up
potential monotony of listening to one person for an extended period of time.
Since the short form version of the First Degree lecture was authorized
in 1983, it has become more commonplace than the original, longer form of the
lecture. While much of the symbology of the omitted portions is contained in
the candidate education courses and questions, they do miss out on them during
the live degree. Breaking up the memorization burden among more than one
individual also increases the chance that the candidates will have an opportunity
to hear the complete long form lecture during their degree.
Passage of this resolution makes no changes in the qualifications for
Junior Warden. It does not change the delivery of the short form lecture; that work
is still to be given by a single person. It also does not preclude delivery of the
entire long form lecture by a single individual.
If passed, notations would be added to future versions of the Cipher
Ritual to mark where the lecturers change but, in the meantime, could be added
by hand.

Lecture delivery involves two ritual portions: (1) The words used in
each lecture and (2) the manner of delivery. Adoption of these resolutions would
be a deviation from our long-established ritual that requires such lectures to be
delivered in their entirety by a single brother and, consequently, would introduce
delivery inconsistency throughout the State.
It has been the policy of the Ritual Committee to not change a practice
unless that practice proved to be a burden to the Fraternity in general or the lodge
in particular over the years.
Additionally, the Ritual Committee will support ritual amendments that
allow us to remain relevant and improves member experience without jeopardizing
our teachings, traditions and heritage.
The key words in this proposal are “who are proficient in such lecture”.
To be proficient both brethren must not only possess delivery confidence but
their interaction must also be rehearsed and choreographed well in advance of
the event. To do otherwise would be a disservice to both the candidate and the
audience and leave us no better off in the future than where we were in the past.
In a recent survey of American Grand Lodges 64% of those that responded
allowed lodges the optional discretion of using multiple brethren to divide and
then deliver their lectures and in doing so have found nothing deleterious to the
candidate or otherwise.
It has become apparent that current delivery of the full-form 1st and
3rd degree lectures by a single brother has become a burden for most lodges.
Additionally, adoption of these resolutions may improve lecture delivery and
improve member experience without jeopardizing our teachings. Consequently,
the Ritual Committee supports these resolutions in concept and believes that their
adoption may be the first of several future innovative steps toward improving
lecture delivery.

Should you adopt this resolution the ritual committee would amend the
next revision of the cipher as the proponents request with the second lecturer
beginning with the moveable jewels for the FIRST DEGREE and with part three
(the hieroglyphical emblems) for the THIRD DEGREE.

There are legitimate concerns that if the transition between lecturers
is not done properly, it could be distracting or confusing to a candidate. Those
concerns apply when any ritual is delivered improperly, whether by a single
brother or multiple brothers. Ritual that is not practiced well, or is ill prepared for,
often results in candidates not understanding the intent of the ritual and can even
deter them from returning to the Lodge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
Since 1898, the Masonic Home in Union City has opened it’s doors to
our less fortunate brothers, their wives, widows and orphans. Thousands have
crossed our threshold, suitcases in hand, seeking a place of respite and relief.
Although the way we provide care has changed over the years, our
commitment to excellence has never waivered. Today we offer a continuum of
services in both our residential and community-based programs for those in need.
Our Masonic Outreach Services and the Masonic Center for Youth and Families
provides services in the community, while our campuses in Union City and Covina
provide residential care, including Skilled Nursing Care and Memory Care at our
Union City Campus.
Our membership demographics continue to shift, creating new challenges
and opportunities. Our younger members will be caring for aging parents as well
as growing families. Many of our aging members will want to age successfully
in place, in their communities, close to their lodges, families, and friends. And
many more will continue to want to live in our Masonic Communities in Covina
and Union City.
At the same time, we are experiencing an evolution in health care. Our
residents are living longer and more active lives. The average age of our residents
is now over 85 and we have a healthy and vibrant group of 90-plus residents on
our campuses, including a few residents that are enjoying life after 100.
We are also experiencing an evolving world of health care, as reform
continues to place new pressures on our Masonic Homes and the care we provide.
We continue to explore potential partnerships with recognized experts in the
health care field in order to be at the forefront of best practices.
This has been an exciting year for the Masonic Homes. Although we
were unsuccessful in our bid to remove the flatlands from an ordinance that
restricts the land from development, we were able to gain invaluable insights
and foster community partnerships with organizations such as Dig Deep Farms,
a program developed by the Alameda County Deputy Sheriffs Association that is
working to help disadvantaged youth in our community and the East Bay Regional
Parks District, the parks district that manages over 119,000 acres of parklands in
Alameda and Contra Costa Counties.
This year we have provided care to more than 300 residents at our skilled
nursing, assisted and independent living communities.

320

321

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Our Skilled Nursing Facility in Union City continues to maintain the
coveted 5-Star Rating from Medicare and both the Skilled Nursing Facility
and Residential Care Facility received zero deficiency surveys from the State
of California.

Our campus master planning process also formed the basis of our plan
to replace aging facilities on our Union City campus that are no longer able to
accommodate the latest models of care. We are also looking to add programs and
facilities that allow us to provide much needed programs and services in Covina.

A yearlong Campus Master planning project, which began last year, was
completed and presented at our February Board Retreat. This new Master Plan
forms the foundation of our five-year strategic plan, Roadmap 2020. This new
strategic plan will allow us to fulfill our mission and provide our members with
state of the art facilities that meet or exceed today’s best practices and prepare us
for the future.

Our Lorber Skilled Nursing facility is based on an outdated model of
care that doesn’t allow us to provide for new best practice models that are based
on a ‘neighborhood’ arrangement. Several other considerations, including a
shortage of parking and State building restrictions which create challenges for
making improvements to other structures on the campus were a critical part of the
decision making process.

Some of this planning has already resulted in changes on our campuses.
In Union City, our new Lorber Memory Care Unit opened in February for skilled
nursing residents suffering from Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia.
Specialized programing is already making a positive difference in the lives of
these residents.

In Covina, the lack of programs and services, due to a lack of facilities, has
challenged our ability to provide a full continuum of care in Southern California.

In June of this year, our new short-term rehab program will be opening
in the newly renovated 3rd floor of our Lorber Skilled Nursing Facility in Union
City. This new program will offer private rooms, a dining room with menu
service, and state of the art in-room rehab equipment as well as specialized care
for Cardiac, Orthopedic, and Neurosurgical Rehab and care for patients needing
short term transitional care. This new program is the result of more than 18 months
of planning with the local healthcare system in the Tri-City area.
Our Union City Campus is also home to our evolving Stepping Stones
Program. This new program encompasses four “stepping stones” aimed at
addressing the ever-changing needs for those suffering from memory loss or
cognitive impairment from Alzheimer’s or other forms of dementia. This new
approach to providing a continuum of care is based upon our understanding
that this disease is a progressive illness that requires different approaches at
different stages.
We have partnered with experts in this field in the creation of a program
that begins with our Brain Fitness Room, an area where our residents can exercise
their minds with the latest in computer stimulation through games and exercises.
The next stepping stone is our Compass Program, which was created as an
interactive daytime program for those residents who are still living in either our
assisted or independent living units and are in need of more structure in their
day and as a means of providing much needed respite care for spouses who act
as the primary care giver. Our Traditions Program continues to provide assisted
living in a safe environment with more specialized programing for residents
whose needs cannot be met in our independent living or other assisted living
units. The Memory Care Unit at Lorber completes our Stepping Stones program
by providing skilled nursing care for those suffering from more acute medical
needs as well as dementia.

Our Covina residents are currently ‘outplaced’ if they need Skilled
Nursing or Memory Care. Spouses are separated and visiting becomes a
challenge. We also have less ability to monitor the quality of care and service in
outside facilities.
In February, the Board of Trustees approved a plan to begin the process
of planning for the replacement of the Lorber Skilled Nursing Building in Union
City with a new Health Center and the building of a new Health Center in Covina.
Both centers will provide state of the art Skilled Nursing and Memory Care
utilizing the new best practice neighborhood models.
Both campuses also lack a central gathering place. New campuses being
developed and built today recognize the important role that the ‘heart of the
campus’ plays in the well being of its residents. Plans are underway to create that
‘Town Center’ concept for both Covina and Union City. These new Town Centers
will be a place where our residents can gather and interact as well as participate
in activities.
These new developments will also help to address our waiting lists.
Currently, the wait time for a residential unit is averaging 12 to 24 months. With
the additional Memory Care units, we will be able to open additional assisted and
independent living units on both campuses.
Our Masonic Senior Outreach Services (MSOS) continues our fraternal
care strategy that allows our brothers and their wives or widows to successfully
age in place, close to their lodges, families, and friends. MSOS provides case
management and financial assistance for those whose needs are greater than their
means. The program continues to grow each year as many more of our elderly
fraternal family members become aware of the services we offer.
MSOS served 316 clients last year, an increase over the total served
in 2013. The majority of these received direct financial assistance and others
received ongoing case management, only. Those clients who are able to repay
their financial assistance enable MSOS to preserve charitable dollars and extend

support to future members in need. And the generous support of Masons to the

Consistent with our values, the Masonic Homes has been helping

Masonic Family Outreach Services (MFOS) began in October 2009 in
response to the economic downturn and the overwhelming needs of our members
under the age of 60. The program extends non-financial assistance, with no
eligibility requirements, to Masons and their wives or widows statewide who
are struggling with today’s complex issues and need assistance with applying for
public benefits and other programs, as well as resource information and referrals.
MFOS care management, which serves families in their own communities,
provides hands-on support that best meets individual needs.
MFOS also provides one-time financial assistance, when eligibility
requirements are met, as a bridge to self-sufficiency. A care plan designed for the
client to reach self-sufficiency is the lynchpin to the success of this program.
This past year, 46 MFOS clients were served; a decrease from the prior
year, which was anticipated and reflects the economic recovery.
As the single point of inquiry for all Masonic Homes services, the
Masonic Assistance line, 888-466-3642, makes it easier for callers with a wide
range of needs and across different age groups to obtain information about our
programs and services, as well as referrals to community resources. Last year, the
Masonic Assistance line handled 1,776 calls just for information and referrals.
The telephone number is printed on the dues cards and appears frequently in
several other communications to members. A satisfaction survey conducted this
past year led to process improvements and the maintenance of excellent service
to members.
Working closely with Grand Lodge Member Services, the Masonic
Assistance office launched the remitted dues project last June, a collaborative
effort to meet member needs, especially those with remitted dues, and reconnect
them to the support of their lodges when possible.
The successful Lodge Outreach Initiative, developed and piloted
by MOS and Division IX lodges in 2012, is activating lodge outreach efforts,
educating members about Masonic Assistance, extending Masonic relief, and
engaging members in a meaningful way that will position us to better meet the
needs of our diverse membership. This initiative strengthens our MOS partnership
with lodges and helps lodges fulfill their fraternal obligation to provide relief to
their members. Lodge Outreach launched in Division II in 2014 and will roll out
next in Division X, followed by the remaining Divisions through March 2017,
when Lodge Outreach will reach all Divisions statewide.

Opened in 2011, MCYAF was created to address the growing need for
professional and integrated help for youth who struggle with behavioral or mental
health issues.
The center is located in San Francisco, but serves Masonic families
throughout the state. While our center also serves non-Masonic youth, Masonic
families are always granted priority.
MCYAF has made a profound difference in the lives of more than 300
children and their families, to date, and continues to attract international attention
for its unique, comprehensive, and integrated diagnostic and treatment model.
In 2014, MCYAF recruited a new Administrator, Kimberly Rich, MS,
a licensed marriage and family therapist with a background in behavioral health
clinic management for children and adolescents. Her early priorities include
reviewing and addressing opportunities for operational efficiencies, introducing
outcomes measures, as well as identifying future directions for MCYAF. Kimberly
shared some of her preliminary thoughts at the Board Retreat in February 2015
on strategies for how MCYAF could potentially reach and serve more clients. She
will also present several immediate priorities for development during 2015.
When the children’s residential program in Covina closed in 2009, a
transition program was created to ensure that each child and her or his family had a
care manager and successful transition plan to a safe and stable living environment
that would also meet the child’s educational needs. Through our financial support
and assistance with accessing public benefits and low-cost programs, the children
continued on their path of success that was established during their residency at
the Masonic Homes.
The last child being served through the Masonic Homes Transition
Program is currently a senior and is expected to graduate this June. Through the
Transition Program, we have provided nominal financial assistance each month
and care management. This high school senior plans to work following high school
and possibly, explore community college. If he finds college to be an interest, then
he will apply to the MH Scholarship Committee in 2016. Following high school,
the Scholarship Coordinator will assist him in seeking employment and using his
independence living skills.
The enduring support from the Masonic Homes has provided these
children the stability and guidance which allows them to fulfill their childhood
dreams. Alumni of our former children’s program continue to receive Masonic
Homes scholarships for undergraduate studies and master’s and doctorate

324

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

degrees at schools of their choice throughout the United States. A hallmark of
this program’s success is the case management support we provide to ensure that
students access school support services and successfully navigate college on their
way to becoming independent adults.

Masonic Homes for Adults Union City
JULY 1, 2014 TO JUNE 30, 2015
POPULATION CHANGES

Last school year, the scholarship program served 21 students. For the
upcoming 2015-2016 school year, the program will serve 20 students. Two are
pursuing a doctorate degrees, one is working on a master’s degree. The remaining
17 students attend a variety of state universities, community colleges, and a trade
school in pursuit of a bachelors or associates degree. It’s clear that our former
children’s program alumni are on the right path, pursuing higher education and
their dreams, with care and support from the Masonic Homes.
We have continued our efforts to reconnect with our lodges. In November
of 2014, the Masonic Home in Union City hosted the first HarvestFest, an event
that we plan to have annually. More than 16,000 invitations we sent and more
than 800 Masons and their families attended a fun filled day. We also had the
opportunity to rededicate DeMolay Drive. At this year’s HarvestFest in October,
we will be dedicating Rainbow Road and Jobs Lane in Union City.
Our SummerFest event will be held in Covina. This annual event will be
open and promoted to all Masons in California and will provide an opportunity
for Southern California Masons to experience our beautiful Covina Campus and
interact with our residents.
We are forever grateful for the generosity that has given us the opportunity
to make such a profound difference in the lives of our Brothers, their wives and
widows, as well as the children that we serve. Generations of Masons gave of
their time and resources to make our Masonic Homes what it is today and it is our
mission to preserve that legacy for generations yet to come.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank all of the Masonic Homes
trustees, our Executive Vice President, our Management Team and our dedicated
staff for their commitment and support. Their leadership, vision, and dedication
to our fraternity have laid the foundation for the future of our Masonic Homes.
It has been a pleasure and an honor to serve with the distinguished
trustees listed below:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Acacia Creek, our continuing care retirement community located
adjacent to the Masonic Home at Union City, is now in its fifth year of operation.
I am pleased to report to you that we continue to grow our occupancy. At the time
of the last Annual Communication our occupancy was at 83%. Today we are at
87% occupancy with additional move-ins scheduled. Our goal is to reach stability
in the coming year as we begin to make payments on our debt as well as on the
loan from Masonic Homes.
The Marketing Program continues to produce deposits and move-ins
consistently. A second duplex cottage has been constructed and was immediately
occupied, another positive indicator of the community’s progress. Based on the
current numbers, Acacia Creek will be applying for a permanent Certificate
of Occupancy from the California Department of Social Services, another
significant milestone.
Current residents’ satisfaction and happiness is apparent to prospective
buyers, and because of this our residents continue to be our best salespeople in
the community and are always involved in the sales process. Residents invite
friends and lodge brothers to join them for meals or for an overnight stay in the
guest apartments, and “host” them for dinner and entertainment, often resulting
in a new deposit.
Masterpiece Living is a national program of physical and mental
wellness which has been adopted by Acacia Creek. Measured against the national
benchmarks for residents in similar communities, our residents again this year
showed a lower level of physical problems and a higher level of nutritional and
physical activity.
The absorption of non-Masons into the Acacia Creek community has
been rewarding for the Fraternity. There is great camaraderie among them and
the community has been strengthened by adding to the mix. Three new residents
have become Master Masons, totaling eight new Master Masons from Acacia
Creek since opening, and more are expected to petition for degrees in the future.
Members of Acacia Creek are actively involved with Siminoff Daylight Lodge
at the Masonic Home at Union City, as members, officers, and in building and
maintaining the new outdoor degree site on the property.
The Acacia Creek staff continues to share feedback about the positive
work environment they enjoy through the team management concept. Employees
are decision makers and feel a sense of ownership in the operations of Acacia
Creek. This results in a very low turnover among staff adding to the comfort level
of the residents.

338

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

When the fraternity planned the Acacia Creek community, we envisioned
that it would include all levels of health care, including independent and assisted
living, skilled nursing, and memory care. To fulfill this goal, Acacia Creek has
worked with the Masonic Homes in designing the renovation of the Traditions
Program of the Masonic Home at Union City, and the planning of the Campus
Master Plan which will create new opportunities for expanded services on the
campus, including the development of a short term rehab center and a unique
Dementia Skilled Nursing program.

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation

A second annual joint meeting of the Acacia Creek and Masonic Homes
Board was held in February2015. This event brought together the two boards
to review and discuss joint strategic initiatives concerning both entities. Topics
discussed involved the improvements and new facilities on the Union City campus
mentioned above as well as a review of the Master Plan for all of the Masonic
Homes holdings. Additional discussion was held about methods of serving the
needs of our prospective clients over the long term and further improving the lives
of our current residents.
The Board wishes to extend our sincere appreciation to Chuck Major,
Executive Vice President of Acacia Creek, who is the heart and soul of the
management team and has been responsible for the high level of morale and
accountability of the staff and the strategic Marketing Program that has been
so successful.
I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee,
the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, and the Acacia
Creek Board for their expertise, their vision, and their passion. Together we
look forward to continuing the mission of bringing Acacia Creek to stability and
financial security.
Respectfully submitted,
Ara Maloyan, President

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F&A.M. of California:
Your California Masonic Foundation continued its focus this year on
our literacy and Investment in Success educational programs to reach a wider
population of students in our communities and to increase the profound difference
we are making in California public education. Our programs continue to be
aligned with the Strategic Plan of the Masons of California and fully supported
by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee. We have increased the visibility of
the Fraternity in our communities and involved larger numbers of our members
through the Public Schools Advisory Councils. We continue to oversee a wide
range of programs supporting various needs within the Jurisdiction.
Strategic Initiatives
Continued progress was made this year in furthering the two 20102015 strategic initiatives the Foundation is responsible for - support to public
education and increasing Lodge involvement in the community. Our now eight
Public Schools Advisory Councils continued their strong leadership by organizing
and conducting eight Public Schools Month Kickoff celebrations in April, 2015,
attended by more than 160 Masons, community leaders, school district staff,
teachers, parents and students. As a part of these events, the Foundation donated
$767,500 to support the Grand Master’s Project Firefighters in Safety Education,
which provides fire safety trainings in K-3 classrooms, and needed scholarships
for deserving high school students. These very successful celebrations further
raised community awareness of Freemasonry and demonstrated our dedication to
both public education and the lifelong learning of our students.
We have evolved our efforts based on our recognition that the role of
families and support networks plays an important part in a student’s ability to
succeed. Whether they are elementary school children or high school students –
the support from those around them can make all the difference. To that end, we
have engaged in partnerships, developed programs and encouraged our brethren
to bring families and communities together to support our schools. We have
identified key entry points in a child’s academic career in an effort to affect the
greatest change by leveraging our resources appropriately.

340

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

341

Literacy

Investment in Success

Having successfully completed our three year pledge to raise $1.2M for
our ground breaking partnership with Raising a Reader (RAR), the national leader
in child literacy programs, we continued the process of disseminating funds and
installing the program in additional classrooms. As of this Annual Communication,
the program is active in 103 schools in 27 school districts, encompassing 381
classrooms. Raising A Reader is also working with Montebello Unified School
District to implement the program this fall in 19 classrooms. This would fulfill our
original goal of 400 classrooms.

The goal of the Foundation is that every dollar invested in a student’s
future has the potential to change a life forever. With Investment in Success, now
completing its fifth year, we have continued to answer this challenge. This year,
80 new young people received a scholarship from the Foundation that few of
them ever dreamed possible, amounting to over $200,000. The scholarship dollars
we continue to invest will change the lives of the nearly 300 students currently
enrolled in our program.

Thanks to this generosity by the Masons of California, Raising a Reader
will be fully installed in California classrooms most at risk of academic failure.
One hundred high quality, professionally chosen books will continue to be
distributed to each family every year. And, by 2020, the Masons of California
will have impacted the lives of more than 50,000 children and their families.
The Fraternity has received positive feedback from parents and educators across
the state, increasing public awareness of Freemasonry as a force for good in our
communities and which will be felt for generations.
In 2013, a grant was received from the prestigious Anne E. Casey
Foundation, an organization that works with disadvantaged children, to allow
research to begin on the effects of this integrated literacy/family engagement
model. A pilot outcomes study in a small group of schools in the San Diego
Unified School District during the 2013‐2014 school year examined the family
reading behaviors and child literacy levels of 187 kindergarten students, 115 of
whom participated in Raising A Reader and 72 who did not.
In February, 2015, we received results of this study, which were positive
and demonstrated Raising A Reader’s impact on family literacy behaviors and
children’s literacy achievement. First, family reading behaviors were measured
using a survey given to parents at the beginning and end of the school year. At
the conclusion of the school year, the study showed that 42% more students who
participated in RAR were reading independently at or above grade level in the fall
of first grade than those who had not received RAR.
Secondly, families who participated in RAR read 22% more minutes per
reading session than families who did not participate in RAR. These additional
minutes add up to approximately 6 additional hours of family reading time over
the course of the school year. These initial findings demonstrate changed family
behaviors, suggesting the positive impact of home literacy behaviors.
The Foundation expresses its gratitude to Most Worshipful Charvonia
and the Executive Committee for their committed leadership in continuing to
support Raising a Reader. This allows an even greater potential for making a
profound and lasting impact on literacy in this jurisdiction.

Investment in Success scholarships are awarded to students attempting
to overcome many of life’s challenges and obstacles to achieve their academic
dreams. Nearly all are first-in-family to college, have little or no resources – yet
all have demonstrated a powerful desire to succeed, a vision for their future, and
the commitment to better themselves and to give back to their communities.
To address these issues, the Foundation continues to include opportunities
for summer or third year courses to increase their chances of graduating and
potentially moving on into a four year school. In addition, our ongoing partnership
with the GLOW Foundation has ensured that our Investment in Success students
enter College Success programs and similar organizations that offer financial
aid, academic advising, and specialized support services – thus increasing their
chances of graduation and success.
Currently, our resources can only reach a limited number of deserving
students, yet each year millions of state financial aid dollars are left unclaimed
by students. To address this situation and allow more students to access these
funds, the Foundation partnered last year with GLOW and the College Access
Foundation of California to create “College Gold Rush,” a one-stop shop for
accessing financial aid resources and information usable by parents, students and
school administrators. The web site is functioning and guiding students through
the maze of college application and financial aid processes, including the first and
most important step – filling out the Federal FAFSA forms.
Public Schools Advisory Councils (PSAC)
As a fraternity, our greatest strength lies in our members. Through our
PSACs, the Foundation is able to maximize our impact by engaging key leaders
and leveraging partnerships with organizations that share our values and strategic
objectives. By working with our members and partners to ensure the success of
Raising A Reader and guaranteeing that our Investment in Success recipients
have a College Success organization supporting them throughout, we provide the
necessary combination of financial support and wrap‐around services needed for
students to achieve academically, and complete college. In addition, our PSACs
allow us to expand our impact beyond our program participants and scholarship
beneficiaries as we collaborate in creating additional resources that are accessible
to families statewide.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is unique among the various Masonicentity boards in California in that it is our only for profit, income tax paying entity
responsible for overseeing the efficient and profitable operations of the garage
located within the California Masonic Memorial Temple building at the top of
Nob Hill. One of our most important responsibilities is to ensure payment of a
dividend to our Grand Lodge at the end of each fiscal year. This dividend helps
fund the many ways in which the California Masons make a profound difference
in the lives of our members and in our communities. I am proud to announce that
the Fiscal Year 2013/2014 was the best year ever for the Nob Hill Masonic Center
and that the dividend provided to our Grand Lodge was also the largest to date.
This year, we engaged in our search to find the right business to contract
for the operations of the garage. To do this, a Request for Proposal (RFP) was sent
to six companies and they were Ace Parking (the incumbent), Propark America,
SP+ Parking, Towne Parking, ABM, and Pacific Park Management. Five of
these six companies were subsequently present for the proposer’s conference
on March 19, 2015. Of the six, Pacific Park Management chose not to proceed.
The remaining five subsequently submitted proposals for review. Three proposals
were eliminated after management review and the exercise of due diligence. The
two finalists were Ace Parking and SP+ Parking and they both presented their
proposals to the NHMC Board at the April 28, 2015 board meeting. Following
further negotiations and a final review, a unanimous consent of the board approved
the execution of an agreement with Ace Parking. This extensive review of a wide
competitive field allowed us to carefully select the best operator of our garage and
the one with the best potential to generate new revenue opportunities to support
the future growth.
ACE is one of the City’s most recognized garage operators and has
managed the day-to-day operations of the facility well. We are working closely
with them to improve the utilization of the garage in the off hours of the late
evening and early morning by engaging the local hotels to have their employees
park there. They also engaged in an internal transportation study to understand the
impact of the use of ride sharing and taxi services on the event parking business
and to further understand how to increase event parking. This competition is seen
as the cause of the decrease in event parking relative to the projections made at
the beginning of the year. Given this, the sustainment of the monthly parking and
daily parking growth will be the key to driving the business.

Report of the Committee
on Insurance
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & .M. of California:
Overview
The Insurance committee is tasked with the responsibility of reviewing
the Grand Lodge property and casualty insurance program and other related
insurance programs, working with the broker selected by Grand Lodge and
making recommendations regarding coverage and other insurance related matters.
The Insurance Committee reports to the Grand Secretary on all insurance matters
(except Life and Medical Coverage and benefits for employees) who then makes
the final decision regarding the different coverages and limits to purchase or
renew. The committee also works closely with the Chief Financial Officer on an
ongoing basis.
Currently there are three meetings a Masonic year of the full Committee
and an additional meeting in December for just the Chairman, Vice Chairman, the
CFO, other Grand Lodge representatives and the Insurance Broker. The purpose
of this meeting is to advise the broker of any changes in Grand Lodge activities
or new programs being contemplated or under way. The broker provides any
information on changes in the insurance market place regarding cost, coverage
and availability. The broker may also make new recommendations regarding
insurance program. The date for the renewal quotes for the new policy year is also
set at this meeting.
Review of Committee Meetings
The three full Committee meetings re as follows:
1.

The first meeting takes place in January. The broker reviews all of the
coverages presently in effect and advises the Committee and Grand
Lodge personnel on the status of the insurance markets as to the
availability of coverage and current pricing. The broker also makes
recommendations for changes that could be made with current coverages
or limits of coverage. The Grand Lodge staff updates the broker of any
changes in operations that are being made or that will be made that
could affect the coverages that will be needed for the upcoming policy
year. The Committee also makes recommendations it sees as necessary
or important.

2.

The second meeting takes place on the date set for the presentation of
the renewal proposals by the broker – this is normally in mid-March.
The broker presents the proposal and also alternate proposals to the
committee and Grand Lodge for consideration. The Committee makes
recommendations to the Grand Secretary and Grand Lodge regarding
how each policy should be renewed regarding coverage and limits. Once
the Grand Secretary has the Insurance Committee recommendations he
makes the final decision. The renewal policies are then ordered.

354

Proceedings of the
3.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The third meeting takes place in June after all of the renewal policies
have been received from the broker. The Committee reviews all of the
policies to make sure that they contain all of the coverages and limits as
ordered and that no new or unusual restrictions or limitations have been
added to the policies. The Committee also reminds the Grand Lodge
staff to be certain that each policy names as an insured each of the Grand
Lodge entities to which a particular cover is to apply.
Review of Key Initiatives

1.

The January 13, 2015 Insurance Committee meeting was held on the
Union City campus of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek. The
purpose of holding the meeting there was so we could view improvements
to the Administrators House, Lorber renovations and other renovations.
This meeting was attended by our broker, representatives from Crum
& Forster, Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek. This gave everyone an
opportunity to better understand the nature of our beautiful homes and
their high quality operation. One result is that our broker recommended
that we add scheduled stained glass coverage for several of the windows.
This recommendation was later recommended by the Committee and
accepted by Grand Lodge.

2.

Volunteer Workers Compensation: During the policy year the Grand
Lodge Executive Committee passed a resolution that provided volunteers
with Workers Comp coverage. At the 166th Annual Communication
Resolution #6 was passed that made the coverage permanent. The
Committee helped arrange with the broker to provide the additional
coverage at a very low additional premium.

3.

Workers Comp claim review at Union City: Insurance Committee
member William Zachary attended the January 20, 2015 Worker Comp
review meeting. His opinion is that our carrier, Crum & Forster, is doing
a good job of handling W.C. claims, controlling costs and providing
benefits to injured employees.

At the conclusion of the renewal process all was well. The renewal premium had
only a 1.21% increase over the previous year – even with some added coverage.
The Insurance Committee is pleased to present this Annual Report. The Committee
will continue to working with the broker to make sure Grand Lodge receives
proper coverage and limits at a fair price.

Report om the Committee
on Lodge Support
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & AM of California
The Committee on Lodge Support is very thankful to be entrusted with
the opportunity by the Grand Master to serve the brethren of California this year.
The 13 very dedicated brethren of the Committee on Lodge Support
have seen increased engagement over previous years by having assisted nearly
40 lodges in various needs during this year. The members of the committee have
generously spent countless hours meeting with and traveling to these lodges to
help meet those needs, often competing with family, professional and fraternal
responsibilities. Several situations required the committee to help the brethren
of a lodge alleviate an unfortunate circumstance and stabilize the lodge for the
benefit of continued Freemasonry in their community. Fortunately, most of our
efforts were focused at assisting the brethren of lodges to develop or rekindle
programs and best practices that embrace Masonic values and enrich the lives
of their lodge members and the communities that each lodge serves. Although at
least two lodges have decided that they could not rebuild at this time and have
therefore surrendered their Charters and two other lodges have consolidated, most
of the remaining lodges are making progress toward improvement, with only a
few still struggling to find their way forward. On the whole, the committee has
thankfully achieved successes in all areas and is pleased to report that lodges
requesting assistance are generally moving in a positive direction.
The Committee on Lodge Support continues to believe that the successful
lodge will utilize a “best practice” approach to focus on four major areas for
growth, relevance and success:
1.

An engaging membership experience whereby each Mason feels
rewarded for being a part of our Craft.

2.

Active community partnership and involvement whereby our individual
communities – and society in general – are beneficiaries of Freemasonry.

3.

Assisting each lodge to operate in a smooth and sound manner financially
and administratively.

4.

Promote methods that develop lodge leadership.

The Committee on Lodge Support recognizes that all lodges are unique
in their history and formation. We assist and facilitate lodges in understanding
their unique responsibility to act as stewards of California Freemasonry, its
historical relevance, precepts, Landmarks, and the preservation of Masonic
values within their own unique communities. Lodge individuality strengthens
our jurisdiction and Freemasonry in general throughout the world. However, with

356

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

certainty, when lodge brethren live by those shared Masonic values of our ritual
and our obligations, harmony prevails and lodges succeed in all their doings. Our
committee therefore encourages lodges to pursue strength from shared values that
are uniquely applied to their lodge.

Report of the
Ritual Task Force

The Committee on Lodge Support further recognizes that lodge
individuality reflects the public community in which it exists, and more
importantly the collective identity of its membership. Therefore, the committee
encourages all lodges to pursue opportunities to engage in programs that enrich
their communities and neighbors, and consequently enhance the lives of its
brethren. These are the best practices of strong vibrant lodges.
The Committee on Lodge Support looks forward to assisting lodges at
the invitation of the individual lodge or its Worshipful Master, the request of the
Inspector or Assistant Grand Lecturer, or at the direction of the Grand Master or
the Executive Committee through mentoring and coaching. The goal for each
engagement is through the prism of the Grand Lodge Strategic Plan to expand and
strengthen Freemasonry in individual communities and throughout California.
It has been said that the Committee on Lodge Support is charged with the
task to eliminate the need for it to exist. With this proud goal we proceed and hope
for increasing Masonic Light in every lodge and a fading need for our committee.
Respectfully submitted,
M. Shawn Donohugh, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
At the direction of Most Worshipful Frank Loui, the Task Force on Ritual
was created and first met on August 16, 2012 under the supervision of co-chairs
Right Worshipful John L. Cooper, Senior Grand Warden and Very Worshipful
Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer. The purpose of the task force was to examine the
practice and teaching of our Ritual and to make recommendations that would
ensure the craft had qualified officers performing quality ritual, so that the degree
experience was deeply meaningful to all candidates, and that all members consider
their experience to be rewarding.
The task force conducted a survey of the Craft and learned that they
wanted to see:
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

Formal Officer’s Coaches training in ritual and teaching skills.
Standardized officer qualification requirements.
Consistent, accurate, and readily available ritual floor work instruction.
Consistent, accurate, and readily available ritual verbiage instruction.
Training on the historical development and meaning of our ritual.
Memory cues to assist ritual presentation and individual performance.
Smaller group training by Inspectors.
Fewer and more focused District Officer Schools of instruction.
Formal Inspector training in interpersonal and teaching skills.
Better advance planning by Inspectors prior to District Officer meetings.
Training on the historical development and meaning of our ritual.
Traveling degree teams to exemplify how each degree is to be performed.

Additionally, the task force conducted a survey of 28 American Grand
Lodges and learned:
•
•

63% allow lectures to be delivered by multiple brethren.
82% held their business meetings in the 3rd Degree.

The task force examined issues relative to changing the term “Holy
Bible” to “Holy Writings”, eliminating the need for the Holy Bible being on the
altar when a candidate chose an alternate Holy Writing to be obligated upon,
alternate lecture delivery (e.g., reduction in the length of the degree lectures,
involvement of multiple brethren during the delivery of degree lectures, use
of standardized tracing boards, and development of 3rd Degree lecture slides),
reduction in the length of the charges, qualifying lodge degree teams opposed
to qualifying specific officers in the delivery of our degrees, requiring ritual
proficiency prior to being elected to office, improved officers’ coaches’ training
and improved Inspector’s schools of ritual instruction.

The Recognition Task Force only held one meeting. It appeared that
major issues of recognition in the international Masonic arena required time to
sort out before the task force could move forward with recommendations to the
Grand Master. The chairman decided that the task force needed to wait until 2016
before making these recommendations. Continuing concerns were the following:
•

France: The United Grand Lodge of England ended its suspension of the
French National Grand Lodge, although the break-away lodges which
had formed their own grand lodge (the Grand Lodge of the French
Masonic Alliance) did not return to the French National Grand Lodge,
and continued to seek independent recognition.

•

Baja California: The break-away group of lodges from the Grand Lodge
of Baja California continued with their own grand lodge, and the latter
continued to have support from the Interamerican Masonic Conference
(CMI) and the World Conference or Regular Grand Lodges. As a result,
Baja California is represented in the international Masonic arena by
a grand lodge which the Grand Lodge of California considers to be
irregular and schismatic.

•

Prince Hall: The mainstream grand lodges in nine Southern states
continued with their non-recognition of their Prince Hall counterparts.
The issue of visitation by Masons from these grand lodges in lodges
of the Grand Lodge of California continued to be a problem for the
Grand Lodge of California. Further exploration of alternatives will
continue in 2016.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code, Section 406.035 E, requires the Committee
on Finance to review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to
be considered at the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact
these items may have on the Grand Lodge budget.
The Committee reviewed Grand Master Charvonia’s Decision and
Recommendations. In the opinion of the Finance Committee, the only Decision or
Recommendation that will have a financial impact on the Grand Lodge budget is
Grand Master’s Recommendation No 1 – Permits All Forms of Electronic Voting.
I will report that Recommendation when it is considered.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Carry-Over Resolutions and
New Resolutions as provided by the Grand Secretary. On August 6, we finalized
our report on the cost impact of each item. The Grand Secretary posted the report
with the legislation. Only one Resolution was found to have any financial impact
on the Grand Lodge budget – Resolution No. 14-14 Adds a Grand Historian. I
will report on this impact at the time the Resolution is considered.
There are a number of Resolutions that would cause changes to the
Ritual or the Monitor. It has been a practice of the Grand Lodge to make the
printed changes and produce new ciphers and monitors only after the current
inventory has been depleted or simply make them available online. Therefore,
there is no additional expense for printing or distribution caused by the adoption of
these Resolutions.
To repeat, in the view of the Committee on Finance, none of the other
Resolutions or the Grand Master’s Decision or Recommendations will have a
financial impact on the Grand Lodge budget other than Grand Master’s Decision
No. 1 and Resolution 14-14.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent handling
of Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist primarily of the General
and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes of California, but also include the
investment portfolios of the California Masonic Foundation, California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the Grand Lodge Retirement plan and the Grand Lodge itself.
We take this charge very seriously. In its simplest terms, we manage the investment
funds with an eye for growing and preserving capital. We strive to maintain an
increasingly diversified portfolio that are designed to generate the necessary funds
for the continuing operation of Masonic functions as well as allow for growth for
future needs. In doing so, we constantly scan the horizon in an attempt to manage
the funds to take advantage of long-term trends as well as near-term opportunities.
The Grand Lodge Investment Committee utilizes the services of professional
investment management firms to gain access to the capital markets. The funds
are invested in the domestic United States, international equity markets, and a
small allocation is invested in fixed income markets. In recent years, we have
increased our investment allocation in less traditional investment vehicles that are
historically not as correlated to the traditional stock and bond markets.
I am pleased to report that the Grand Lodge and related entities had
positive performance over the preceding fiscal year (ending June 30, 2015). Of
particular note is the fact that early indicators point to the hard work accomplished
by the committee and our consultants over the last five years are bearing fruit.
After an amazingly strong and resilient rise in global capital markets over the last
number of years, we expect increasing headwinds and higher market volatility
ahead. However, the portfolio is better positioned than we ever have been, and
while volatility is expected, we remain committed to our investment process and
the responsibilities with which we are charged.
Grand Lodge Investment Performance for the year ended 6-30-15
Amid more volatile global capital markets, the Total Grand Lodge and
Related Entities portfolio advanced 2.1% for the year ending June 30, 2015. This
result fell just short of our Policy Benchmark return of 4.1%.
The U.S. equity allocation of the portfolio was up 7.5% compared to
7.2% for the Dow Jones Total Stock Market Index. The Non-U.S. equity portfolio
had a good year relative to the broad non-U.S. equity market. The portfolio
advanced 0.3%, while the broad market, as measured by the MSCI All Country
World ex-U.S. Index, was down 5.3%. Global Equities struggled with a negative
return of 4.7%. The MSCI All-Country World Index returned 0.7% during the

362

363

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

year. The fixed income portfolio was up 1.5%, compared to a 1.9% return for the
broad fixed income market. Our Alternative Investments were up 2.4% during a
period when global equities advanced only by 0.7% and fixed income returned
1.9%. As compared to the custom Alternatives benchmark, which returned 7.7%,
the portfolio disappointed. Overall, the allocation to U.S. equities helped offset
disappointing returns from other asset classes during the year. A detailed manager
performance review can be found in the tables following this report.

Another major strategic asset allocation change implemented by the
Investment Committee in response to the changing market environment is in
the fixed income portfolio. Over. In recent years, we have reduced the portfolio
allocation to fixed income. In addition, the fixed income portfolio is managed
in an “unconstrained” manner. This means that the investment manager has the
ability to position their fixed income portfolio to withstand a rising interest rate
environment. When interest rates increase, bond prices decrease. Utilizing the
skills of a bond manager with multiple tools at their disposal can minimize the
damage of a rising interest rate environment on a bond portfolio.

The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most recent
top performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended allocation to
stocks and bonds and other asset classes only after very careful due diligence
and consideration. The purpose of the funds, respective spending requirements,
investment time horizon and ability to assume risk are all factored into these
recommendations. The probability and duration of potential losses are carefully
weighed against the long-term potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals
are taken into account. The Investment Committee recommends asset allocations
that will provide the highest probability that the funds will be able to meet their
respective objectives over the long-term.
Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance for the year
ended 6-30-15
The market value of the Masonic Home’s portfolio as of June 30, 2015,
was $901.9 million compared to $864.6 million a year earlier. For the twelvemonth period, ending June 30, 2015, the combined funds of Grand Lodge and
the related Masonic entities were up 2.1%. This compares to 4.1% for the custom
benchmark index. For the three-year period ending June 30, 2015, the combined
Grand Lodge and related entities returned 9.8% versus 10.3% for the benchmark.
Since inception, our funds have returned 7.9% annually versus 7.9% return of the
benchmark. All returns are net of fees. Detailed Entity performance can be found
in the tables following this report.
Summary of Recent Changes
Over the past six years, the Grand Lodge and Related Entities asset
allocation has evolved in an effort to better position the portfolio to withstand
downturns in the market while still maintaining the overall expected return. For
example, six years ago, the asset allocation included approximately 73% in public
equities. While public equities are an essential piece of the asset allocation, the
Investment Committee of the Grand Lodge of California has taken steps over
the past five years to reduce this allocation in favor of strategies that provide
diversification to equity risk. As such, the current asset allocation includes
approximately 55% in public equities. Capital has been re-allocated to alternative
strategies that are designed to perform well when the public equity market
struggles, thereby smoothing out the inevitable “ups and downs” of the markets.

Grand Lodge Investment Management for the year ended 6-30-15
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand
Lodge Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee meets
quarterly with our Investment Consultant, Aon Hewitt Investment Consulting
and our individual portfolio managers. We review their respective performance
compared to various indices representing their objective. This process provides
the Investment Committee with the necessary data to evaluate each investment
manager on a timely basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve the
objectives of their mandate.
The committee also holds monthly WebEx conference calls to discuss
any outstanding business on a timelier basis, or discuss the implementation of
tactical changes within the portfolio.
In addition, the committee makes regular calls to the managers to assess
if there have been any material changes at the respective investment company that
may affect the management of assets, or that may be a sign of bigger potential
issues that requires further review and analysis.
Finally, we have scheduled bi-annual retreats to take time to review
our overall strategic initiatives implemented over the prior two years, review the
macro environment and opportunities therein and chart a course for the following
two-year period.
We continue to work with our investment consultant, Aon Hewitt
Investment Consulting.
Not only is the Investment Committee responsible for managing the
portfolios of our various organizations, but it also oversees the management of
our planned gift investments. The current portfolio of planned gifts includes
approximately $24.1 million. Despite the obvious difficulties in our economy,
the Grand Lodge philanthropy staff had another successful year in the solicitation
of planned gifts. The Investment Committee is grateful to the entire staff at the
offices of Philanthropy and Finance for their support and hard work this past year,
and look forward to another successful philanthropic campaign in 2014-2015.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The
Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Charvonia’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
In the Committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on August 6th of this year is sufficient to carry out the intent
of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Charvonia’s
recommendations which he will present in his message is sufficient to carry out
his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set
forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no
recommendations as to the action you should take with it. While the Committee
has written the title and introductory explanation for each resolution before
you and assisted the proponents in drafting the Code changes required to effect
their intent, the proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own.
The Committee does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no
comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge
website on August 6th of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master
Charvonia’s recommendations require no separate motion because they are
automatically before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will
announce the vote required for the passage of each item before discussion begins.
Any legislation which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual
requires a simple majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California
Masonic Code or the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote.

368

369

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

If the amendment receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative
vote, it carries over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds
affirmative vote is required for adoption.

The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of
all trials held during the past Masonic year. All Committee votes were unanimous
except where otherwise noted.
