Joseph P. Tabrisky
R. Stephen Doan, P.G.M., Consultant

In each of the following matters, the Committee finds there was
compliance with the procedural requirements of the California Masonic Code and
that the findings were supported by the evidence.
The following cases were decided by the Trial Masters after investigation
as provided for in California Masonic Code section 1404.410, Procedure if the
Accused Fails To Plead, or section 1404.420, Procedure if the Accused Pleads
Guilty or No Contest.
1. Trial Numbers 2617, 2618 and 2619 are related matters and charges
and were consolidated for trial. They involve the failure of several
brethren to properly account for funds received and expended. In one
case the funds had been collected from candidates to be used for a
meal or refreshments in conjunction with a degree. No accounting
for those funds was presented to the Lodge. A contribution by a
candidate for a meal or refreshments served in conjunction with a
degree requires proper accounting and reporting to the Lodge. In
another instance there was a failure to properly record and report
funds received and expended in a Junior Warden’s refreshment fund.
In yet another instance a brother failed to document for appropriated
funds totaling over $5,575.
This case was first presented to Grand Lodge at the 2013 Annual
Communication and reversed when, due to mechanical failures of
the recording equipment, there was an inadequate record of the trial.
The Committee on Trial Review could not determine if the evidence
presented supported the findings of the Trial Master and the penalty
imposed. Because we could not carry out our mandated function
we recommended and the Grand Lodge voted to reverse the matters
for new trials. The trial proceeding were started anew and are again
before the Grand Lodge.
In trials 2617 and 2618 the matter pursuant to Code section 1404.535.L
was mediated by the Trial Master and an agreement reached. It was
agreed that after entering a no contest plea, both brothers would
be suspended for a definite period of time of one year. The Trial
Master agreed to this penalty. After the first trial and the problems
related thereto, these two brothers had, for practical purposes, been
suspended as active Masons for more than a year. The Trial Master
“stayed” all the definite suspension period except for one day. The
Committee on Trial Review concurs in this penalty and agrees the
staying of all but one day was appropriate.

In remaining portion of the consolidated cases, that is trial 2619, the
brother failed to respond to both written and telephonic notices of the
recommencement of the trial proceedings. Since he had previously
been served and had subjected himself to the jurisdiction of our
Masonic trial process, the Trial Master treated the failure to respond
in the same manner as a failure to answer charges and conducted
an investigation pursuant to Code section 1404.410. He determined
that in excess of $5,575 had been entrusted to the accused for Lodge
events as well as for Trestleboard printing and mailings costs. The
brother provided no bills or other accounting of how those funds
were used. The Trial Master determined the conduct was unmasonic
and imposed the same penalty as had been put into effect prior to
the case being reversed, that is, expulsion. The Committee concurs
in this result.
2. In trial 2657 the Accuser, the Senior Warden of the Lodge, alleged
that the Accused, without provocation punched him. The incident
occurred in November, 2012, in the parking lot of a restaurant.
The Accuser, the Senior Warden of the Lodge, and Accused met in
a parking lot at the request of another brother whose purpose was
to try to quell the ill feelings between the Accuser and the Accused.
Apparently the animus between the Accuser and the Accused arose
when the Accused learned that he would not be appointed an officer
of the Lodge if and when the Accuser was elected Master. When
the Accused and the Accuser approached each other, the Accuser
extended his hand to the Accused and stated he was sorry. At this time
the Accused punched the Accuser in the chest with a closed fist. The
next day, the Accused noticed that the area where he was punched had
a reddish mark. Because of the incident The Accuser withdrew from
the line and was not installed as Master.
The Trial Master found the conduct to be a violation of both the Moral
Law and it also involved moral turpitude. He found no mitigation
of the conduct and that there was aggravation since there was no
showing of remorse, there was no response to the charges and no
justification for the conduct of the Accused; he set the penalty at
expulsion. It is noted that the Accused filed two documents pursuant
to Code section 1404.910, Grand Lodge Review. Neither satisfies the
requirements of the section and the second document was received
after the mandatory fifteen days before the Annual Communication
due date for such a filing. The committee agrees with the Trial Master
findings and the penalty he imposed.

3. In trial 2671 the Accuser alleged that he was intimidated and punched
by the Accused, cursed and subjected to defamatory, vile and indecent
language directed at him in the presence of several brothers. During
the trial process the Trial Master was active and in constant contact
with the counsels of both the Accuser and Accused. During the
pretrial discovery phase it came to light that the Accuser could not
produce any brothers he had alleged to have witnessed the conduct
and could attest to the facts. Additionally there was no evidence of
a physical injury to the Accuser. The Trial Master gave each side
every opportunity to present evidence or information relevant to the
case at hand. The parties entered into discussions in an attempt to
reach an agreed to disposition. They were unable to do so. A Trial by
commission had not been requested in a timely fashion, therefore the
matter was to proceed to trial before the Trial Master only. After all the
pretrial discussions and discovery proceedings had been completed it
was clear to the Trial Master that the case could not be proven by
a preponderance of the evidence as our Code requires, therefore he
dismissed the case. Though this case did not proceed to trial it appears
all parties are satisfied with the dismissal of the charges. Since both
sides had openly and completely discussed the available evidence
with the Trial Master there was nothing that could or would have
been changed during a trial; a trial at which after hearing the evidence
the Trial Master would have the authority to do exactly what he did,
dismiss the case. The Committee agrees with the decision of the Trial
Master and recommends approval.
4. In trial 2704, the Brother submitted an application for degrees. He
answered “No” to the question “Have you ever been arrested, taken
into custody, pleaded guilty or nolo contendre to, or been convicted of,
a criminal offence [sic] (other than a minor traffic violation)?”
At an undisclosed time, but after the application was filed and before
May 30, 2014, a brother became aware that the Accused had been
untruthful in his answer and had in fact been arrested and convict of
crimes. Charges were preferred, the Accused was served, but failed
to respond. Investigation revealed the brother had been convicted
of criminal conduct at least four times, including a violation of
California Penal Code section 242, battery; a misdemeanor violation
of California Penal Code section 273.5.9(a), spousal abuse; and for
violating Vehicle Code section 23152(b), driving under the influence
with a prior driving under the influence conviction.
The Trial Master set the penalty for lying on the application at
expulsion, the Committee concurs.

372

Proceedings of the
5. In trial 2673, the Accused was a member of the Hall Association
and lived near the Lodge. He was not the building manager, but was
given a key to the building for the purpose of showing the facility
to prospective renters. The charges arose when he allowed a group
to use the building without a contract, proof of liability insurance,
a vote by the hall association and without a rental fee. There was
no written agreement or contract between the Lodge and the group.
Additionally, the Lodge’s name was used by the gratuitous user
on a website in a manner which some could infer that the Lodge
endorsed a particular political candidate. The Charges alleged five
separate instances of unauthorized use of the building by the group.
During the Trial Master’s investigation the Accuser provided proof
of the conduct. This met the burden of showing the Accused allowed
the use of the Masonic hall for the benefit of a third party, without
compensation to the Hall Association, proper insurance or contract.
The proof also proved that the Lodge’s name had been used in a way
that imply endorsement of a political candidate. The actions of the
Accuser caused the Lodge to do extensive clean up after the group left.
Allowing the hall to be used for a political purpose and to imply either
intentionally or inadvertently that the meeting was a Lodge function
violated the spirit, if not the words of both a specific Masonic Code
section and a Grand Masters decision which state in part. “Racial or
ethnic background, color of skin, political views or religious belief
.., shall not be a consideration either for membership or visitation.”
The Trial Master determined that the Accused’s conduct, at a minimum,
breached the fiduciary duty he owed to the Hall Association and to
the Lodge; he determined the appropriate penalty to be an indefinite
suspension; the Committee concurs in the determination.
Note: The Committee also discussed this case with the legal counsel
for the Grand Lodge who opined that very careful attention should
be given when considering renting to a political group so that any
publicity of the event makes it clear that the renter is using the
facilities and there is no endorsement of the political purpose or
person by the Lodge. Failure to make this clear could possibly cause
a loss of the Lodge’s tax exempt status.
6. In trial 2696 it was determined that the Accused on the evening
March 27, 2013 and through the morning of March 28 violently
assaulted his wife, hitting her in the face causing serious injuries. The
Accused was arrested and wife was granted a protective order and,
for her safety, she moved to a battered women’s center. The Accused,
while out on bail and using his training as a former peace officer, was
able to trace the wife’s whereabouts and on March 29, 2013 went to
the shelter and again assaulted her. The Superior Court sentenced the
Accused to an aggregate sentence of five years and eight months in the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

373

State Prison for the following: California Penal Code (PC) 273.5 a, as
a felony corporal injury to a spouse, two years; Penal Code 273.6A,
a misdemeanor for disobeying a criminal protective order, one year;
a misdemeanor for disobeying a protective order, one year; Penal
Code 136.1(B(1); a felony for preventing or dissuading a witness,
eight months and violation of Penal Code 647, a misdemeanor for
public intoxication, six months. These charges include both felonies
and misdemeanors, but under California Law none are considered
crimes of moral turpitude even though he could be and was sentenced
to state prison. The Trial Master determined that his conduct was
certainly unmasonic; he set the punishment at expulsion, with which
the Committee on Trial Review agrees.
7. 
In trial 2699 the Accused was charged with hazing during the
second section of 3rd Degree. After an extensive investigation the
Trial Master held a conference with the parties. The Accuser and
the Accused expressed a desire to settle the case in order to promote
harmony within their Lodge. Having satisfied himself that the outcome
of the investigation serves the best interest of the principles in the
case in particular, the Lodge, and freemasonry in general, the Trial
Master accepted the Accuser’s, request to withdraw his complaint,
contingent upon the delivery of a presentation to the Lodge by the
Accused, entitled, “Hazing Rituals Are an Anathema to Masonic
Fraternalism.” On February 4, 2015, at the Lodge’s Stated Meeting,
the Accused delivered the subject presentation in an articulate and
passionate manner, thereby satisfying the final contingency to
the agreement.
The Committee finds that the dismissal of the charges by the
Trial Master was a proper exercise of his authority and concurs
in the action.
8. In Trial Number 2710 the Accused had been charged in the Superior
Court with molesting a child under the age of fourteen, a crime of
moral turpitude. The charges were amended and the Accused agreed
to and entered a guilty plea to felony Child Endangering, which
under California law is not a crime of moral turpitude. The Trial
Master caused Masonic charges to be delivered to the Accused who
acknowledged receipt of the charges and responded to them in a
letter stating “To Whom it May Concern, I … do hereby tender my
resignation effective immediately to all rights and privileges in the
Masonic Lodge. Thank you for allowing my [sic] to serve for all these
years in this organization.” The Trial Master deemed this to be an
acknowledgement of the receipt of the charges and that the brother
had submitted himself to the jurisdiction of the Masonic trial process.
There being no plea of “not guilty” the Trial Master conducted an
investigation as if the response was a no contest plea.

374

Proceedings of the
The Trial Master determined that the conduct underlying the child
endangering conviction was of a sexual nature, that the Accused had
plead guilty to that charge, that the Superior Court had exercised its
discretion and ruled the offense was a felony, sentenced the brother
to jail as a condition to the grant of probation, and order that he enter
a program for the treatment of sexual offenders. The Trial Master
determined that the conduct of the Accused, the criminal plea
notwithstanding, involved moral turpitude, violated the moral law
and was unmasonic; he set the penalty at expulsion. The committee
concurs in the decision and the penalty imposed.
9. In trial 2724 the events which resulted in charges started in the
dining room of the lodge during an informal organizational meeting
of Lodge leadership and prior to a regularly scheduled meeting. The
Accused, the Master of the Lodge and the Accuser, the Secretary,
had a verbal disagreement which resulted in the Accuser telling the
Master he would not serve under him and attempting to leave the
meeting. The Accused physically blocked the Accuser from leaving
the meeting and the Accuser, in what turned out to be his final attempt
after several prior ones to get around the Accused and exit the
building, placed a hand on Accused’s chest and was able to get past
him. After passing the Accused and as he approached the elevator,
the Accused kicked the Accuser behind the knee and knocked him
to the ground. A scuffle ensued, with both Accused and Accuser on
the floor; the Accuser called to his brothers for help, they did and
the Accused was pulled away from the Accuser and restrained.
The Accuser suffered a significant amount of scrapes and bruising.
The injuries were supported by a color photograph of the injuries.
Additionally a tablet computer with an estimated value of $560 was
damaged beyond repair.
The Accused failed to respond to the charges which had been properly
served and after which the Trial Master had telephone contact with
him. The Accused ended the telephone conversation by stating “I
want nothing to do with Masons ever again” and hung up on the
Trial Master. An investigation in compliance with California Masonic
Code section 1404.410 was conducted and the Trial Master found
that the conduct was in violation of section1401.010, Section G,
Subsection 2c, physical violence against a Mason. The aggravating
circumstances outweighed the mitigating circumstances and fixed the
penalty at expulsion. The Committee concurs.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

375

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for adoption the
following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Numbers 2617, 2618, 2619, 2657, 2671, 2673,
2696, 2699, 2710 and 2724 the Trial Masters’ procedures, findings and
the penalties affixed by are affirmed.”
The following cases were dismissed by the Trial Master:
10. In consolidated trials 2655, 2687 and 2688 two elected pillar officers
and one pro tem officer were accused of fraudulently reporting the
true ballot box contents after a vote on an application. The Accuser
alleged that he had deposited a cube.
California Masonic Code section 804.450, Ballot Secrecy, states:
“Except for the three officers whose duty it is to examine the
ballot box, no one is entitled to know the number of votes cast for
or against an applicant. There shall be no discussion regarding
an unfavorable ballot. No member of a Lodge shall be required,
requested, or allowed to divulge his vote upon a ballot, or to
assign reasons for such vote, if it be known, except to the Master
for the purpose of correcting a mistake.” [Emphasis added.]
The minutes of the Lodge do not reflect that the Accuser or any other
brother made known to the Master that a correction of a mistake
was need.
The Trial Master ruled that the specific language of section 804.450
was controlling, therefore no one could be required, requested or
allowed to provide the necessary information to prove the case. The
code language “no member of a Lodge…” includes the person who
cast the cube, the Accuser or any other Mason. Without the legal
authority to allow any testimony about the balloting the Trial Master
had to dismiss the charges. In his report he strongly recommended
that the California Masonic Code be modified to allow disclosure for
the purpose of the trial process. The Committee reluctantly concurs
in the decision and is studying appropriate legislation to present to
this Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for adoption the
following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Numbers 2655, 2687 and 2688 the Trial Master’s
dismissal of the charges is affirmed.

376

Proceedings of the

The following trials were conducted with testimony taken.
11. Trial 2665 arose due to the accused acting in a verbally abusive
manner to multiple brethren, their ladies and to tenants of the Lodge’s
hall association. This conduct occurred over an extended period
of time and with escalating frequency and magnitude. Multiple
brothers counselled the Accused and endeavored to bring about
a change in his conduct. Many brethren testified to the Accused’s
conduct. They also testified that they believe that the conduct was
the result of the multiple surgeries the Accused had undergone over
several years, his obvious suffering of pain and the medications he
was required to take. After considering the evidence a Commission
found the Accused guilty of unmasonic conduct. The Trial Master
set the penalty at an indefinite suspension. The Committee concurs
in the finding and the penalty.
One member of the committee recused himself from discussing and
voting on this matter.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for adoption the
following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Number 2665 the findings and penalty
affixed are affirmed.
12. Trial 2685 involved multiple counts some of which were stricken by
the Jurisprudence Committee in the review process and by the Trial
Master in the trial process; others resulted in not guilty decisions
and other resulted in guilty findings. In this report the Committee
on Trial Review will report only on those charges which impact the
resolution below.
The accused was charged with six specifications although five other
accusations had been made, but did not proceed to trial. The trial
was conducted without a commission as none was requested.
Specification one: The Accused was alleged to have committed
un-masonic conduct by acts which resulted in material harm to his
wife and child in violation of CMC 1401.010 G. 2(a), G.2(c) and
G. 4. occurring on January 2, 1986 which was before he applied to
Masonry. (It should be noted that although requested, the Accused’s
Lodge was unable to locate his application.) Court documents show
that on January 3, 1986 the Accused’s wife asked the civil court
to issue a restraining order against the accused. In her application,
she alleged the accused pushed her head through the wall and
punched her with resulting bruises and told her he would like to

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

377

kill her and all this was done in front of their minor child. While
a temporary restraining order was issued, it would by law expire
unless a permanent restraining order was issues. On the day of the
hearing, the wife had the matter taken off the court’s calendar and
no contested hearing was ever held. No evidence was present to the
civil court and no permanent restraining order was issued.
Wife did not testify at the Masonic Trial and the only evidence of
the January event was the certified copy of the wife’s declaration
under penalty of perjury and the temporary restraining order based
on that declaration. The Trial Master correctly determined that even
though the declaration was a certified copy of the court filing and
the foundation as to its authenticity was established, the content,
that is the wife’s declaration constituted inadmissible hearsay in so
far as establishing a relevant fact. Its only probative value may have
related to the character of the accused. As to this specification, the
Accused was properly found not guilty.
Specification Two: The accused is alleged to have committed a
similar offense on April 10, 1989 for the same Masonic Code
violations as that alleged in Specification One. In this instance there
were again a certified record of the civil court proceedings. That
record contained a declaration of the wife that alleged the Accused
struck her with his fist in the nose causing substantial bleeding.
The sheriffs photographed the scene and arrested the accused. On
10/23/89 after a formal court hearing with wife and the accused
present the court minutes show a restraining order was issued. The
only allegations of conduct and injury was the striking the wife
in the nose with his fist. The court ordered, after a hearing that a
restraining order issue; this indicates that the court, with both parties
present and available to be questioned, received enough evidence to
believed the allegations in the application for the restraining order,
to wit, the Accused struck and injured his wife. The Trial Master, a
non-attorney, in reaching his decision as to this specification may
not have realized the legal implication and the nuances of the civil
court’s action. The Committee on Trial Review believes that the
accused was guilty of the un-masonic conduct as alleged. The Trial
Review Committee recommends a reversal of the Trial Master’s
decision as to that specification because there was a formal hearing
at which both the accused and his wife were present and the court
rendered a factual judgment thereon.
Specification Four: The accused is alleged to have committed
un-masonic conduct by inflicting physical injury to his wife on
September 4, 1998 in violation of California Masonic Code section
1401.010 G.2 C and G. 4. (7).

378

Proceedings of the
On September 15, 1998 a criminal complaint was filed alleging the
accused violated Penal Code Section 273.5(A), a misdemeanor, by
willfully and unlawfully inflicting corporal injury upon his wife. On
10/29/98 the accused plead nolo contest. The accused was sentenced
to three years probation, to pay $200 fine to the battered women’s
shelter, perform twenty hours of volunteer service and complete a
thirty day anger management program.
The Trial Master’s decision stated that under the 2009 Grand Master’s
Decision No. 2 this behavior does not necessarily constitute moral
turpitude as only a very slight injury is required under the Penal
Code section. However, the Trial Master correctly concluded that
the conduct violates California Masonic Code section 1401.010 B, a
violation of the Moral Law and G (1) and (2a, c, d and e). The Trial
Master therefore found the accused guilty of un-masonic conduct.
Specifications Eight and Nine: The Trial Master found these to
be companion matters relating to the same pattern of conduct
and incidents.
Specification Eight and Nine alleges the accused violated California
Masonic Code section 1401.010 G.2. (b), G2 (d) and G. 4. (7) by
stalking, yelling at and threatening an eighty five year old mason.
The accused is alleged to have hidden in the bushes outside of
said brother’s residence, disabling the lights on a nearby covered
bridge where the brother mason walks his dog; further the accused
flashed a camera or other light in the brother’s face several times
and stating “this is because your daughter’s cost me so many fines.”
The brother’s wife was hospitalized due to the stress caused by
the accused.
On 8/5/13 the 85 year old brother filed for a restraining order
against the accused. A temporary restraining order was issued and
set for hearing on 8/20/13. Also on 8/5/13 the same brother filed a
restraining order against the accused to restrain the Accused from
harassing his wife, his three adult daughters and adult granddaughter,
alleging the accused harassed, stalked, screamed (for 15 minutes
including profanities) in front of the brother’s house on July 23,
2013 and shined a flashlight into the family residence windows and
intimidated the entire family.
At the Masonic trial, in addition to extensive testimony by the
Accuser and others, a settlement agreement executed by all parties
and signed by the judge presiding over the hearing for the restraining
orders in the Superior Court, was introduced into evidence. In that
agreement the Accused agreed to be restrained from contacting,
communicating disturbing the peace, or coming within 100 feet of
the 85 year old brother or his wife.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

379

Based on the testimony and the exhibits the Trial Master found
that Specification 8 and 9 were true and the Accused guilty of unmasonic conduct under California Masonic Code section 1401.010,
Sections G.2. a and c.
The Trial Master set the penalty as an indefinite suspension. Except
for the modification discuss above, the Committee on Trial Review
agrees with this decision and the penalty.
It should be noted that some of the above acts occurred before the
Accused had applied to be a Mason. Masonic Trials are concerned
with unmasonic conduct. The passage of time, the nature of the
conduct and the indications of rehabilitation may affect the penalty,
should one be called for, but not whether or not the conduct was
“unmasonic.” Unmasonic is concerned with conduct of an individual
not when it occurs.
One member of the committee recused himself from discussing and
voting on this matter.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for adoption the
following Resolution:
“Resolved, that verdict of “not guilty” to the charge set forth in
Specification 2 of Trial 2685 be modified to a verdict of “guilty” and a
finding that the conduct was “unmasonic.” Be it further resolved that the
penalty in Trial 2685 be an indefinite suspension.
Finally, the Committee on Trial Review reviewed the automatic
expulsions for crimes of moral turpitude as authorized by Code section 1404.820.
There were eight automatic expulsions, trial numbers 2692, 2717, 2719, 2720,
2722, 2727, 2729, 2736 and 2746. The charges were one for bank fraud; one for
petty theft, one for discharging a firearm into a dwelling, four for child molestation
and one for attempted murder. The expulsions were proper and met the criteria of
California Masonic Code section 1404.820.

Report of the Committee on
Youth Orders

The following brothers were recommended to the Grand Master for
recognition by this committee and received the Grand Master’s Youth Support
Award at the Public Ceremonies of the 166th Annual Communication:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Russell Charvonia, and the members of the
Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:

Brother Jeffrey G. Dotson of Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469 and Gateway
Lodge No. 339

The Youth Orders Committee proudly continues the work of supporting
and advocating for our Masonic youth orders—DeMolay International, Job’s
Daughters International and the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls.

Brother Russell W. (Bill) Keel of Redlands Lodge No. 300

The Jurisdiction was organized into fifty-two geographical areas for
Youth Orders purposes with a Committeeman assigned to each. Each Area
contained designated Lodges, DeMolay Chapters, Rainbow Assemblies and Job’s
Daughters Bethels. The assigned Committeeman was asked to “take ownership”
of his Area and the organizations contained therein. A detailed database of
each Youth organization in the Jurisdiction was created and furnished to the
Committeemen.

Brother Jacob F. Galba-Bright of Temescal Palms Lodge No. 314 and
Moreno Valley Lodge No. 804

While each Committeeman was asked to make contact with the Youth
organizations in his Area, introduce himself and offer support, emphasis was
placed on their working with the Lodges in the Area to encourage increased
involvement with and support for the Youth Groups.
The Committeemen were asked to make contact with the incoming
Worshipful Masters of their assigned Lodges to foster activities with the Youth
Groups in their 2015 calendar. A list of suggested activities with the Youth Groups
was created for use by the Lodges. Lodges were to be encouraged to include
Youth Group activities, past and future, in each month’s Trestleboard.
The guiding vision was to leverage the energy of the Youth Orders
Committeemen by developing the personal involvement of Lodge officers and
members with the Youth Groups in their Area. The Committeemen submitted
quarterly reports of their activities for the Committee.
Quarterly meetings of the Committee were held by conference call.
The Committee continued to sponsor the Youth Orders Adult Volunteer
Training sessions by Larry Newman.

Brother David E. Killmer of Roseville Lodge No. 222

Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges 2015

CANADA: Grand Lodge of Alberta (205); Grand Lodge British Columbia &
Yukon (206); Grand Lodge of Manitoba (207); Grand Lodge of New Brunswick
(208); Grand Lodge of Newfoundland and Labrador (209); Grand Lodge of Nova

(210); Grand Lodge of Prince Edward Island (215); Grand Lodge of Quebec
(215); Grand Lodge of Saskatchewan (216); CHILE: Grand Lodge of Chile
(217); CHINA: Grand Lodge of China (219); COLOMBIA: National Grand

of Serenisima of Columbia (219); Grand Lodge Occidental of Columbia (220);

of Cuba (225); CYPRUS: Grand Lodge of Cyprus (224) CZECH REPUBLIC:
Grand Lodge of the Czech Republic (229);

The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the Grand Lodges in the United
States published in the 2015 List of Lodges Masonic, which includes all 50
states and the District of Columbia. In addition, the Grand Lodge of California
recognizes a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges and foreign Grand Lodges
around the world. The Grand Lodge of California recognizes some, but not all, of
the foreign Grand Lodges in the 2015 List of Lodges Masonic as well as a number
of foreign Grand Lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign Grand Lodges that are recognized by the Grand Lodge of
California are listed belowalphabetically by country. For those that are published
in the 2015 List of Lodges Masonic, the corresponding page number is provided
in parenthesis. Recognized Grand Lodges that are not published in the 2015
List of Lodges Masonic are marked with an asterisk (*). The Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all correspondence with these
Grand Lodges and the Lodges under their jurisdiction. Please contact his office
for assistance.

The Grand Lodge of California has mutual recognition with a number of Prince
Hall Grand Lodges in the United States. In addition, the Grand Lodge of California
has extended an offer of recognition to a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges
throughout the country where mutual recognition does not yet exist.
The Grand Lodge of California maintains mutual recognition with following
Prince Hall Grand Lodges. Some of these Grand Lodges are published in the
List of Lodges Masonic so the same markings follow the name of the Grand
Lodge to indicate whether or not the Grand Lodge is published in the List of
Lodges Masonic, and if so, the 2015 edition page number is provided. The terms
of recognition are the same with each Prince Hall Grand Lodge and are consistent
with the agreement of mutual recognition between the Grand Lodge of California
and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. In essence, dual membership
in Lodges under the two jurisdictions is not allowed. Visitation may be had
between members of Lodges of both jurisdictions. For these purposes, visitation
means visiting tiled meetings.
ALASKA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Alaska and Its Jurisdiction, Inc. (20);
CALIFORNIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. (27); COLORADO
(Wyoming and Utah): Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Colorado, Wyoming and
Utah*, DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the District
of Columbia* (includes Lodges in Maryland); MARYLAND: Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of Maryland and Its Jurisdiction*, MASSACHUSETTS (Maine): Prince
Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Massachusetts* (includes Lodges in New
Hampshire and Maine); MISSOURI: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Missouri
and Jurisdiction*; NEBRASKA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Nebraska and Its
Jurisdiction*; NEVADA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Nevada and Jurisdiction,
Inc.*, NEW MEXICO: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the State of New Mexico,
Inc.*; OREGON: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Oregon*; PENNSYLVANIA:
Prince Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Pennsylvania* (includes Lodges in
Ohio); TEXAS: Prince Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Texas*.
The Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of mutual recognition with
the following Prince Hall Grand Lodges, but mutual recognition has not yet
been established. Visitation between our members and members of Lodges
under the jurisdiction of these Grand Lodges cannot yet be made. When mutual
recognition is established, the Grand Secretary will notify our Lodges in writing.

REPORT OF INDEPENDENT AUDITORS

Other Matters
Report on Summarized Comparative Information

Board of Trustees
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
Report on Consolidated Financial Statements

We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand Lodge”), which comprise the
consolidated statements of financial position as of October 31, 2015, and the related consolidated
statements of activities and changes in net assets, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related
notes to the consolidated financial statements.
Management’s Responsibility for the Consolidated Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these consolidated financial
statements in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America;
this includes the design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation
and fair presentation of consolidated financial statements that are free from material misstatement,
whether due to fraud or error.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these consolidated financial statements based on our audit.
We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance
about whether the consolidated financial statements are free from material misstatement.
An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures in
the consolidated financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment,
including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,
whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk assessments, the auditor considers internal control
relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the consolidated financial statements in order
to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of
expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the
reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the
overall presentation of the consolidated financial statements.

We have previously audited the Grand Lodge’s 2014 consolidated financial statements, and we expressed
an unmodified opinion on those audited consolidated financial statements in our report dated March 20,
2015. In our opinion, the summarized comparative information presented herein as of and for the year
ended October 31, 2014, is consistent, in all material respects, with the audited consolidated financial
statements, from which it has been derived.
Supplementary Information

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements
as a whole. The accompanying 2015 consolidating statement of financial position and consolidating
schedule of changes in net assets, are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a required
part of the consolidated financial statements. Such information is the responsibility of management and
was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other records used to prepare the
consolidated financial statements. The information has been subjected to the auditing procedures applied
in the audit of the 2015 consolidated financial statements and certain additional procedures, including
comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting and other records used
to prepare the 2015 consolidated financial statements or to the 2015 consolidated financial statements
themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in
the United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all material respects in
relation to the consolidated financial statements as a whole.

The accompanying supplemental schedule of fraternal expenses, supplemental schedule of program
appropriations, and supplemental schedule of general and administrative expenses are presented for
purposes of additional analysis and are not a required part of the 2015 consolidated financial statements.
Such information has not been subjected to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the 2015
consolidated financial statements, information from which is presented only in summarized comparative
form in the accompanying consolidated financial statements. Accordingly, we do not express an opinion
or provide any assurance on it.
San Francisco, California
March 18, 2016

We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for
our audit opinion.
Opinion

In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material
respects, the financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California as of October 31, 2015, and the changes in net assets and its cash flows for the year
then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.

NOTE 1 – SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
History and organization – The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand
Lodge”) is a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal organization and governed by a constitution and ordinances setting forth its
jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all lodges and Masons within the state of California, and
members of lodges of California, wherever residing.

The Grand Lodge provides general and administrative services to its related entities: the Masonic Homes of California (the
“Masonic Homes”); the California Masonic Memorial Temple (the “Temple”); and the California Masonic Foundation (the
“Foundation”); (collectively, the “Masonic Entities”). These services are reimbursed by the related entities.

On February 15, 2007, the Temple transferred operation of the auditorium and garage to a new entity, Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.
(the “Nob Hill”), an entity created for this purpose. The Nob Hill is a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge. Accordingly, the financial
statements of the Nob Hill have been consolidated in the financial statements of the Grand Lodge.
On October 30, 2008, the Temple transferred the operation of the auditorium from the Nob Hill to Live Nation, not an affiliate.

Principles of consolidation – The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Grand Lodge and its subsidiary,
the Nob Hill. All significant inter-company accounts and transactions have been eliminated.

Net assets classifications – The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the
standards set forth in Statements of Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”)
958-605 “Revenue Recognition,” ASC 958-205 “Presentation of Financial Statements” and the guidelines set forth in the industry
audit and accounting guide “Not-for-Profit Entities” issued by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. Under these
guidelines, contributions of cash and other assets are classified as one of the following three categories:

Unrestricted – Unrestricted net assets represent resources that are not subject to donor-imposed stipulations and are available
to support all activities of the Grand Lodge, including the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund (the “Endowment Fund”). At the
2011 annual communication the Grand Master revoked the charter of Covina lodge 334 and all assets were then transferred to
Grand Lodge. In 2012, the assets of Covina lodge 334 were liquidated and designated for a future lodge in Covina. At the 2014
Annual Communication a charter was granted to Destiny Lodge No. 856 located in Covina and all previously designated assets
were transferred from Grand Lodge to Destiny Lodge 856 in October 2014. The amount transferred to Destiny Lodge 856 was
2,494,081.

At the 2014 annual communication the Charter of Sublime Benicia lodge No. 5 was revoked and all assets were transferred to
Grand Lodge for a future lodge in Benicia. The amount transferred to Grand Lodge was $426,095 and $58,445 for the years
ended October 31, 2015 and 2014, respectively.

The Endowment Fund was established at the Grand Lodge’s October 1993 Annual Communication. If, in any fiscal year, there
is an excess of support and revenues over expenses, as defined by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee, the excess shall be
added to the Endowment Fund. For the years ended October 31, 2015 and 2014, there were no excess of support and revenues
over expenses.
Temporarily restricted – Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions that are limited in use in accordance with
donor-imposed stipulations. These stipulations may expire with time and/or may be satisfied by the actions of the Grand
Lodge according to the intention of the donor. Upon satisfaction of such stipulations, the associated net assets are released
from temporarily restricted net assets and reported as unrestricted.

Permanently restricted – Permanently restricted net assets represent contributions to be invested and held in perpetuity as
directed by the donor. As of October 31, 2015 and 2014, there were no permanently restricted net assets.

NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Use of estimates – The preparation of consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the
consolidated financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual results
could differ from those estimates.

Fair value of financial instruments – The carrying amounts reported in the accompanying consolidated statements of financial
position for cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and accrued liabilities, and due from/due to related
entities, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature. Discussion on the fair value of financial instruments is included in
Note 2.

Fair value process – The Organization determines fair value measure policies and procedures for assets and liabilities under the
supervision of the Investment Committee. These policies and procedures are reassessed annually to determine if the current
valuation techniques are still appropriate. A variety of qualitative factors are used to subjectively determine the most appropriate
valuation methodologies. Methodologies are consistent with the market, income and cost approaches. Unobservable inputs used in
fair value measurements are evaluated and adjusted on an annual basis, or as necessary based on current market conditions and
other third party information. In determining the reasonableness of the methodology Grand Lodge evaluates a variety of factors
including a review of existing agreements, economic conditions, industry, and market developments. Certain unobservable inputs
are assessed through review of contract terms while others are substantiated utilizing available market data including but not
limited to market comparables, qualified opinions, and discount rates and mortality tables for split interest agreements.
Cash and cash equivalents – Cash and cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less at the time of purchase, with the exception of cash and cash equivalents held as investments.
Prepaid expenses – Prepaid expenses consist primarily of prepaid insurance coverage.

Investments – Investments in debt and equity securities are stated at estimated fair values based on quoted market prices.
Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair values at the dates of donation. The fair value of alternative
investments is recorded at the investment manger’s Net Asset Value (“NAV”), as the managers have the greatest insight into the
investments of their funds and the related industry and have the appropriate expertise to determine the NAV. The Grand Lodge
assesses the NAV and takes into consideration events such as suspended redemptions, restructuring, secondary sales, and investor
defaults to determine if an adjustment is necessary. Additionally, asset holdings are reviewed within the investment manager’s
audited financial statements, as are interim financial statements and fund manager communications, for the purposes of assessing
valuation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market fluctuations are recorded in the period in which such fluctuations
occur. Realized gains or losses resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on a cost basis.
Property and equipment – Property and equipment, including leasehold improvements, greater than $1,000 are recorded at cost
and are depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of 3 to 25 years.

The Grand Lodge periodically evaluates the carrying value of its long-lived assets for impairment. The evaluations address the
estimated recoverability of the assets’ carrying value, which is principally determined based on projected undiscounted cash flows
generated by the underlying tangible assets. When the carrying value of an asset exceeds its estimated recoverability, a write-down
is recorded. No impairment was recorded during the years ended October 31, 2015 and 2014.
Other assets – Other assets consist primarily of a collection of jewelry used in lodge ceremonies.

Deferred per capita dues revenue – Deferred per capita dues revenue consists of dues received in the current year for the
subsequent fiscal year. These amounts are recognized as revenue using the straight-line method over the period to which they
relate.

Assets held in trust for lodge life membership – Assets held in trust for lodge life membership consists of lodges’ participation in
Grand Lodge’s investment pool. Investments are held and managed by Grand Lodge.

Revenue recognition – Contributions are recognized as revenue when received or unconditionally promised. Non-cash donations
are recognized at fair value at the time of the donation. Dues are recognized as revenue ratably over the period to which they
relate.

Concentration of credit risk – Financial instruments potentially subjecting the Grand Lodge to concentrations of credit risk
consist primarily of bank demand deposits in excess of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) insurance thresholds, cash
held in money market accounts in excess of the amounts insured by the U.S. Treasury insurance for money market funds, and
various debt and equity investments in excess of Securities Investor Protection Corporation (“SIPC”) insurance. Demand deposits
are placed with a local financial institution, and management has not experienced any loss related to these demand deposits in the
past. Investment securities are exposed to various risks, such as interest rate, market, and credit risk. It is at least reasonably
possible, given the level of risk associated with investment securities, that changes in the near term could materially affect the
amount reported in the consolidated statements. The risk associated with the investments is mitigated through diversification.
Income tax status – The Grand Lodge has been granted tax-exempt status for both federal income and California franchise tax
purposes; while Nob Hill, a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge, is subject to federal income and California franchise tax.

ASC 820 “Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures” defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to
transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. ASC 820 also establishes a fair
value hierarchy which requires an entity to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs
when measuring fair value. The standard describes three levels of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:
Level 1 – Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

Level 2 – Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; quoted prices in
markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by observable market data
for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities; or net asset value per share (or its equivalent) with the
ability to redeem the investments in the near term.

Level 3 – Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the fair value of the
assets or liabilities.

Following is a description of the valuation methodologies used for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis and
recognized in the accompanying consolidated financial statements, as well as the general classification of such instruments
pursuant to the valuation hierarchy:

Investments – Where quoted market prices are available in an active market, securities are classified within Level 1 of the
valuation hierarchy. Level 1 securities include exchange traded equities. If quoted market prices are not available, then fair
values are estimated by using pricing models, quoted prices of securities with identical characteristics or discounted cash
flows. In certain cases where Level 1 or Level 2 inputs are not available, securities are classified within Level 3 of the hierarchy
and include certain real estate investments, hedge funds of funds, and other less liquid securities using investment appropriate
models like the income approach for real estate investments and a net asset value approach for the hedge funds.

As required by FASB ASC Topic 820, the investments are classified within the level of the lowest significant input considered in
determining fair value. In evaluating the level at which the Grand Lodge’s investments have been classified, the Grand Lodge has
assessed factors including, but not limited to the ability to redeem at net asset value (“NAV”) at the measurement date and the
existence or absence of certain restrictions at the measurement date. In accordance with the guidance, if the Grand Lodge has the
ability to redeem from the investment at the measurement date or in the near-term at NAV, the investment would be classified as a
Level 2 fair value measurement. Alternatively, if the Grand Lodge will never have the ability to redeem from the investment or is
restricted from redeeming for an uncertain or extended period of time from the measurement date, the investment would be
classified as a Level 3 fair value measurement.

investments and cash equivalents, and investing its assets accordingly.

NOTE 7 – RETIREMENT PLANS
Defined benefit plan – Masonic Homes, the Grand Lodge, and the Temple participate in a defined benefit pension plan (the “Plan”)
that covers all employees. The allocation of Grand Lodge and Nob Hill employees represent 16.16% of the Plan. The Grand Lodge is
the sponsoring employer of the Plan.
Plan termination – The Plan was frozen effective March 31, 2007, and all benefits ceased to accrue. On February 28, 2014, the
board of directors of the Grand Lodge, voted to terminate the Plan effective July 30, 2014. The board also approved an amendment
to the plan to offer a one-time opportunity to elect lump sum for all non-retired participants. The amendment also provides for late
retirement benefits and in-service retirement income.

The accrued benefits of each participant became nonforfeitable, and the net assets of the Plan will be allocated, as prescribed by the
terms and provisions of the Plan in accordance with ERISA and its related regulations, to provide benefits, subject to any required
approval of the IRS and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC). Participants in the plan are fully vested and may elect to
have their benefit in the Plan distributed in the form of a lump sum payment or in an annuity purchased by the plan for the benefit
of the participant.

NOTE 9 – ENDOWMENT FUND - UNRESTRICTED
Spending policy, investing policy, and strategy
Return objectives and risk parameters – The Grand Lodge has adopted investment and spending policies for endowment assets that
attempt to provide a predictable stream of funding to programs supported by its endowment while seeking to maintain the
purchasing power of the endowment assets. Endowment assets include those assets of donor-restricted funds that the Grand Lodge
must hold in perpetuity or for a donor-specified period(s) as well as board-designated funds. Under this policy, as approved by the
Board of Trustees, the endowment assets are invested in a manner that is intended to produce results that exceed the price and
yield results of various market benchmarks appropriate to the investment classes utilized while assuming a moderate level of
investment risk. The Grand Lodge expects its endowment funds, over time, to provide an average rate of return of approximately
7.0%-7.5% annually. Actual returns in any given year may vary from this amount.

Strategies employed for achieving objectives – To satisfy its long-term rate-of-return objectives, the Grand Lodge relies on a total
return strategy in which investment returns are achieved through both capital appreciation (realized and unrealized) and current
yield (interest and dividends). The Grand Lodge targets a diversified asset allocation that places a greater emphasis on equitybased investments to achieve its long-term return objectives within prudent risk constraints.

Spending policy and how the investment objectives relate to the spending policy – For 2015/2014, the Grand Lodge has a policy of
appropriating for distribution 4.25% – 5.00% of its endowment fund’s average fair value over the prior twenty quarters through
the calendar year-end preceding the fiscal year in which the distribution is planned. In establishing this policy, the Grand Lodge
considered the long-term expected return on its endowment. Accordingly, over the long term, the Grand Lodge expects the current
spending policy to allow its endowment to grow at an average of 2.00% annually. This is consistent with the Grand Lodge’s
objective to maintain the purchasing power of the endowment assets held in perpetuity or for a specified term as well as to provide
additional real growth through new gifts and investment return.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION REQUIRED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR
Schedule H, Line 4(j) - Schedule of Reportable Transactions ........................................................................................................................................... 10

We have audited the accompanying financial statements in liquidation of California Masonic Retirement Plan
(the Plan), which comprise the statements of net assets available for benefits as of December 31, 2014 and
2013, the related statements of changes in net assets available for benefits for the years then ended, and the
related notes to the financial statements.
Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the
design, implementation, and maintenance of internal controls relevant to the preparation and fair
presentation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audits. We conducted
our audits in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the
financial statements are free from material misstatement.

An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures in the
financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment including the assessment of
the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error. In making those
risk assessments, the auditor considers internal control relevant to the Plan’s preparation and fair
presentation of the financial statements in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the
circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Plan’s internal
control. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of
accounting policies used and the reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as
well as evaluating the overall presentation of the financial statements.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our
audit opinion.
Opinion

In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the financial
status of the Plan as of December 31, 2014 and 2013, and the changes in its financial status for the years ended
December 31, 2014 and 2013, in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United
States of America.

additional procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying
accounting and other records used to prepare the financial statements or to the financial statements

CALIFORNIA MASONIC RETIREMENT PLAN

CALIFORNIA MASONIC RETIREMENT PLAN

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS IN LIQUIDATION

NOTE 1 – DESCRIPTION OF PLAN
The following brief description of the California Masonic Retirement Plan (the Plan) provides only general information.
Participants should refer to the Plan agreement for more complete description of the Plan’s provisions.

General – The Plan was a defined benefit plan that provided retirement benefits for substantially all employees of the Grand Lodge
of Free & Accepted Masons of California, Masonic Homes of California, and other Masonic organizations (collectively, the Grand
Lodge). Eligible employees must have reached the age of 21 and completed one year of service during which they have been paid
for at least 1,000 hours of service. The Plan was subject to the provisions of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974,
as amended (ERISA).
The Plan’s assets were maintained in a trust established pursuant to a trust agreement between the Grand Lodge and the Bank of
New York/Mellon. Assets were held by the Bank of New York/Mellon.
The Grand Lodge of Free & Accepted Masons of California was the plan sponsor and plan administrator.

The Plan was frozen effective March 31, 2007, and all benefits ceased to accrue. On February 28, 2014, the trustees of the plan
elected to terminate the plan effective July 30, 2014. As of December 31, 2014, all assets of the plan have been distributed (see
Note 4).

Payment of benefits and vesting – The benefit formula varied based on an employee’s date of retirement. For current employees,
the annual retirement benefit at normal retirement was equal to the sum of: (1) 2% of the participant’s average annual
compensation earned during the five calendar years prior to January 1, 2002, multiplied by the participant’s years of service
earned prior to January 1, 2002; and (2) the sum of 2% of the participant’s compensation in each full and partial year of service
earned after January 1, 2002, through March 31, 2007, when the Plan was frozen. Benefits were generally paid in the form of
annuities prior to the plan termination. If the value of the vested accrued benefit was $5,000 or less, it was paid as a single lumpsum amount. To facilitate the termination, the Plan was amended to provide participants a one time opportunity to elect a lump
sum payment. The Plan provided normal retirement benefits for participants upon reaching age 65 and had provisions for reduced
early retirement benefits.

Death and disability benefits – Disability benefits were payable to qualified employees who became totally and permanently
disabled. The benefit amount was equal to the accrued benefit amount, as determined above, reduced for early withdrawal.

Death benefits were available to a participant’s spouse in the form of a single life annuity for participants who died before their
retirement date.
Investment management and administrative expenses – Investment management and administrative expenses were paid
principally by the Plan.
NOTE 2 – SUMMARY OF ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Basis of accounting – The accompanying financial statements are prepared on the liquidation basis of accounting.

Use of estimates – The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles required
management to make estimates and assumptions that affected the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, and changes therein;
disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities; and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits at the date of the
financial statements. Actual results could have differed from those estimates.

607

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS IN LIQUIDATION

Benefit payments – Benefit payments to participants were recorded upon distribution.

Risks and uncertainties – Investment securities were exposed to various risks, such as interest rate, market, and credit risks. Due
to the level of risk associated with certain investment securities, it was at least reasonably possible that changes in the values of
investment securities could have occurred, and such changes in the near term could have materially affected the amounts reported
in the financial statements.

Plan contributions were made, and the actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits were reported, based on certain
assumptions pertaining to interest rates, inflation rates, and employee demographics, all of which are subject to change. Due to
uncertainties inherent in the estimations and assumptions process, it is at least reasonably possible that changes in those estimates
and assumptions in the near term could have been material to the financial statements.

Subsequent events – Subsequent events are events or transactions that occur after the statement of net assets available for
benefits date but before financial statements are available to be issued. The Plan recognizes in the financial statements the effects
of all subsequent events that provide additional evidence about conditions that existed at the date of the statement of net assets
available for benefits, including the estimates inherent in the process of preparing the financial statements. The Plan’s financial
statements do not recognize subsequent events that provide evidence about conditions that did not exist at the date of the
statement of net assets available for benefits but arose after the statement of net assets available for benefits date and before
financial statements are available to be issued.
The Plan has evaluated subsequent events through October 6, 2015, which is the date the financial statements were available to be
issued.
NOTE 3 – ACCUMULATED PLAN BENEFITS
Accumulated plan benefits were those future periodic payments, including lump-sum distributions, that were attributable under
the Plan’s provisions for services that employees have rendered. Accumulated plan benefits included benefits expected to be paid
to: (a) retired or terminated employees or their beneficiaries; (b) beneficiaries of employees who have died; and (c) present
employees or their beneficiaries.

The actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits was the amount that results from applying actuarial assumptions to adjust
the accumulated plan benefits earned by the participants to reflect the time value of money, through discounts for interest, and the
probability of payment, by means of decrements, such as for death, disability, withdrawal, or retirement, between the valuation
date and the expected date of payment. The actuarial present value of accumulated plan benefits and plan assets as of January 1,
2013, was as follows:

Investment valuation and income recognition – Cash and money market funds included cash held in financial institutions and
other highly-liquid, short-term investments with original maturities of three months or less when purchased.

Investments are stated at fair value. If available, quoted market prices are used to value investments. The related net appreciation
or depreciation in fair value of investments is recorded in the statements of changes in net assets available for benefits. Net
appreciation or depreciation includes gains and losses in investments bought and sold, as well as held, during the year. Purchases
and sales of investments are recorded on a trade-date basis. Interest income is recorded on the accrual basis. Dividends are
recorded on the ex-dividend date.

NOTE 4 – PLAN TERMINATION
The Plan was frozen effective March 31, 2007 and all benefits ceased to accrue. On February 28, 2014, the board of directors of the
Grand Lodge, voted to terminate the Plan effective July 30, 2014. The board also approved an amendment to the plan to offer a onetime opportunity to elect lump sum for all non-retired participants. The amendment also provides for late retirement benefits and
in-service retirement income.

The accrued benefits of each participant became nonforfeitable, and the net assets of the Plan were allocated, as prescribed by the
terms and provisions of the Plan in accordance with ERISA and its related regulations, to provide benefits, subject to any required
approval of the IRS and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC). Participants in the plan were fully vested and could elect
to have their benefit in the Plan distributed in the form of a lump sum payment or in an annuity purchased by the plan for the
benefit of the participant.
As of October 31, 2014, the Plan paid out all benefits in the form of lump sum payments to terminated vested employees and active
employees or through the purchase of an annuity for retired participants and those participants who did not choose a lump sum
payment.

During October 2014, the Plan entered into an agreement to purchase annuity contracts from Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance
Company (MassMutual) in the amount of $23,586,479 to provide retirement benefits to all remaining plan participants.
MassMutual assumed the liability as of December 1, 2014. The plan sponsor paid an additional premium of $110,040 to
MassMutual for post-sale adjustments to the annuity contract. This amount was paid to MassMutual in December 2014.
NOTE 5 – INVESTMENTS
During 2013, the trustees of the Plan moved the investments into a fixed income fund to immunize the Plan against interest rate
volatility in anticipation of termination of the Plan. All investments of the plan were held in the Vanguard Long Term fund.

The Plan classified its investments based upon an established fair value hierarchy that prioritizes the inputs to valuation techniques
used to measure fair value. The hierarchy gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets
or liabilities (Level 1 measurement) and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs (Level 3 measurements).

Methods used in arriving at fair value may produce a fair value calculation that may not be indicative of net realizable value or
reflective of future fair values. Furthermore, although the Plan believes the valuation methods used are appropriate and consistent
with other market participants, the use of different methodologies or assumptions to determine the fair value of certain financial
instruments could result in a different fair value measurement at the reporting date.

Page 7

609

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The three levels of inputs used to establish fair value are as follows:

Level 1 – Unadjusted quoted prices in active markets that are accessible at the measurement date for identical, unrestricted
assets or liabilities.

Level 2 – Inputs to the valuation methodology include: quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets; quoted
prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets; inputs other than quoted prices that are
observable for the asset or liability; and inputs that are derived principally from or corroborated by observable market
data by correlation or other means. If the asset or liability has a specified (contractual) term, the Level 2 input must be
observable for substantially the full term of the asset or liability.
Level 3 – Prices or valuations that require inputs that are both significant to the fair value measurement and unobservable.

A financial instrument’s level within the fair value hierarchy is based on the lowest level of any input that is significant to the fair value
measurement.
Following is a description of the valuation methodologies used for assets measured at fair value:
Money market funds are valued at cost, which represents fair market value.

Mutual funds are shares of registered investment company funds (or mutual funds) valued at the net asset value (NAV) of shares held
by the Plan at the closing price reported on the active market on which the individual securities are traded.
Common stocks are valued based upon quoted market prices.

NOTE 6 – TAX STATUS
The Internal Revenue Service determined and informed the Plan’s sponsor by a letter dated April 10, 2014, that the Plan and
related trust were designed in accordance with applicable sections of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). The Plan had since been
amended. However, the plan administrator believes the Plan was designed and was currently being operated in compliance with
the applicable requirements of the IRC.

The Plan received a favorable determination letter from the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) for the termination of
the Plan.

In accordance with guidance on accounting for uncertainty in income taxes (ASC 740-10), management evaluated the Plan’s tax
positions and does not believe the Plan has any uncertain tax positions that require disclosure or adjustment to the financial
statements. The Plan is subject to routine audits by taxing jurisdictions; however, there are currently no audits for any tax periods
in progress.
NOTE 7 – TRANSACTIONS WITH PARTIES IN INTEREST
The Grand Lodge of Free & Accepted Masons of California was the plan sponsor and administrator. Trustees that served on the
Plan’s administrative committee were also participants of the Plan.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION REQUIRED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR

Schedule H, Line 4(i) - Schedule of Assets (Held at End of Year) .................................................................................................................................... 10

We were engaged to audit the accompanying financial statements of California Masonic Retirement Plan II
(the Plan), which comprise the statements of net assets available for benefits as of December 31, 2014 and
2013, and the related statement of changes in net assets available for benefits for the year ended
December 31, 2014, and the related notes to the financial statements.
Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the
design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair
presentation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud
or error.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on conducting the audit in
accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America. Because of the
matter described in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion paragraph, however, we were not able to obtain
sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion.
Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion

As permitted by 29 CFR 2520.103-8 of the Department of Labor’s (DOL’s) Rules and Regulations for
Reporting and Disclosure under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), the plan
administrator instructed us not to perform, and we did not perform, any auditing procedures with respect
to the information summarized in Note 7, which was certified by Fidelity Management Trust Company, the
trustee of the Plan, except for comparing such information with the related information included in the
financial statements. We have been informed by the plan administrator that the trustee holds the Plan’s
investment assets and executes investment transactions. The plan administrator has obtained a
certification from the trustee as of December 31, 2014 and 2013, and for the year ended December 31,
2014, that the information provided to the plan administrator by the trustee is complete and accurate.
Disclaimer of Opinion

Because of the significance of the matter described in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion paragraph, we
have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion.
Accordingly, we do not express an opinion on these financial statements.

The form and content of the information included in the financial statements and supplementary
